review_text:
First of all, my first order arrived with a small crack in the wooden cabinet and it would not turn on. I am going to give Sangean the benefit of the doubt and assume that it was shipping damage even though the box from the outside did not look like it was damaged, so I won't let this affect my rating.

But this did give me a chance to test Amazon's return policy, and I must say it was great. When I realized that I had to return the radio, I went to Amazon's website and clicked on the radio and selected "return." Then I was prompted to print a return shipping label to attach to the box when I sent it back. By the time I did that, there was an email in my in box from Amazon telling me that they were shipping a replacement to me via UPS Air. So I packed up the unit in it's original box, attached the label I had printed, and then the next day when the replacement arrived I gave the box to the UPS driver. Of course, all of this was at no additional cost to me. I was quite impressed with the whole process.

Now to the radio itself. Overall I am quite impressed with it and I am giving it four stars. For a radio of it's size, it sounds great. I have never heard a radio that small with the tight bass response that this one has. And AM radio sounds better than than it does even on my Onkyo receiver that I have in my family room.

The radio with it's wooden cabinet looks great on my nightstand and you can just tell by looking at it that it is a quality product.

The tuner's sensitivity on the FM band is good with the external wire antenna that is supplied with it. Selectivity between adjacent stations is also good. And I am getting good stereo separation when I listen with headphones. I do have one small quibble however. There is a button to switch any FM station to mono, but you have to do this individually for each station. It would have been better if you could toggle between stereo and mono for all the stations at once rather than having to do it individually for each one.

AM sensitivity is pretty good using the built in antenna. Weak stations in my area come in better than they did with my old clock radio, but I still do have some problems with the very weak stations. I could probably improve this if I bought a good external AM antenna, but I don't think I will bother to do that since I don't really listen to any of the weak stations anyway.

One reason why I got this radio was because it has a line in jack. I have connected my Directv box to it so that I can listen to the Directv music channels through the radio without having my TV set on. All I had to do was to go to Radio Shack and buy a Y adapter with two RCA plugs on one end and a 1/8" plug on the other. It works like a charm.

I also like that the display has large enough numerals that I can read it without my glasses on. However, as others have mentioned, the display defaults to the radio station frequency or the RDS display rather than to the time. To get the time display back I have to tap the display button, and it's hard to do at night in a dark room. I think it would have been better if it defaulted to the time in the first place.

Another quibble that I have is that the power button uses a bright blue light which is distracting in a dark room. They shouldn't have made it so bright. That will take some getting used to.

Also, as others have mentioned, setting the alarm is needlessly complicated as is turning it off. You need to hit three different buttons to do it. I am starting to get the hang of it, but I wish they would have just included a button which toggles the alarm on and off.

But overall I am rating this as a good four star product that could use some minor improvements. The most important thing to me is the sound quality, and that is unmatched for a radio of this size.

review_text:
All I can politely write is that what an amazing experience. The headphones are small and just sit over the ears (like their noise canceling headphones). The Bluetooth component sits neatly inside the headphones, as we have another Bose Bluetooth headphones and the Bluetooth component sits outside of the headphones. I synced this with iPad, iPhone and iPod Classic (using Kokkia I10). The quality of the sound is fabulous as you would expect from BOSE ( a lot of bass) you will not be disappointed. I played a range of music from rock, pop and classical music...awesomeness is the experience with Bose! The range is not miles...more like 20 feet..and not through too many walls. ...terrific design of compactness and total comfort on my ears. In terms of external noise, it really did cut out the concrete jungle living of traffic hum.

I listened to my music for over an hour now and no pain on my ears...bliss and worth every cent and pennies. I love these new BOSE Bluetooth headphones. Note, they come fully charged. There are little and discreet volume up and down buttons, which are elevated a little so it is easy to find and you will not end up pushing the wrong button. I didn't have to press any additional button to synch..there is a voice telling you that it is seeking to synch..and will let you know when it has connected. There is a button to switch from music to speak on the phone. Crystal clear. It comes with a power charge..a micro USB cable and a RCA cable.(hmm redundant with Bluetooth, but if you have digital piano, you can connect it via the RCA. I am going to get the Bluetooth adaptor to test it with these head phones).

The headphones remember all the names of the gadgets, and will play from which ever one that is 'on', which is a huge plus. There appears to be an intelligence here that we do not see in the Bose over the ear wireless headphones.

In term of play time, after a full charge, which took less than 2 hours: total playtime is more like 8 hours, not 15 hours claimed, but it must be related to the volume too. I had my volume pretty high most of the time. Given, how quickly it charged up, and the number of hours of playtime, I really don't need to charge it up for more than one every three days.
Also comes with a compact and stylish case to store the wires and headphones when not in use.

After two years of research, many many visits to the local Bose store, lots of questions asked, we finally took the plunge with the latest model and enjoyed a 10% sale that was offered at the time! We were looking to replace our current home theatre system with the very large Kiplisch speakers (one of the main reasons for the search and hence was attracted to the jewel boxes) and we were looking for a replacement that was more befitting an apartment space. Addtional extra was the remote ended up operating more like a harmony, which was not what we had orginally thought (we remain a harmony-run family, with this one exception). All hooked up to the receiver include the TV, tivo, xbox, apple tv, and play station.

We love the slim line look of the receiver and without all the huge speakers in the room, we feel we have gained back a lot of space. The receiver has inputs/outputs that really reflects the current modern day demands and entertainment devices. The speakers are amazing: the centre one offers the best sound in terms of hearing speach in any genre and we are not raising the volume to hear the talking part of a program and then having to turn down the volume when all the sound effects come into play!

The set up takes a while, even for my husband who is a technical nerd, but that maybe because of all the additional devices we had to program the remote to learn. The sound testing system is cool and I am sure that is why we are so enjoying the surround sound effects and the clarity of the voices is beautiful. The speakers bring music to life - seriously. we played so many genre and each one just echoed with such depth that you would have thought you were in the recording studio. We were impressed with the integration of the receiver with the speakers and the sound testing that came with the set-up.

One thing to note, we opted to have wireless back speakers which required additional hardware to be purchased. The sound quality is a tad better with the back speakers wired; but we opted for wireless and we will probably end up not noticing in the long run!

The remote was a dream and it did take a little time to learn the language of all our devices. We thought we couldnt use the infra-red wireless headphones with it - well you can! The cord has be be jacked in the front panel of the receiver and you have to turn up the volume to hear.

Like everyone, we were also aware of the high costs, but when you break it down, tangible and tangible benefits do out weigh the 'cost number'. For those of you who are looking for a cleaner look and good sound quality (loves movies and many genre of music: I am trying to differentiate from those who have ears that pick up a whole lot more than the average population and are very fussy about what they listen to): this being said, it is really worth a look and a serious investigation at this latest Bose Model.

This product was not bought on a whim and we had a lot of high demands and requirements, especially where the hamrony-like features and the wireless headphones were concerned! Seriously, we held back from buying the model earlier as we were still investigating on whether the Harmony could be trained for the Bose system: in the end we were impressed with the Bose remote!

We have had the system for over a week now and we cant stop pinching ourselves on the recent purchase and wonder why we had waited so long.

I compared the sound with another portable 2-speaker ipod dock (ihome iH16GX), which also has an amazing sound: they were both about the same. But this little speaker wins it hands down for being so compact. I am looking forward to throwing this speaker into my bag and listening to it at work. I also loved this speaker as it allows me to use my shuffle, nano or classic (which the ihome only allows for the bottom insert to be used) whereas the x-mini uses the earphone port (more universal for the different ipod models).

I also like this speaker as it uses the universal USB port to charge the chargeable battery in the speakers. I hope these rechargeable batteries last a long time! I dont think they are replaceable looking at the build of the speaker.

For the price,this is a great little speaker and so easy to carry around. I just ordered two more for family members. I noticed the x-mini max is about to be released (two speakers) and ~$30 more expensive, but I think this one is so more fun!

review_text:
I don't think I asked a lot in a iPad cover, but I'm impressed how well this cover has delivered. Mostly I was looking for functional protection and a look that classy looks. This cover delivered both in spades.

Protection:

I love the way the iPad is held in place by the four rubber corner holder. The case makes contact with the iPad in the most minimal way and does not allow grit to get between the case and the ipad to scratch surfaces. I have never had the iPad slip out of these feet either, it is very snugly held in place.

The outside materials are rugged and there are 3/16th inches of touch material between the iPad and the harsh world. It will not protect it in a long fall, but it is safe from scratches and smudges.

Looks:

I was originally looking for a leather case for looks, but this is just as classy as the leather cases I have found for twice the price. I like the leatherlike surface and the black with white stitching is subtly striking. I even like the Belkin logo, it's a cute representation of the human form.

Functionality:

The magnet is well placed to hold the case closed, then when open, it holds the front flap securely attached to the back of the iPad. Magnet strength seems to be strong enough to be functional. Also well designed are the multiple positions the case folds into. It has a great adjustable angle fold for watching movies and using my bluetooth keyboard.

I don't use the camera ever, but this case does have a strategically placed hole so it is available.

Failings:

In general this is a great case. The two things I can think of for constructive criticism are the inside materials and the fact that the magnet causes the iPad to wake in transit. For the inside material, it is a velvety black material that picks up dust. Not a huge thing, but noticeable. As for the magnet, I guess this is not uncommon, but I do completely power down the iPad if I am putting it in my laptop bag. Otherwise it occassionally turns on and runs down the battery. Again not a bad thing and not an issue in general.

Summary:

All in all, I love this case. It's classy and functional. Recommend.

review_title: Judging Price vs. Performance, A Decent Kid/Camping-Proof Camera
review_text:
To let you know where I am coming from on this review, I have two sons, 9 and 4. We do a lot of camping without mom, but want to share our adventures. So far, our trips have destroyed a Canon Powershot 450 (overly hydrated while canoeing) and a Powershot 980IS (smashed into ground during a fall.) So the idea of a waterproof, shockproof and hopefully kid-proof camera sounded perfect.

Purpose for camera: Rugged camera to take along canoeing, fishing, camping, and hiking for snapshots and quick, shareable movies.

I have never owned a camera in this class, and the one thing I am trying to keep in mind is the price point. This is not intended to be a high-end performance device, but more a rugged snapshot camera. I was a little suspect on 1080P on a hand held device under $175 (still am,) but the 5 MP camera is adequate for photos to email to grandparents and to show off our catches and camps to mom.

Design -

The camera is very nicely designed. It is physically attractive and comfortable in the hand. The winged doors lock into place well in their watertight positions and are, well kind of cool. The screen is adequate for playback and we spend a lot of time watching what we filmed over and over. The controls are spare, but easy to understand and operate. The four major flaws I found are; the embedded battery, lack of a flash, lack of lens cover, and no headphone jack for previewing sound.

Battery-

It is unfortunate that the design team decided to go with an internal non-removable battery. This seems to move the device into the "disposable" class since it is useless once the battery dies. I suspect that the battery can be replaced fairly easily, judging by the hex screws in the camera body, but there is a big difference between slipping a battery in and out and sending the camera out for replacement. Also, I can make a huge argument for being able to carry a back up battery. At least for now though, the battery seems to have a decent charge. We have filmed and played back films for at least two hours between recharges and have never seen the battery near empty.

Performance -

Image capture: 1080p is a lot to ask from such a small sensor. For that matter, so is 720p. So I am satisfied with the images I am getting, not great but what I would expect. I usually shoot Canon DSLR's (except when camping with kids) so I am at times frustrated by the lack of manual controls of any kind. Autofocus, autoexposure... with no way to change anything beyond file format and resolution. The images and video I am getting are a little noisy and especially so in low light. Blurring from camera or subject motion is common on stills. This is where the flash option would be nice. But in daylight, or decently lit interior shots the images are definitely passable. Again, judging this camera on its price point and function, it really is decent. If I want good stills, I'll go with a Canon 50D, if I want a snapshot of my kid pulling a bass into the canoe, this is perfect.

I am uploading a video with more details on picture and movie quality.

Sound: For a single source mike on the camera, it does pretty good. Definitely picks up footsteps or breathing, so don't film while walking up hill. Truly emphasizes if you are out of shape. Picks up ambient sound well and in tests in a light breeze, did fine.

Interface: I had the interface lock up on me once and I was unable to get it to power off or get out of a locked state. I had to use the small reset button to get it to reboot and clear the freeze. So I have thrown a very small paper clip in its case. Without being able to pull the battery, the reset button seems to have been the only option. Otherwise the device is very fast loading up, and the interface is intuitive and easy to use. Although occasionally when browsing I end up in fast forward or reverse when watching a movie and it takes a little to get it back to play or browse.

Summary:

All in all, I am really happy with this camera. It is full of limitations which you should understand before purchase. For the price, it is a decent camera and it fits our intended purpose to a Tee. My kids love the ability to take a movie, then watch it immediately. I like the feeling that it might survive the kids for a while. I feel like I'm being pretty critical of the camera, and I guess I am. But I'm giving it four stars because it does what I want it to, and after using it for a couple weeks, I really like it. Just don't expect the world from a inexpensive camera.

Pros-
Price (under $175 is not a high end price)
Images are decent (under daylight or bright light conditions)
Kidproof
Quick to startup
Well thought-out design
Just all round cute and useful

Cons (in order of importance to me)
Internal Battery (cannot be replaced, nor can you carry a spare)
No Flash (can't stop motion blur, fill flash)
Low-light performance (weak performance, noisy video and stills)
Complete lack of manual controls
Occasional lock-ups on interface
No Head phones for reviewing movies
When switching through modes it keeps defaulting to zoomed out

review_text:
I have always puttered around with graphics programs and fought with the mouse the whole way. I have tried tablets in the past either through my role as IT support to designers or with a smaller [[ASIN:B002OOWC3S Wacom Bamboo Pen and Touch Small Tablet]] which proved to be too small to be very useful. When I started using this device it was eye opening. Suddenly I was able to out line items in photoshop with the ease of sketching with a pencil.

The design is beautiful and rich. My earlier memories of Wacom tablets were stacks of obsolete and yellowing plastic. This device has a beautiful dark gray surface which should age gracefully and avoid the yellowing of the earlier models. Opening the packaging felt like Christmas.

Functionally the device is amazing. I have used it on quite a few projects and the preset keys are great for adding or removing selected areas on the fly without going back to the keyboard. Zooming in and out with the touch wheel also flows well. Once in drawing mode, I never need to return to the computer keyboard at all. Initially I was disappointed to find that the USB port on the tablet appeared to be on the wrong side, then I realized a small switch closed that port and opened one on the other side - an amazing little detail. As a leftie, I was worried how it would work for us minority handers, it works exactly the same - again, amazing.

If I had to knock the device for anything, I find the tablets surface a little rough for my taste and I have noticed that the stylus point wears and marks the surface when using it. It's not horrible, but a little irritating. Other than that I can do little more than gush about how surprisingly much I have loved this tablet. The pressure controls in brushes are - I have to say it again - amazing.

After using it for some time, I'm not sure how I got along without it. The pixel for pixel mapping is far better than my earlier Bamboo tablet. I love it! highly recommend it to everyone I know.

review_title: Very Nice Sound, Very Portable, Not Very Loud, But Overall a Nice Speaker System
review_text:
This has proven to be a very nice little acquisition. We got it primarily as a way to unlock the songs on our iPods so we could share them, or enjoy music without being tethered to headphones, but it has ended up being our bed stand iPhone charger and portable music player.

The sound put out by these speakers has a Bose-like quality (not exactly Bose equivalent, but a similar, warm, full sound.) This is not a particularly loud sound system, but it does fill our small bedroom adequately to a reasonable volume. It will not fill a large room or outdoor area for sure, or belt out heavy metal, but does great at an adult contemporary listening level.

After getting this, one thing became quickly evident. The lack of a remote kind of sucks. At first I figured it wouldn't be a problem, but since you must use the controls on the ipod, (the speakers only have volume and power controls built in) you need to move to the speakers to skip songs, change volume or turn off. This doesn't seem like a big idea, and for the price, it is understandable that there is no remote, but I found that it is worth the extra money to get a speaker system with a remote.

One thing I really like about it is the portability and the ability to run off of batteries. We have used it a couple times at night to play owl calls to hear owls call back to us. Also, since it is so portable we move it all around the house and garage which is very handy.

Pros:
Nice full sound (although not overly loud)
Highly portable
Battery power option
Nice and small
Well designed

Cons:
No Remote
Picks up dust quickly, hard to keep clean
Limited controls, you must use controls on iPod
No equalizer controls

All in all, it fills a niche for us and we are happy with the quality of the product an the sound. It is all around nice set of speakers at a nice price.

review_title: Decent Router, Love the speed, Setup was Quick and Easy
review_text:
I have been using B for way too long now, so I was looking forward to upgrading to G. The instructions and setup were straight forward and clear so set up went very well. Although I should point out that I am an IT worker. Setup took literally less than five minutes including plugging in the hardware, setting up WEP protection, configuring... Once up and running, I have been very happy with the speed boost. My old Linksys B router was more of a bottleneck than I had thought.

My hopes and expectations were pretty limited, I just wanted a device that worked. The elegant design was just a plus. Set up in it's vertical orientation, it has a much smaller footprint than the Linksys it is replacing as well as a classier look.

Now that wireless routers have become a basic home appliance, perhaps the best feedback to give on this one is to say that it just plain works. With the ease of set up and the reliability I have seen, I would recommend this to anyone (not sure that I would have done the same with my Linksys.) Solid product.

review_title: Plug and Play; So Far, Works Great
review_text:
I selected this hub/docking station for a new laptop that did not come with an SD card reader, a tool I used almost daily with my older system. As I looked for options and features I began to realize that I can use extra ports and interfaces too, though the card reader was the main consideration. After doing a good bit of research I settled on this hub and I am very pleased with it so far.

This is a small device, about the size of a deck of playing cards. It’s shelled in an aluminum casing so it is durable enough to handle getting battered around my desk a little which is a good thing. It comes with a USB-C cable, but I have not used the included cable, opting instead to use a cable that is able to handle higher wattage and was purchased at the same time; I’ll keep the included cable as a spare.

I had no issues with connection and my Windows 11 system was able to see it and set it up automatically with no manual effort at all. It quite literally has been plug and play for me.

The card reader works flawlessly for me. I have used it with two different cards and the system sees the cards as soon as they’re inserted into the reader.

I have not tried all of the other interfaces this device offers, but I did plug an external USB drive into the hub and it worked exactly as if it was plugged into one of the onboard ports. Speeds are excellent and I have had no problems with time-outs or stalls when moving large amounts of data across the interface.

What I have not tried yet, because I haven’t had the time, is connecting to my Linux system. My Linux system has an odd issue with the HDMI port (a known hardware issue with the graphics card model), and I want to see how well this hub addresses the conversion from USB-C to HDMI. If this solves the issue with that system’s HDMI connectivity when I try it, I’ll be buying another one. Once I have tried this I will update my review. If it doesn’t work with Linux it’s okay – the product description does not mention Linux as a supported platform, so if it does happen to work it’s a bonus.

My experience with this hub/dock has been very positive and for me it has been worth the expense. It’s expensive when considering I just needed an external card reader, but when considering everything else it does it’s a good investment for my system.

I have a gold streak filter that I use occasionally with my main lens. This is the first blue streak filter I have used and I use it with my most versatile (and newer) lens, and so far I am pleased with it. It's a specialty filter that is useful in certain situations.

The idea behind this filter is that it has grooves in the glass that trap light and the result is a long, blue streak in the image when a light source is bright enough or is in the frame. This kind of filter is very similar to star filters that create 4-, 6- and 8-point stars, though this one creates just straight lines. When used properly this can cause some very dramatic effects in images, such as when photographing street lights or approaching cars at night.

I do need to say, though, that this kind of filter can easily be overused if not thoughtful. When used a lot, the effect can get dull and be more of an annoyance; however, when it is sparingly used it can evoke that "oh wow!" type of response for the unexpected effect.

This is a screw-on filter that will fit most standard lenses with threads. Make sure you select a filter size that is matched to your lens.

I like this lens filter and the effect it brings to the table. It is a niche product that should be used sparingly, but when used at the right time it can create an eye-popping streak effect.

review_title: Very Fine Light Stick for Photography
review_text:
I have a strong interest in photography and I always keep an eye open for lights and equipment that will help me take more creative or impactful pictures. I selected this light with the intent of using it for creative photography and so far I am pleased with it. I have other LED lights that have similar functions, but this one is different in a few ways that set it apart.

This is a wand light as opposed to a square LED bank. As such, the light distribution is a bit different. It can directly cover a longer (wider) area which is handy when putting together a mock-up with miniatures. It has a couple of mounting options too, utilizing either a miniature tripod (included) or magnetically attaching to a metal surface. I do wish a clamp was included such that it could attach to the tripod horizontally, but such clamps are available if they're needed.

This light is VERY bright and can easily light a small room when at full brightness. It can be dimmed to cast a soft light too which is good. It's not exactly the most ideal light source but it will work for general lighting in a pinch.

The temperature range goes from 2500k (very warm and orange-y) to 9900k (blistering cold white) and everywhere in between. Getting the color just right is relatively easy though it does take a little patience and experimentation to get it right. Do keep in mind that because this is an LED-based light, the temperature band setting is quite narrow and presents a different light profile, one that the camera can see but the human eye cannot. In addition to "natural lighting" modes it can be set for specific colors too such as purple, red, blue and so on.

Charging is done via a USB-C port, and the charging cable is included. I have not tried using this as a power source to charge my phone though the documentation doesn't say much about that. A full charge on this light lasts a while, though I have not drained it all the way down to find out how long it will last. Obviously the runtime is variable based on mode and brightness, and what is interesting about this light in particular is that it displays the estimated runtime on the screen based on current settings - this is a nice feature that I have not seen on a lot of these lights.

There are some creative modes for use with video or for special effects in a live setting, though the usefulness of these modes is dependent on the user. I personally will never use them. However, in the right hands these might be very useful for a project. There are several effects available, including police flashers, tube TV glow simulation, flickering candle and more.

The light comes with a nice canvas carrying pouch that provides basic storage and protection.

I really like this light and will be working with it more in the coming weeks and months. It has some nice features and it has good color and brightness ranges. It's not terribly expensive either.

review_title: Bass Boost that Can Be Turned Off!
review_text:
I am usually not a big fan of on-ear headphones. I have learned through experience that Philips makes good headphones, though, and based on the brand name I selected this set of headphones to try out. So far I am pleased with them.

As mentioned, these are on-ear phones. For me, I prefer over-the-ear phones which are more comfortable most of the time, and that is probably the only complaint I have with these. After wearing these for a while I need to take them off for a short time before I can put them back on and keep going. This is true with most on-ear phones I have tried. For on-ear phones, though, these aren't bad and the ear fatigue is less than many I have used.

This particular set boasts an on-demand bass boost, and for me that's a huge plus. Most headphones have the bass boost baked right in and there's no way to turn it off. I don't care for heavy-handed bass (gives me headaches), so for me it is a feature I will leave turned off most of the time. However, there are times when the bass needs some help, and these deliver. When activated, there is a very noticeable increase in bass response that will certainly make some people happy.

So, about the sound profile... A set of headphones isn't worth any amount of money if they sound bad. These are fairly balanced phones when the bass booster is turned off. The highs are bright and clear, the midrange is warm and the bass is present but not overwhelming. The bass becomes front and center when the boost is turned on.

I selected this light for working with my camera, though I have other lights that are good for the tasks I have in mind. I have had good experiences with Logitech products and I had good expectations for this light. For the most part I am pleased with it.

This is a small LED-based light that is designed to attach to a flat screen monitor and be used for video lighting. The target audience is very clearly vloggers and video makers, though it can be adapted for other uses with some thought. The main feature of this light which is important enough to mention is that it is a non-strobing LED, meaning no striping when at high shutter speeds.

The light has a couple of settings that can be adjusted by buttons on the back. It can be brightened or darkened, and the color temperature can be adjusted as needed. I personally like using a warm setting more than a cool setting, but that's a preference and it changes based on what I am doing. There is some graduation in the levels though they are granular enough for my needs.

The head of the light can be tilted forward and backward, so there is some adjustment that can be made. It is not adjustable from side to side, though. Also, it must be mounted on a surface where it can hang, not placed on a desk stand-alone. As such, it is specifically designed for hanging on a monitor.

The one thing about this light that I do not care for is that it does not have any battery capacity. That is, it must be plugged in to a USB outlet to work. That's probably again related to being marketed as a vlogging tool, but it does reduce portability when a USB port is unavailable for use. It can be rigged to work with a power bank which is a sloppy work-around, but this is simply a patch.

This is a decent light for video work and it is very definitely a tool for vloggers and video makers. It has no battery capacity so it must be plugged in to work, but otherwise it is a nice light that works well.

I have worked with K&F Concept filters in the past and generally had good experiences with them. They're good, mid-range quality filters at (usually) a budget price. I haven't worked with any black diffusion filters prior to this one so I have no basis against which to compare, but so far it seems to work as designed and seems to be made very well.

In a nutshell, this type of filter softens light a bit, causing some gentle halos around light sources, without impacting image sharpness or detail. Where I have seen the most noticeable impact is in images where there otherwise would be a lot of shadows and contrast; instead of stark contrast and strong shadows, the filter has the effect of brightening up the shadows somewhat and creating smoother color gradients. Sure, this can be done in software after the fact, but it is a lot easier to do this at the time the image is taken and it certainly is a lot less work.

The filter is very easy to install. This is my first magnetic filter and it is as easy to attach to my camera as I could have hoped. The threaded ring attaches to the lens in the same manner as a step ring or another filter, and the filter itself just snaps securely into place due to the magnetics. Removing the filter is just as simple, especially if you choose to leave the magnetic ring in place on the lens.

The assembly seems to be well made. I have had filters in the past that have been poorly constructed and rattle in the frames when shaken, or have been mildly blemished, or just felt cheap. This filter has none of those issues and appears to be well made.

This is a nice black diffusion filter. It's easy to install and use, and it just works. I will be using it more in the coming weeks.

review_title: Good Improvements Over Older Smart Watch Models
review_text:
I have used smart watches for a while now and I have seen a steady progression in the technology. This is my first Gen 6 watch. It is a big improvement from what I have used before (beyond just battery life) and so far I am pleased with it.

This is an Android-based smart watch, and it is similar in interface to previous smart watches I have seen and used. If you have used any generation of smart watch before this one the experience is very similar. I won't get too deep into the nuts and bolts of that or the WearOS app.

There are two big areas of improvement I have seen with this new watch. First, the battery life is much better than previous smart watches I have used which is very encouraging. I have a Gen 2 watch that I love but it lasts only about 3 days on a charge, and my Gen 5 is not much better. This one lasts several days before the battery runs out.

The more important improvement to me, though, is the way it doesn't interfere with the Bluetooth in my car. Previous watches messed up my ability to stream to the car's sound system to the point that the sound would sputter and simply die. I did trace it to the watch by powering off the watch completely after which the problem went away and would come back when the watch was powered on. This watch does not interfere at all and my car's Bluetooth works whether the watch is on or not.

This is a stylish watch, a bit more upscale than some of the others I have seen and used. The band is a non-stretch link band that is a little snug but not unworkable.

So far this watch works well for me. I am pleased with the improved battery life and even more happy that it doesn't mess with my car's Bluetooth connectivity.

USB-C cables are the one cable type I usually have trouble putting my hands on in my house, and I need them for charging my tablet as well as my video lights. I selected this one because I like cables with braided insulation and so far this one has worked out well for me.

This is a 6' cable which is just about right for my needs. It is long enough to reach my devices when I have it plugged into my USB brick on my desk without requiring rearrangement of everything on my desk just to make it fit. Longer would be handy but unnecessary, but shorter would make it a lot less useful for me.

I have not used it for data transfer, just charging up devices, and so far it has worked out well in that capacity. The connection is snug and I have not noticed any particular difference in charging speeds between this cable and the OEM cables that came with my devices.

I am especially pleased with the build quality. The cable is stiff (as to be expected) and it should hold up for a long time against kinks and twists. The junctions where the cable goes into the plastic casings for the connectors are tight and allow no play which is a big plus for me as these are the spots where I have had cables fail most often. Overall, I am not unhappy with the build quality.

This is a decent third-party USB-C cable that works very well for me. It is made well and it does a fine job charging my devices. It isn’t too expensive either, making it easy to recommend.

review_title: Better ANC than Most; Outstanding in the Price Range
review_text:
I have worked with numerous pairs of active noise canceling (ANC phones) and I’ve seen a wide variation in sound profiles, features, and the quality of the ANC function. Some are better than others. I was a bit skeptical of these because of the price; most of the ANC phones I have used that were worth anything have a higher price tag. These are better than the price suggests.

Right out of the box, these headphones do not draw much attention to themselves. They’re not flashy and do not have any noticeable markings on them unless you’re looking for them. They are over-the-ear headphones which tend to be more comfortable than on-ear phones, and these have a snug fit without clamping down tightly. They adjust easily to fit almost any size head too. The padding on the cans is soft enough to not pinch, though after extended wear they do start to get a little warm.

Pairing and connection with my computer was a painless affair and these were ready very quickly after they were powered on.

The ANC function is far and away better than any other headphones I have worked with in this price range. They’re almost as aggressive as that of the Bose QC-15’s that I own, without that weird faux pressure sensation when the ANC is turned on. Even with the volume down low, these cancel out enough background noise to make them a serious contender. I have no complaints with the ANC.

The sound quality is very good, though not quite to my tastes. The bass is very strong – much stronger than I like personally, but not out of line with what has been trending in the last decade. Where Skullcandy got it right, though, is in how well they’ve implemented the bass enhancement. Even though the bass is very strong (enough to give me a headache at higher volumes), it does not distort or turn into just low-frequency noise. More importantly, the bass enhancement does not stomp on the midrange which is the usual casualty. The midrange is warm and fairly balanced. The highs are bright and clear without being piercing. The end result is a sound profile that sounds full and rich. So many headphones with enhanced bass I have used have killed the midrange which makes music sound hollow, or distort the bass so much as to make music sound like a low-fidelity render. These are refreshing in that regard.

Some headphones detect when you take them off and pause music or playback when you take them off. These do not.

These come in a carry pouch that offers little in the way of drop and crush protection but it does keep them clean and free of scuffs and scratches. Also included is an audio cable for wired use as well as a USB Type C cable for charging.

Overall, these are far and away better than the price would suggest. They are very comfortable to wear, they have a good sound profile (particularly if you like heavy bass) and the ANC function is better than average and competitive with much more expensive headphones. These are budget-friendly ANC headphones with higher-end performance.

review_text:
I use rechargeable AA batteries frequently, specifically in my handheld GPS receivers, so keeping them charged up is sometimes a challenge when I have had more than one device in use. My previous charger only allowed for charging two batteries at a time, so I was excited to have the ability to charge eight at once. This charger works well for this, though it is on the slow side.

This is a very small and lightweight charger, without a lot of bells and whistles. It does not have a refresh option, it is simply a charger. The cost is lower than I would have expected, running about $13 as I write this.

I was startled when I opened the box and found that this is a USB-powered charger, not a AC-powered charger. It’s not even a USB-C device but a Micro USB device. My immediate thought was that it will be slow, and this thought was correct. To be fair, I missed the detail that it works via USB so that’s on me. The fact that it uses a Micro USB interface is listed as well, though it is buried in the details.

I popped in 8 batteries and let it go. I wasn’t sure how long it would take to charge them all, and it finished them at varying times over about a 4-hour period. Most had some charge already and finished earlier, while others had little power already and needed more time. It did charge them all, and it gave me a clear visual indicator when it had finished each battery. I’m not dissatisfied there.

While it is slower than my 2-battery charger that runs on AC power, it ultimately is faster as it can charge 4 times as many at once and the net time consumed is less.

The one improvement I would make for this charger would be to have it use USB-C instead of Micro USB, though that would likely drive up the asking price. Otherwise, I have no real complaints. This charger works well and it handles 8 batteries simultaneously. Price-wise, this is a good deal, too.

review_text:
I am no videographer though I have a camera that is well-suited for video recording (even though it is primarily a stills camera). I selected the Scorpion EX as a possible aid in taking shots close to the ground. In my case this device is absolutely overkill and likely will see less use than it would in the hands of someone shooting video, but I do have my uses for it and I do very much like it.

The concept is pretty simple. This is really just a fancy holster of sorts, not unrelated to a tripod, and it has all of the hardware you need to attach your camera, video camera, or even your phone to it (I will generically say just “camera” moving forward). It is roughly the shape of a horseshoe (hence the name) and it has numerous mounting holes for attaching your camera. It has an easy grip handle and is lightweight enough to be easy to handle, even for people with smaller hands.

There are no electronics involved here – no remote shutter, no stabilization like with a gimbal, or any other fancy electronic smarts that would drive up the cost. What stabilization is there is gravity-based and this works surprisingly well, though not as well as a gimbal. My camera does not have on-board stabilization, and in experimentation the Scorpion did reduce but not eliminate some of the shakes. So, do not expect miracles, but it will definitely make a stabilization improvement when you use it.

This has a surprising amount of flexibility built-in (not in the sense of being pliable, but versatile). The harnesses can be attached almost anywhere on the handle so that everything can be optimally positioned. I have found this to be especially useful for attaching a COB light near the forwardmost point, so that the light is cast wonderfully when I am trying to get a head-on shot.

As for being low to the ground when I need a ground level shot, this is better than a tripod because I can get the camera lower than with even the smallest tripod and I can use adjustable feet to make everything level. This is really useful for when I am taking long exposures.

While this is very definitely overkill for my uses I am pleased I have this in my toolbox. It is a simple tool but it is very useful, and in the hands of someone who needs to better stabilize a video recorder it will be more useful still. As I mentioned above, it won’t work absolute miracles, but it reduces the camera shakes enough to make a noticeable difference.

My son participates in an online meeting weekly, and he needed a new webcam to replace the one he was using. The old one worked but was not of good quality. Based on the asking price for this webcam I was not especially hopeful. That said, it has proven to be better than either of us expected.

It's easy to set up - plug it in and let the OS configure it. It's easy enough to use, too, by selecting the camera desired if there's more than one.

We have seen no issues with clarity or audio/video quality, which have both been solid and reliable. In his meeting, others have commented that his feed seems to be the clearest and most glitch-free.

At least one other reviewer noticed issues with lag and skipping. This has not been an issue for us and so far this little camera has performed well without incident.

The model we received did not have the mini tripod. However, it has a standard mount for a tripod and those little tripods are easy enough to find. If you already have a tripod of any size, this webcam will mount without issue.

Could it be better? Sure. But, improvement would drive up the cost, and the quality is good as it is. For the asking price, this is a great little webcam.

review_title: Keyboard Slipped Past the QC Department
review_text:
For the most part I have had good fortune with Logitech peripherals. As I write this I am using an MX Ergo trackball which is the best mouse/trackball I have ever used. I looked to the MK470 mouse/keyboard combination with the idea of using it with a laptop running Linux. I had high expectations for the keyboard but lower expectations for the mouse due to the size and shape. Both failed me, but in completely different ways.

I will start with this: this combo does not use a unifying receiver so if you want to use another peripheral with this combo you’ll need either another USB port or connect via Bluetooth. That’s all right as long as you recognize that up front. It’s a mild disappointment, but it was clear up front so this was not a surprise.

The mouse and the keyboard both have the batteries installed already. The keyboard takes 2 AAA batteries and the mouse takes one AA battery. I question the logic behind using different battery sizes.

I plugged the receiver into my laptop running Linux with the latest kernel, and both peripherals were immediately usable. That’s a plus.

The first problem I have is with the mouse. The mouse works just fine but is such a low-profile device that it is uncomfortable for me to use. I have a travel mouse that actually fits my hand a little better and that says a lot. For someone with very small hands this one will serve acceptably as a basic two-button travel mouse. To be fair, I knew this ahead of time so I cannot complain too much. It does work correctly and in a pinch I can work with it.

The keyboard is a completely different matter entirely. It works just fine – except for the “P” key. For that specific key, I have to bear down very hard to get it to register at all. I tried leaning the keyboard on its side and tapping it gently in case something was caught in the switch and I have tried my best to clean it without disassembly. No matter what I have tried, the “P” key continues to be insensitive to the point of rendering the keyboard unusable.

I really wanted to like this keyboard, and I knew the mouse would be small. Unfortunately, because the keyboard I received doesn’t work properly I can’t use it and can’t rate it favorably. It’s a shame – I imagine I got a bad unit (it happens), but I cannot recommend a product based on an assumption.

UPDATE 10/31/2019:

I popped off the "P" key and looked at the mechanism underneath, since the keyboard was not otherwise useful. It does not appear to be broken, damaged or obstructed in any way. For this particular key, the plastic key cover needs a small bead in the center underneath to push down the silicone membrane to make contact. Using a very small piece of tape and a tiny ball (about the size of a pin head) I was able to add such to the key cover to get it working without damaging any parts, without changing the feel while typing, and without spending any money. However, this should not have been necessary as this should have been tested properly before pack-and-ship; my review and rating stand.

review_text:
This is the first digital picture frame with which I have worked so I do not have any basis of comparison with others to know if it compares well against other ones or not. That said, it does what it is supposed to do, it does it well and I am happy with it.

Setup is simple and easy. If you have your media ready to go, copy it to the included SD card and pop it in.

On a side note, the card that came with it is 32GB which is huge. That can hold literally thousands of full-resolution images from a digital camera. Assuming that the average high-resolution JPG image is 8mb (which is what comes off my mirrorless camera) it can hold about 4,000 pictures. That all said, this frame can also play back video and sound, so there is more to it than just showing pictures. In that light, the size of the card makes a lot of sense.

The frame is approximately 10” of viewing area. The images are bright and clear which should please most users.

The unit handles a number of audio, video and image formats. The list is not exhaustive, but it does handle the main types in each category.

Included is a little remote. The remote isn’t fancy but it is sufficient for changing settings, moving to the next media element, power on/off, etc.

There’s really only one negative, and that’s the documentation which is written in very poorly-translated English. I would lower my rating of the overall package on this basis except that the product is so self-explanatory and easy to use/understand that the documentation isn’t necessary.

Overall, we are happy with this frame. It works well and it is very easy and straightforward to understand. It handles a lot of formats and can play back audio and video in addition to showing still images.

review_title: Sound Profile is Very Good, ANC is Ok
review_text:
My experience with JVC up to this point has been with video equipment and televisions. My experiences have been positive so I hoped that this would be a good set of Active Noise Canceling (ANC) phones. I have worked with a lot of ANC phones – Bose, Sennheiser, Sony, Philips and more. Almost every set I have used has had some flaw, either in the ANC or in the sound profile. These JVC phones are interesting in that regard. The sound profile is nearly spot on, but the ANC is on the conservative side.

I’ll go over the ANC first. This is not a real competitor for the high end Sony or Bose sets and if the main thing you want from a set of ANC phones is noise elimination then these are far from the strongest or most aggressive. I have a fan that I use as the main test for ANC phones, and with the most aggressive phones the fan is almost completely wiped out. The JVC phones do cancel a good bit of noise, but it leaves a good bit of sound behind that Bose in particular eliminates. Now, that said, ANC headphones that can cancel more than these are almost universally much more expensive, often by double the price. These are what can probably be called “good enough for most”. For me, I like a more aggressive headphone, but these cancel enough ambient noise that when I am listening to music I don’t hear much else.

Many ANC phones fiddle with the sound profile to compensate for some of the lost frequency response, usually in the bass range and at the expense of the midrange. These phones are very unusual in that they don’t really seem to impact the sound profile much at all. And, the sound is very balanced. The bass is good, not overdriven (if you have ever used Dre Beats or Monster phones, you know exactly what I’m talking about). The midrange is warm and music sounds like it has the right depth as a result. The highs are clear and vocals sound very clean. The sound profile does not seem to be different between when the ANC function is on or off, though turning on the ANC does enhance the volume (which you can observe by having the headphones off when you activate the ANC in the middle of playback.

The ear cups are comfortable and I can wear these for a while before I need to take them off for comfort reasons. They don’t seem to get too warm when wearing for a while which is good. They’re not the most comfortable phones I have used, but they are better than many.

They connect via Bluetooth and I had no issues pairing and connecting them to my phone.

My favorite feature is that there is an independent volume control on the headphones themselves that does not change the volume setting on the source device. This is a feature that is a bit unusual; often, when the phones have a volume control on them it impacts the system volume when adjusted.

So, there is one thing about these phones that I think needs some improvement. Included with them is a cloth bag for protection, and that’s just not going to cut it, particularly in this price range. A bag prevents the contents from getting dirty but provides no damage protection. For the asking price (presently $149) these should have a hard case that at a minimum provides crush resistance.

I am very pleased with these headphones, more than I expected to be. They sound great, though the ANC is passable. My biggest issue isn’t with the phones themselves but with the lack of a suitable protective case. Hopefully JVC will resolve that issue in the near future. If you want a good set of ANC phones without spending north of $300, these are worth a look.

review_title: Works Great in an MX ERGO
review_text:
I bought this replacement ball for my Logitech MX ERGO, which worked well for me before I accidentally dropped it and subsequently put a pock mark on the original ball. The ERGO still worked but would occasionally get stuck when the support pegs would catch the pock and cause the ball to resist - not enough to really hurt anything but just enough to make digital drawing difficult and just enough to annoy me. This replacement ball has taken care of that for me and has proven to be a worthwhile expense for me.

The ERGO and the M570 have the same size ball, so this ball can be used in either (I was using the ball from my old M570 in the ERGO while I waited for this ball to arrive). Replacement is a 30-second procedure and requires no special tools, though a pencil does make getting the old ball out a lot easier.

There are two different finish types available, glossy and matte. I chose the glossy in red. Operation has been absolutely smooth with no resistance at all and no catches. I haven’t noticed any operational differences between it and the original gray ball that came in my ERGO. And, in my opinion, the dark red of this ball actually looks a little nicer than the original silver ball as well as the blue M570 ball.

This wasn’t an expensive replacement and so far it has worked out very well for me. It has restored operation of my trackball to what it was before I damaged the original ball, which is really all I needed. Based on my experience with it, this is an easy replacement ball to recommend if you need to replace the ball in either a Logitech M570 or an MX ERGO.

review_title: Bluetooth Connectivity a Big Plus; Pen is Mediocre at Best
review_text:
NOTE: This review is written for the Small, Bluetooth edition.

I have been using Wacom Intuos and Bamboo tablets for years, not really for graphic arts but more for digital handwriting and for use as an alternative to traditional mice and trackballs. My present solution is an Intuos 5 medium which seems to be about the right fit for my hands and my work space. The one drawback has been that it’s a wired solution. This new Intuos is a Bluetooth solution and it is definitely a step forward. For me the challenge is downgrading to the small from the medium, but it’s a good fit for me when traveling and when working in cluttered spaces.

To approximate the size, it is roughly equivalent to 7” tablet in size. It’s small enough to tuck away in a corner of a desk when not in use, and when it is being used it does not take up large amounts of real estate. The design itself makes it suitable for use just about anywhere it can be set down and kept stable - one of the reasons I like drawing tablets more than traditional mice.

The Bluetooth connectivity is new to me, and I was pleasantly surprised to find that this unit can connect via USB as well. So, if your system is like one of mine and the Bluetooth doesn’t work, this drawing tablet still will work.

I have it connected to my Windows 10 system. I have not yet made the effort to get it working with my Linux system, though I expect there will be some labor involved to make that work. I’ll revisit that later.

In operation, this is a straightforward drawing tablet though it is an improvement over my Intuos 5 in some ways. Of course the Bluetooth is a step up, but I was surprised by the increased number of pressure levels which is effectively doubled over my old tablet - 4096 vs 2048. For someone like me, this is not a huge difference and I don’t take advantage, but for someone who is very serious about fine digital artwork this can be a huge benefit. For use in handwriting, it is not especially important as even 512 pressure levels (like my original Bamboo small) is more than sufficient.

When you register, you get a choice between three Corel titles, of which you can select two (for the medium you get all three). Some may find the choice difficult - Painter Essentials 6, AfterShot 6 and Clip Studio Paint Pro (2 years) - but for me, having AfterShot is more than enough.

There is a downside to this little tablet, though - the pen is mediocre. There is no comfort grip, changing the nib is a pain, and there’s a very limited number of replacement nibs for it. It’s the one weak spot in an otherwise nice product, and even then it’s not all that bad.

The hardest part for me with this specific tablet is the move from a medium to a small, but this this counterbalanced by the Bluetooth connectivity and the inclusion of the Corel titles, specifically AfterShot. This is a very nice drawing solution and is it priced nicely. I’d recommend the small for anyone either just getting started or experimenting; the medium is a better fit for those more experienced or needing more real estate. I would choose a different pen if available, though.

review_title: Solid Performance; Slightly Pricier than Competitors
review_text:
I have built systems with SSDs for the last several years and I have come to see where they have their strengths and weaknesses. Not all SSDs are the same, and some have distinct advantages over others though the gap is definitely narrowing. This is my first experience with Samsung’s SSDs, and so far it has been a very positive experience. It has given me no issues at all and has performed well.

I installed the drive in a Dell Inspiron laptop which was running Windows 8. On the SSD, I installed Linux instead. Installation was very smooth, it was quick and I had a working system up and running in no time. I have now been running the system constantly for over a week (no powering off or hibernating) and the drive has shown no signs of trouble.

I loaded up a virtual machine and ran it on top of the main installation. The VM and the host install both have performed admirably and have not suffered from any noticeable I/O lag. Running smartctl against the drive after the past week of testing, it has reported no errors and a very healthy drive across the board.

Aside from the speed advantages of an SSD over a platter-based drive, this drive is absolutely silent (no surprise there) and so far I have not had any heat issues. It has given me no indications of any trouble in operation and my system is running as smoothly as should be expected.

The one issue I have with this drive, and it’s not a performance or quality issue, is the pricing. It is a little more expensive than most, and so far I have not seen any real justification for it over the likes of Crucial, Kingston or other branded drives. There may be justifiable reasons that reveal themselves later (I do not know how long this drive will continue to work but it should literally last for several years, even under very heavy use), but for now it seems a tad expensive compared to competitors.

Operationally I cannot find fault with this drive. It works well, it’s fast and quiet (as should be expected) and so far I’ve not had heat issues with it. Utilities I have run against it have shown that the drive is very healthy and has reported no problems out of the box. This is a good drive that will serve well. Time will tell, though, if it is worth the slightly higher asking price.

review_text:
There are two of us in the house that use iPhones with the lightning port and as such we do need extra cables. Lightning cables are great but they do have a tendency to break. Also, not all third-party cables are the same and some are not worth the box they ship in. I was anxious to try this cable and I have found it to be a perfectly acceptable replacement for the one that came with my phone. Actually, it’s better.

First things first - it is important to note that this cable is MFI-certified which is actually a big deal. I have worked with cables that are certified and those that are not. Those that carry certification are guaranteed to work properly with your device, while those that are not certified are a roll of the dice. This cable is certified so it means two things you can expect from it: it will allow you to charge your phone without worry, and it will allow you to connect your phone to your computer without complaining about the cable being unauthorized. It just works.

The cable is shielded in a heavy nylon weave and that is a double-edged sword. On one hand it means the cable is very stiff and not very bendy which may or may not be an issue. More importantly, though, it means it is going to last longer than plastic coated cables which tend to flex and break.

The ends are terminated well too, with a hard plastic sleeve at the end of each plug where the cable connects. This spot is where most cables fail, and it is nice to see that some thought was put into reinforcing the cable at this point.

The weighted ball is interesting but to me it gets in the way. It can be slid up and down the cable which has its uses, but it is large enough and bulky enough to be more of a hindrance to me than a help. That said, if you are putting this cable in an area where it will not be moved and you intend to leave it there for the long term, it does prevent tangles and it allows for keeping gently tension on the cable.

Overall, I am pleased with this cable. It’s a lot less expensive than Apple-branded cables and it definitely is more durable and should last a long time.

It just works. The cable is shielded in a heavy nylon weave and that is a double-edged sword. On one hand it means the cable is very stiff and not very bendy which may or may not be an issue. This spot is where most cables fail, and it is nice to see that some thought was put into reinforcing the cable at this point. The weighted ball is interesting but to me it gets in the way. review_title: Fast, Quiet, and Works Great Under Windows and Linux
review_text:
NOTE: I am writing this review for the 1TB platter-based Passport drive.

I have a 250GB Passport I bought several years ago and it has served me well, though it has gotten close to full over time (I never imagined at the time that I would fill that thing up). I have had good fortune with it so I expected the same from this 1TB version, and so far I have been right. In addition to the larger capacity, it is very definitely a speed upgrade from my old Passport.

This is a small drive in terms of physical footprint, approximately 4”x3”x0.5” in dimension. That’s a double-edged sword. On one hand, it is small enough to stuff in a shirt pocket which makes it an excellent on-the-go storage solution that’s almost as convenient as a thumb drive. But, that also means it is easy to misplace or lose (or have stolen if left unattended).

It comes with software that allows you to password-protect the drive which is a nice deterrent in the event that the drive is taken. It’s certainly not foolproof, but it’s sufficient to keep the large majority of unauthorized access out. To be honest, since the drive does not leave my home I have not used the software at all.

When you plug in the drive to a Windows or Linux system, the OS immediately recognizes the drive and it is available immediately for use. In the case of Windows, you can immediately explore the drive and read from it and write to it. For Linux, it depends on how you have configured automount and which desktop management software you use, but the kernel does register the presence of the drive and you can display the partition table.

This is a USB 3.0 drive, making it a huge speed upgrade from my older 2.0-based Passport. This is a great solution for storing all of your pictures, movies, important documents, and as in my case large downloads and purchased software packages. With 1TB of space, I don’t think I am going to run out of space anytime soon.

As a bonus, this is a very quiet drive.

I put this drive on a USB power meter to see how much it draws from the USB port. At rest it pulls 0.17A. When actively reading, it peaks just under 0.6A which is surprisingly low. My concern was that this would add some strain on the USB port over a longer period of time but this seems to be an unjustified concern. That said, I am more likely to connect it to a USB hub instead of directly to a USB port.

So far I have no complaints with this drive. It’s a big step up for me from my older Passport, being larger, faster and more quiet. It’s not cost prohibitive either which is just a bonus. If you need a decent backup drive with large capacity and a small footprint, this one is worth consideration.

review_title: Outstanding Sound and Solid ANC Function
review_text:
I have used active noise canceling (ANC) headphones for many years and I have come to expect - and look for - the subtle differences between them. I have worked with ANC phones from Bose, Sennheiser, Monster, Noontec and quite a few more. All of them have their strengths and weaknesses. This is my first experience with Sony ANC phones, and I anticipated good ANC functionality and a solid sound profile. At the price point ($300 as I write this) they need to be excellent to be worth any kind of consideration. These were a huge shock to me: the ANC is nearly on par with Bose and the sound profile is solid, giving better results than I imagined.

I will address the ANC function first, then the sound profile, and afterward I will discuss design and features. I apologize ahead of time for being long-winded, but I’d rather give too much feedback than not enough.

The ANC function is, in a single word, outstanding. Bose is the standard by which I compare others and very, very few headphones get anywhere near the same level of noise cancellation as my Bose sets (QC-15 and QC-20i, by the way). Those that get close usually have the same weird pressure sensation for which Bose is known. My primary test is a loud fan that I use for generating white noise when I want to drown out everything around me at night. I turned the fan on high speed, plugged the Sony’s buds into my ears and turned them on. I put them in ANC mode and the fan all but disappeared. All that remained of the noise was a faint, higher-frequency hiss (distinct from the ANC hiss which I will explain later). Of all the phones I have used, this set and the Bose are the only ones to wipe out that much noise. I also went into the bathroom and turned on the ventilation fan to test, and these phones again wiped out a large majority of the fan noise. For this fan, the Bose sets have a very slight edge but you have to be looking for it to notice.

The main difference between the Bose sets and these is the utter lack of that weird pressure sensation with these. If you don’t like that sensation but you want very high ANC, these are simply excellent. Like a lot of ANC phones, these generate a faint hiss that you really won’t notice unless you’re not feeding any sound at all to them and you’re listening for it.

The sound profile is also quite solid. Usually with ANC phones, because of the cancellation of certain bandwidths the phones compensate by twiddling the sound profile to fill in what was dropped, and usually this means overcompensation in the bass range (if you use Dre Beats, you know exactly what I mean). Heavy bass gives me headaches so I avoid headphones where the bass has been given too much boost. With these, Sony did not overdrive the bass at all but it’s still very solid and full - love it. The midrange is very warm and rich and music has the right depth. The highs are very bright and clear but not piercing. Overall, I am very pleased with the sound profile - not audiophile quality but closer than most.

In terms of design, these are a wireless earbud product with a neck harness. So, these are neither on-ear or over-ear phones. The harness and slack but adjustable wiring to the actual earbuds ensures that they can be set up so they won’t tug or pull when you’re working out, running or otherwise doing physical activity. Being wireless, there’s no cord to tangle up either. And, one size really does fit all which is a problem with some regular phones. The neck assembly has a leatherette padding that is soft and will not chafe.

The Bluetooth functionality works great. I paired these to my phone and they paired and connected in less than 5 seconds which is really all I could ask. After a full power-off, I turned them back on and they immediately connected to my phone again. I have no complaints there.

One of the really interesting features of these is the ability to turn off the ANC and use them without any cancellation, but they have another unusual mode that I have only seen in one other pair of phones - they have an “ambient sound” mode that you can turn on that dampens the feed in the buds and slightly increases the surrounding noise without turning off the ANC. Assuming the volume is not turned up too loud, this allows for carrying on a conversation without turning off the feed. I will say, though, that listening to my own voice coming through in this mode is disconcerting.

I do not know yet how long the battery in these lasts. So far I have not run them all the way down.

Included in the box are the phones themselves, a conversion cable so that they can be used with an audio jack (handy when Bluetooth is not an option), a cable for charging, an in-flight audio adapter, several silicone tips fo the buds so you can get the size right, and a protective carry bag.

The carry bag is the only complaint I have with the whole package - it offers little protection from drops and crushes. If you only are concerned about keeping everything together and keeping the set very clean, the bag is acceptable, but if you need better protection that consider getting a third-party hard case or use the original packaging box.

Sony got these right and even at the price tag these are easy to recommend. They’re comfortable (more comfortable than I expected for ear buds), they have excellent sound and the ANC function is outstanding. I prefer these to my Bose phones and will be using these instead.

review_title: Good NAS Drive; Can Work in USB Enclosure with Some Effort
review_text:
A NAS is a great way to add storage for the whole network where everything can be reached from any system connected. It is not as simple as a USB mass storage device like a thumb drive, of course, but it addresses a completely different issue. So far, this drive has proven to be a good one, though its reliability remains to be demonstrated over the long haul.

I have the 8TB drive, and it is great for dumping huge numbers of videos, music, documents and other media needed across a small network. It is fairly fast too, so streaming video from the NAS to any given device on the network is reasonably smooth as long as the network can handle the bandwidth (keep this detail in mind if you are wanting to stream video over a slower wireless network - the lag isn’t necessarily the drive’s fault). The drive is very quiet, though not silent, and so far seems to stay acceptably cool.

I did learn that it does not work all that well in a USB drive enclosure right out of the packaging. I have an enclosure that is capable of handling drives up to 8TB so I decided to try an experiment with the drive when it first arrived. I put it in the enclosure and connected it to my Windows 10 laptop. The system saw the device, and it even saw the drive and recognized the model and serial number, but it was unable to access the drive or even format it. I had more success with my Linux system which recognized the drive and was able to access the partition table and display drive parameters. I did not repartition the drive or create a file system for my experiment though I believe it would have worked.

Time will tell if this drive will be reliable over the long haul. Based on my experience so far, it has worked out well and I have had no issues. It’s the largest drive I have worked with and can handle a LOT of data. If you need wide open spaces for your network storage solution (or you are willing to fiddle with it to get it working as a USB solution) this is a good choice.

review_text:
My parents used to have a Polaroid camera and it was everything that we remember those old cameras for – it spat out a white square of plastic that slowly developed into a grainy, faded-looking picture within a few minutes, it was bulky and it had a very distinct sound. It was a great old camera but when Polaroid quit making film for it it became a paperweight. It's nice to see that some of these old cameras are available with film again. That said, there are some oversights with this package.

I will start with the two negatives (no pun intended). First, the way the camera was packaged for shipment was sub-par and the package was partially crushed when I received it. It did not appear to be damaged beyond the packaging, but it was a disappointment to open the package and find the merchandise box partially crushed. Second, the camera comes with no film or batteries at all. So, the camera by itself is still a paperweight. It would have been nice to have at least a lower capacity pack for film to get started.

The camera came out of the box without a mark on it. It looks to be brand new, in spite of being an older unit. Some of the other reviewers have complained that the camera they received either was scratched up or was partially damaged, but mine is pristine. It's a simple, straightforward device too, and it does not require much thought to use.

In use, it works just like it would have when new. It fires the flash, spits out one exposure with that same distinctive sound I remember and the film develops in front of you. The exposure still looks grainy and old when it is all done, but it is a real photograph that does not need a separate printer or software to get a hard copy. This is not the kind of camera a photographer would use, but rather it is for the tourist or enthusiast.

Why would you want a camera like this? For me, it is a trip down memory lane to a time years ago, when candid pictures were a part of daily life and the exposures were lined up on the pinboard for all to see without needing a computer or tablet. It is not going to make pictures that look like they could be in a magazine, but it will produce pictures you can enjoy right away.
