review_title: Good Speedlight for Someone Trying to Learn
review_text:
If you are seriously into photography a speedlight is a valuable asset that can help you get the lighting just right, which I have found to be particularly helpful when dealing with portrait shots. I have worked with other K&F Concept products and have had consistently good experiences with them so I expected the same from this speedlight. I have not been disappointed. I encountered a couple of minor speed bumps along the way, based largely on learning curve.

This is a sizeable device, and it has a bit of heft to it when the batteries are installed. Please make sure you have proper support for the camera when you are using this light as it can unbalance the camera and make it awkward to use. This is not specific to this particular speedlight but to speedlights in general.

First things first – this thing takes 4 AA batteries and that adds weight. The battery compartment is easily accessible and it is easy enough to install the batteries.

The controls on this light are very straightforward though knowing what the settings do is a different matter. If you do not know what slave mode is or how the settings relate to the zoom, you are going to find yourself frustrated. It took a little bit of research and some experimentation to get the hang of this light and I have found the best use for me is to use it in slave mode to supplement the lighting my the flash that came with my camera, though through the hot shoe I can install it on my camera.

Read the manual that comes with it. It will help a lot in learning how to use this light properly.

The light comes with a small stand so it can be set up independently from the camera and in that manner it can be used as a standalone flash. Turning on slave mode allows for positioning it so that it can add the right balance of light in reaction to the flash on the camera and as a result you can get very good backlighting.

The mode button on the back of this light allows for switching between modal settings and making adjustments, There are also 4 directional buttons that are used for making individual setting adjustments such as zoom. There is the on/off switch which toggles power but also toggles the backlight on the LCD display. Finally, there is a flash button that allows for activating the flash manually. The flash can be fired repeatedly in manual mode but seems to be on a 3-second recharge when not so.

The light has 90 degrees of freedom of movement so that it can be positioned as desired. I like the fact that the neck has angular measures on it for 45, 60 and 75 degrees,

Be aware that this speedlight is not universal and does not work on all cameras. It works fine with a Canon camera; my Samsung camera does not register the presence of this flash at all so to use it with my Samsung camera I have no choice but to use it in manual or slave mode.

This is a nice speedlight and it works well, It is not the fanciest or most expensive but it gets the basics down very well and it has not let me down. This is an affordable speedlight and it is good for the photographer who wants to learn how to improve their lighting techniques.

Disclosure: I was provided a sample of this product in exchange for a fair, honest and thorough review. Even though I received this product at no/minimal cost I have rated and reviewed this product without bias, based solely on my experience with it.

review_text:
Projectors for home use are typically set up for home theater systems. I have seen a number of systems set up with projectors suspended from the ceiling, and I have seen a few that rely on being mounted on a table top. This is a table top model and it is a very good and easy-to-use projector.

This is a 300-lumen projector which is fine for home theater systems, though it would be a little underpowered to use in a larger room or something like a small church. It is good for small presentations too and is a good option if you want to take it with you for meetings instead of keeping it permanently placed somewhere.

There are several input sources for which the projector is configured. For testing and experimentation I found it easiest to work with HDMI though I was able to use some of the other sources as well. It accepts VGA (which is great for older computer systems and other hardware), it can read files from an SD card or even a USB drive. Using a USB drive or SD card, this projector becomes very compact and portable and doesn't even need an external source of input.

This projector even has a pair of speakers inside so you can use this projector for the entire A/V experience, though you will get better sound from a dedicated sound system. This projector is capable of receiving sound as well as outputting it.

I used the HDMI input to feed the image from my computer to the projector and it did a fine job of displaying my desktop on the wall for me. I was also able to configure Windows to use it as an extended display so I could then look at PowerPoint on the computer screen and use the projector to output the slide show. This is very, very convenient and makes this configuration ideal for presentations. I was able to adjust the focus manually and get the image as sharp as I wanted too.

review_title: Spacious and Well-Designed Backpack Camera Bag
review_text:
I have a growing interest in photography and I have been learning as I go. One of the things I have discovered is that a good camera bag – sufficiently large to hold the camera, lenses you need and any accessories – is absolutely essential. I have a messenger-style camera bag that works well enough but I have run out of room in it and it does not have the capacity to hold all of my extra lenses and filters. I looked to this camera bag as a solution. It definitely holds more than my old bag, it seems to be made well and there are some nice features to this bag.

This is a backpack style bag and it is about the same size as a small travel backpack, though it is an order of magnitude thicker. There are zippers and pockets everywhere. There's a lot of padding to protect the camera and multiple movable partitions.

The main compartment is large enough to hold a small laptop if all of the partitions are pulled out. There are three small partitions and two large ones and these can be arranged in any configuration to accommodate a wide array of accessories. As shipped, the partitions are arranged to allow for the camera lens and camera to sit through the middle of the pack which maximizes the padding and protection for the most valuable parts of your setup, and the smaller partitions are about right for 2-3 lens kits. I have a smaller camera – a Samsung NX300 with the 18-55mm lens – so I need less room for my camera and rearranged the configuration to permit room for several filter kits, a telephoto lens, a fisheye lens and a few smaller accessories, all in the main compartment. I have not yet purchased additional lenses but will rearrange when I do.

The main compartment also has a pocket that is suitable for either a thin book or a tablet. So, even with all of my other gear in the main compartment, I still have room for my tablet. I really can't ask for much more than that.

There is a smaller zippered compartment on the front that has room for even more accessories. In this I have loaded up a spare set of macro lenses that would not fit in the main compartment. Inside this compartment there is yet another pocket suitable for holding a tablet as well as a mesh pocket for loose items, my choice being a couple of pens. However, the most interesting item in there, attached by a tether, is a waterproof nylon cover for the whole bag. So, if you need to go out in the rain with this backpack, you can do so without fear of getting your equipment wet.

On the sides there are two small pockets, sufficient for holding a couple of small items like a filter or two or even a very small flashlight.

On the front there is one more zippered pocket that is well suited for thin items, like a map, magazine or papers.

The shoulder straps are adjustable and padded so getting the pack to fit just right is not an issue. However, there is a carrying handle loop on the top of this bag and I prefer carrying this bag using that instead (I have always preferred carrying backpacks this way).

This is a very nice camera bag. A lot of thought went into the design and it can hold a lot of equipment for its size. It has replaced my other camera bag outright.

review_title: Better than the Strap that Came with my Camera
review_text:
I have come to understand the value of a good camera strap. It is more than just a designer item and more than just a simple strap to keep the camera hanging around your neck. It needs to be strong enough to keep the camera secure and it needs to be long enough to allow for grabbing the camera and taking a quick shot instead of having to struggle with getting the camera from around your neck and risk missing the shot by a second or two. The strap that came with my camera is functional but much too short and I expect it to rip eventually. This strap by Orota is a much better strap than that provided with my camera.

This is a well-made strap. One side is a heavy weave not unlike a car’s seat belt but not as smooth and shiny. It is also quite a bit thicker than a seat belt and will have no issue with supporting the camera. Sewn to it is a decorative layer that is also a heavy weave, similar to but not exactly like canvas. These are stitched together with heavy thread and I see little risk of them separating.

Each end is clamped with a leather reinforcement that is held in place with four metal rivets. The leather ends each hold a metal buckle with the thinner nylon straps that actually connect to the camera. Looking closely at each component I found no loose threads, no uneven seams, no flaws in fabric or materials. There is nothing about this strap that suggests it will fail under daily use.

This is a much longer strap than what came with my camera, measuring a little less than 3' long. I like the fact that with this trap attached to my camera I can lift my camera and quickly get the shot I want and I don’t have to take it from my neck in order to focus on it. I can hold it far enough from my face to actually focus on the camera. This is a very big improvement over my old strap which was short enough that I could not get the camera in front of my face at a comfortable distance.

This is a very well-made strap and I am very pleased with it. It is stylish, well constructed and it is long enough to make it much more useful to me than my old strap.

review_text:
Sound Intone makes good, inexpensive headphones and the HD-680 headphones is one of their newest offerings. I will admit to initially disliking this particular set of headphones, but a conversation with the manufacturer and persistence with a 16-channel equalizer has brought my opinion of these headphones up substantially. I can’t say these are my favorite headphones as I am not into heavy bass, but I am pleased enough with them to use them when working on my computer.

Right out of the box, these are striking phones that are quite attractive. I have the blue and white edition and my teenage son’s first words upon seeing them was, “those look great!” These are very lightweight and as a result they have a light fit. I personally prefer a headphone that fits more tightly but that’s a personal preference, not a criticism. The padding is firm but not hard and I did notice that these phones get a little warm on the ears over time - again not a big deal but worth mentioning.

When it comes to the build quality, the strongest feature of these phones is the cord - I am exceptionally partial to woven tangle-free cords versus plastic coated wire.

The difficulty I had with these phones initially was the sound profile. The bass is exceptionally heavy, so heavy that it drowns out the highs quite a bit and the result is a sound that is muddy and unclear. It took some time to realize that this is very reminiscent of the sound you get at an outdoor concert - the bass carries forever and the highs get lost. The midrange is absolutely solid. I don’t care for bass that’s so heavy (it gives me a headache) so I fed everything through a 16-channel equalizer. It took a good bit of experimentation and persistence but I finally was able to find the balance to get the sound right and now these phones sound great. The issue is overdriven bass; once I squelched some of the bass and boosted the treble channels just right the profile is solid. They still sound a little like being in a concert hall but that’s more than acceptable.

Oddly enough, these sound good when listening to straight speech, even without an equalizer.

These headphones are different than most other phones I have used. The typical headphone I use does not boost the bass to an extreme. If you really, really like bass, then these phones are for you and will not disappoint. If you prefer something a little more balanced, feed the sound through an equalizer and the sound can be made near-perfect. Although I did not initially like these phones I have come to appreciate them and can recommend them.

FOSCAM is a well-known name when it comes to security cameras and security equipment and they make a good variety of security solutions for home and business use. The F19803P camera is a wireless IP camera that is weatherproof, has night vision and can be accessed via smartphone. One configured and set up on the network it works great but the setup process can be a very painful one.

In the box is the actual camera, the antenna, power adapter, mounting kit, installation software and an Ethernet cable. The camera housing is roughly the size of a new roll of bathroom tissue - very small, compact and lightweight. The mounting kit is a small but solid painted aluminum bracket plus the screws needed to secure it. When mounted properly, this camera can be very inconspicuous.

Following the included directions, I installed the software first and then hooked up the camera to the router. According to the included documentation the IPCamera application should immediately see the camera and from there one can select the camera, log into it and manipulate it as needed. This did not work for me and the camera never did appear. I tried downing my firewall, I tried connecting to a different router and even tried directly connecting to the camera and still was unable to see it. I finally managed to reach the camera by opening the FOSCAM client software and telling it to search for cameras. When I did this, the camera finally appeared, and the IPCamera application showed it too. This works but runs contrary to the documentation.

I did get into the camera finally and was able to change the username and password. I also set up the wireless network settings and found other settings to adjust like IR timer, time source and more.

I found that the camera’s administration settings can be accessed as needed through the IP address and specifying port 88 (unless the port is deliberately changed). I strongly encourage assigning a fixed IP address to the camera via DHCP through the router; otherwise, the IP address can change and accessing the camera gets more difficult. I learned this the hard way, when I had the Ethernet MAC defined but not the WiFi MAC in my router’s DHCP table. My fault, but this was made more difficult by the IPCamera application still not seeing the camera and I had to let the client software scan again.

I made one more mistake and reset the camera via the reset button and it cleared everything I had set already: user name, password, everything. I was concerned that I would lose everything again with a power failure so as a test I unplugged the camera for a few hours and plugged it in again, and fortunately it retained its configuration.

The camera cannot see my 5G network, only my 2.4G network. However, even though my computer is on the 5G network it still can access the camera. Both networks are handled by my one router so I assume that this is normal. If you have a 5G network, make sure you also have the 2.4G network configured or keep the camera connected via Ethernet. The fact that it does not support 5G networks is not necessarily a problem but is worth knowing beforehand.

Once I made it through the configuration (which was all of two hours, most of it trying to figure out how to talk to the camera), the client software allowed me to add it to the configuration and stream a live video feed from it. The video quality is actually very good and when not in IR mode is in full color. When streaming IR video the image is straight black and white, but the image is very clear. Testing with the camera indoors I killed all the lights in the room and the IR kicked in, my intent being to see how clear the image is. The image is clear enough to read text off a white sheet of paper when angled right. Specifically I held up the instruction manual to the camera at about a 2' distance and was able to read the front page without difficulty. The only complaint I have with the IR is that it does not seem to kick in early enough; when in a dimly lit room the camera still tries to use non-IR and the result is a very dark feed. I have found no way to adjust this in the camera settings other than to set the IR to cut on at a specific time which may or may not be the most useful thing.

I like the fact that this camera does not need a specialized hub to work and can be run from a PC or MAC instead. This makes the system a lot more flexible and easier to manage.

The real power of this camera comes in the client software. It allows for adding additional cameras (the screen settings suggest up to 64 cameras) and monitoring all of them at once on one screen. Some of the camera settings can be manipulated such as setting up recording times, setting alarms and more. Adding a camera is as simple as running a search and then adding the camera to an area. There is even the ability to play back the video that has been recorded built right in.

This is a nice security camera and it works well. It has very good IR capability, it works wirelessly and has full-color video that is clear and workable. Configuring this camera can be very unpleasant, though once configured it’s a great solution. If you need a good outdoor wireless camera and you have some patience for an install that’s not necessarily smooth, consider this one.

I work with a sound mixing board that is used to connect multiple instruments and sound inputs to an amplification system. The limitation of the system is the cabling which prevents relocating certain pieces of equipment. One of the biggest trouble spots in the system happens to be audio cabling between the mixing board and the computer used to process the data. This audio cable has helped remedy that situation.

This is one of the better-made cables I have used. Instead of a cheap, plastic-coated cable made of low-gauge wire, it is instead a heavy-gauge wire insulated in a thick nylon braid. I have had bad fortune with cheaper cables as they have a bad tendency to degrade when twisted or pulled tight. Another point of failure is the connection between the plug and the cable which is usually molded plastic that is much too flexible and allows the cable to break. This cable has a metal cap that screws down over the plug and adds a lot of stiffness to the connector. This is probably one of the heaviest audio cables I have used.

This particular cable is 12' and using it as an extension in the sound system it has added a lot of flexibility to the configuration.

This is a very good audio cable. It works as it is supposed to work and it is designed to last much longer than the average cable. This is an excellent choice if you need an audio cable that will not wear out or break quickly, and at 12' there is plenty of cable for almost any use.

review_title: Very Slow Install Process but Wicked Fast Performance
review_text:
We have a router that supports the 802.11ac standard but until we got this router we had no way of connecting to it beyond the 802.11n standard. I was very interested in trying this adapter to see if it really is that much faster. It’s absolutely very fast and has wonderful connection reliability but suffers from a very slow software installation process.

I connected it to a Windows 7 64-bit system and allowed Windows to search for a driver. When that failed (as I assumed it would since this is a new product) I put in the installation CD and started the installer. The process took a surprisingly long time just to install and load the driver, to the point that I considered rebooting the box and starting over. It did finish though and then was ready to connect.

It connected without effort to our 5GHz network and immediately was able to serve up content. Everything seemed to be faster but we were not sure - until my teenage son connected to a Minecraft server and started playing. In addition to a lag-free connection he noticed about a 20% gain in frame rates sustained.

So far I can’t find anything beyond the clunky install that stands out as a negative. This is a fast adapter and it worth the one-time install time if you want fast, reliable connections and have a router that can handle the 802.11ac standard.

review_title: Fast and Reliable Connections for Your Windows System
review_text:
We have several networked devices in our house and also several individualized networks configured. Not all of the networks can be seen by all devices so I looked to this Belkin USB WiFi adapter to allow one of the older computer systems to access the most reliable network in the house - a 5GHz network that only one or two of the systems can see.

Installation was a snap. I popped in the CD, told it to install the drivers and we were off to the races. The particular target system was a 32-bit Windows Vista laptop. After just a couple of minutes the driver was completely installed and when I plugged in the USB adapter is was picked up immediately. I could see the desired network as well as several other networks in the neighborhood that were previously invisible to the computer. I shut off the built-in adapter, connected to the 5GHz network and went to the net.

So far, the connection has been very stable and speeds have been excellent. The router to which it is connected is a TP-Link router and so far we have seen no issues between the two devices. I have not had this adapter very long so it is still early to say it’s completely stable but all indicators up to this point have been very favorable.

Several other reviewers have mentioned that this adapter does not work with Linux. This is true - there are no drivers available for this adapter other than for Windows XP/Vista/7/8. If you need an adapter that will allow you to connect a Linux or Mac system to a wireless network, this is not the device you need right now.

So far I can’t find too much about which to complain concerning this router. It seems to be stable and reliable on the system to which it is attached here. I am satisfied with it and based on my experience with it can recommend it - if you’re sticking with Windows.

review_text:
A good headset is a fun and very useful accessory when playing online games with friends and can really add to the gaming experience. Such is also useful when interacting with software that uses voice recognition and interpretation (a good example being Rosetta Stone). Creative Labs’ Tactic3D Rage wireless headset is a very good midrange headset and boasts some really nice features, but it suffers from one issue that otherwise would make it perfect.

My teenage son is a frequent online gamer and he assisted me in evaluating this headset.

This is a lightweight and comfortable headset. It can be worn for extended periods of time and not cause ear pain like some other headsets can. I was a little apprehensive when I first put them on, thinking that they would be uncomfortable after a while but it turns out I was mistaken. Some other reviewers have reported discomfort when wearing this headset but so far this has not been the case for us.

Being wireless this headset does not require a wired connection to the computer to work. It does come with a USB cable that allows for charging, but the headset needs instead a USB receiver in order to work properly. Without the USB connection the headset stays charged for a good while. The packaging claims that the headset can be used for 16 hours on a single charge, though so far we have not tried to go that long.

Sound quality is excellent. We loaded up a few music tracks that cover a wide range of the spectrum and the overall sound was balanced, not too heavy on the bass and not muddled on the highs. When communicating with someone online with this headset, he told us we were coming through loud and clear.

The way the headset works can be customized through the use of a Control Panel application. This Control Panel allows one to tweak the voice properties (such as adding robotic effects or greatly twiddling the pitch/volume), change the color of the LED glow on the cups, volume settings and more. My son and I had fun playing with the settings, though we agreed the headset was must useful with the default voice settings.

I have only one complaint with this headset - the control panel is not included on a CD in the box and tracking it down online proved to be a lot more challenging than it should have been. It took a bit of searching before I finally was able to find the correct download package - and then the download kept timing out. I think this is the one area where Creative dropped the ball with this headset - if there is no CD in the box, it should not require a lot of effort for customers to find the application on the Creative website, especially when the application is touted on the packaging.

Overall, my son and I are very pleased with this headset. It delivers good sound on both ends of the connection, it is comfortable and it is not absurdly expensive. It would have been nice to have the software on a CD in the box, but otherwise we have no complaints. This is a good mid-range headset that is worth consideration if you’re looking for a headset you can customize.

review_title: Good GPS Unit with Outstanding Support Behind It
review_text:
This is my third (and final) write-up on the Magellan RoadMate 2220-LM. I decided to rewrite my review again after making more discoveries regarding this unit, enough that my previous attempts at writing a review were no longer satisfactory. In a nutshell, this is actually a very decent GPS navigator with a generous feature set and a few minor quirks. One of this navigator's greatest strengths is the level of support they receive when a problem is reported.

Up to this point I have used a TomTom Start as my primary navigator and my wife uses a Garmin Nuvi. Both of these units have their strengths and weaknesses, but both navigate well and do a good job of selecting routes. I have always been curious about Magellan GPS navigators so I was pleased to get the opportunity to do a side-by-side comparison with the Garmin and the TomTom.

Right off the bat, the Magellan maps look a lot more simplistic and basic compared to the Garmin and TomTom maps. Where Garmin and TomTom have opted for more colorful and polished-looking road maps, Magellan uses much more simple graphics when it comes to the maps. At first I looked at the Magellan's maps with disappointment, but as I have used them I realized that there is an advantage with their approach. Because the maps show the roads as more basic, single-color and narrow pathways, the maps are actually less cluttered, making them easier to read.

I ran into a serious issue with the Magellan when I was trying it out during the first few days. Navigation was reasonable but the position showed me at roughly 10 yards behind my actual location, regardless of the direction of travel. Unable to find a calibration option, I contacted technical support. I got very immediate assistance and was walked through a procedure that was supposed to reset the unit, and what it did was more of a hard reboot. After several emails back and forth my issue was resolved and the navigator now tracks accurately. I am very pleased with Magellan's support - highly professional and very eager to make things right.

So, with the accuracy issue out of the way I mounted the Magellan next to the TomTom and the Garmin and went for a drive along a known route I frequently take. All three navigators tracked the same, though I observed something interesting regarding the Magellan. The Magellan marks position with a blue triangular icon and the others use a cartoony icon that can be selected from a palette of choices. With the Magellan, actual position is the top point of the triangle, but with Garmin and TomTom the position is the center of the icon. Even more interesting is that, because of the roads being represented as more narrow at all zoom levels, the Magellan is more likely to show slight inaccuracy while the others show the same location and appear more accurate due to the wider road representation.

There are a number of features that the Garmin and TomTom have that the Magellan does NOT have, though these are more personal preference options more than functionality options. Magellan has one voice - period. If you do not like the Magellan voice the only option you have is to mute it. Also, there is no option for changing the icon that represents the current location, it will always be a blue triangle. Garmin and TomTom also have content communities for upgrades where Magellan does not.

Of the three navigators, the Magellan has the very best mounting bracket and suction cup. Attaching it to the window is quick and easy and removing it is almost just as easy. Like any other mounting cup, it does not do so well when the window is very cold, so if mounted on a cold windshield it can suddenly let go and fall.

For my particular car, the Magellan's car charger is all but useless, due to the size of the plug and the placement of the 12V outlet. That said, because the Magellan has a standard mini-USB plug it can be used with a typical USB cable and a 12V-to-USB adapter. This is the configuration I use and it has worked out well. I did notice that the Magellan does not necessarily charge completely when it is plugged in and operating simultaneously.

Magellan's navigator offers four routing options: Shortest Distance, Fastest Route, Most Use of Freeways and finally Least Use of Freeways. These vary in usefulness, the first two being by far the most helpful to most people. When using Shortest or Fastest I have found the routing to be very sensible most of the time, though the routes usually differ just a little bit from what my TomTom offers up. I have not mapped out a route by hand to see which is more accurate but I believe them to be roughly equivalent.

I decided to try "Least Use of Freeways" for a 45-mile one-way trip. The route offered up was reasonable but because of the traffic at that time of day I knew better than to take that specific route so I took another way. The Magellan then continuously told me to make a U-turn until I was probably 5 miles from the turn I skipped, after which it finally calculated a new route - way out of my way and making little sense. It recommended turns going farther from my destination, continuously trying to steer me back to whatever route it had chosen. I finally got on the freeway for a three-mile stretch, and it recommended I take the very first exit (west-bound) followed by a U-turn, when what I needed was the east-bound exit maybe 0.1 mile further down the interstate. After the exit, it tracked just fine. To make matters worse, every route after that seemed to have some quirky turns in it regardless of the method I chose for routing. I finally reset the unit using the suggestions that technical support had made earlier, after which the navigator has been just fine. Bottom-line: the Least Use of Freeways routing is not very good.

Probably the biggest weakness of this navigator is the software used to interface with the unit. Content Manager, which can be downloaded directly from Magellan's website, is a rather unintelligent application that provides basic connectivity to the GPS unit, with a poor interface and the inability to recognize that an update was made already without requiring a relaunch of the software. It continuously tells me that there is a map update when it says I have the current version. Magellan could have done a much nicer job with the software.

The actual interface on the navigator itself is very well thought-out and designed. It is very much icon-driven and it shows a little more polish and refinement than that of Garmin or TomTom. Hiding in this interface is a good amount of functionality - access to POI databases, traffic camera alerts, "phantom" alerts, navigation by landmark instead of by street name and many, many more features. Magellan got something important right with their interface - it is very uncluttered and clean, making it a lot less distracting while driving.

One feature of which I was completely unaware revealed itself on my commute home one afternoon. My unit did not come with traffic alerts. When I reached the portion of my commute that requires access to the interstate, traffic came to an abrupt stop. Without prompting, an icon popped up on the Magellan screen, offering three alternative routes. I had no clue the Magellan would do that since I did not get traffic alerts, but the feature is very much welcome, regardless.

The Magellan 2220-LM GPS navigator is a nice unit with a good feature set. It is different than Garmin and TomTom navigators and some of those differences really set it apart in good ways. Support is outstanding. The software used to interface with it is acceptable though could be better. I think this is a fine unit that will serve the owner well. If you're looking for a good, basic navigation system at a reasonable cost, this is a unit that is worth a look.

review_title: Disappointing - The Low Price is Justified
review_text:
This is my first exposure to Panasonic Active Noise Canceling (ANC) headphones. This particular model is very inexpensive relative to most ANC phones on the market, and unfortunately the low price is justified. These phones fall short in a couple of important areas.

First and foremost, these are ANC phones and the ANC function does indeed work. That said, the degree to which it works is in line with the pricing. I have a very specific fan in the house that I use as a benchmark, as most ANC phones are able to nearly completely wipe out the white noise that this fan generates when on the lowest speed setting. The Panasonic phones kill a good bit of the fan noise but allow more noise than almost every other ANC set I have tried. In the office I tried these phones in an area serviced by two large air handlers that generate a lot of noise and these headphones did remarkably well though still not as well as most other phones I have tried in the same environment. Now, when compared to the likes of Bose, Panasonic does a very poor job but then again they cost maybe 15% of what Bose costs. When considering this price differential the Panasonic phones do a decent job with their ANC which should be acceptable by most for traveling.

One area where these phones fail, though, is in build quality. These headphones are extremely lightweight and they feel very flimsy and fragile. These are not the headphones to take when traveling frequently. To add insult to injury, they come with a cloth carry bag which offers absolutely no protection at all beyond serving as a dust cover.

Worse, though, is the miserable sound quality. I don't know if my specific headset is the problem but while I have a decent full range of sound, everything across the spectrum sounds slightly tinny and hollow. I was encouraged that Panasonic does not overdrive the bass as many manufacturers tend to do and instead delivers a fairly balanced spectrum, but this does not make up for the poor quality of sound. As these are inexpensive headphones I would never expect them to be audiophile quality, but the sound should absolutely be much better than it is.

I was encouraged to see that Panasonic includes a 2-prong adapter in the package, but then they omit the 1/4" adapter which is something I actually use.

Panasonic has made a very inexpensive ANC headphone and unfortunately the low cost is justified. While the ANC capabilities are within reason for the price range, the sound quality and build quality are severely lacking. If looking for ANC phones for the purpose of using the ANC function, and keeping costs low is important, then these phones may fill that need acceptably. However, if sound quality is in any way important, these are the wrong phones and will sorely disappoint.

review_text:
Let me begin by saying that I am not gifted in the arena of art. I am more technically oriented and as such I use tablets in different ways than most people. For that reason, this is likely going to be a very different review than that of most others on here.

I use pen tablets for handwriting and as general pointing devices as I find them to be more comfortable than mice and trackballs. I started experimenting with tablets a couple of years ago with a Bamboo small, which worked well but was just too small for me. I then compared a Bamboo Fun Pen & Touch to an Intuos4 and it took no time at all to determine that for me, the Intuos4 was a much better choice. With the release of the Intuos5 I jumped at the chance to compare it to the Intuos4, and so far I like it but I have found a couple of things about it that are, in my opinion, less than ideal.

I am using an Intuos5 on a Core i7-based laptop with 8 GB RAM and Windows 7 64-bit.

The very first thing - installation. Installation was about as painless as could be. I plugged in the tablet, installed the drivers and I was able to start using my tablet immediately without any issue. That's a big plus right off the bat. I have had trouble with installs in the past, in particular with the Bamboo Fun Pen & Touch, so having a smooth install is a great relief.

There is one thing about the install that troubles me, though. This tablet is capable of left- or right-handed use, so by simply rotating the tablet it is easy for anyone to use it. However, unlike the Intuos4 the Intuos5 only has a USB plug on one side, and it's the edge that always faces away from the computer. This means that the cord will always run above or below the tablet when plugged in unless it's plugged in to a USB hub of some sort. Perhaps that is not a big deal to some, but to me it is a minor irritant. The included USB cable is long enough, though, that I can hang most of it off the far edge of my desk. I suppose it's a good thing that my desk faces the wall.

I immediately grabbed the pen and started writing, and what I have found is that the Intuos5 seems to be a little more sensitive than the Intuos4, which means I can write a little more softly and still get what I want from it. Wacom did a good job of adjusting the sensitivity to the pen and subsequently turning off the touch feature. With my Bamboo Fun Pen & Touch the pen had to be very, very close to the surface of the tablet before touch was disabled, and even then the tablet kept trying to zoom on me as I wrote. Not so with the Intuos5 - the sensitivity to the pen seems to be good up to about an inch from the surface, which is fine for my purposes.

The surface of the Intuos5 does seem to be a little rougher than that of the Intuos4, so expect the nibs to wear more quickly. Though it has more texture it still feels very natural to me and I have no issue with writing on the surface. That said, why make it rougher so that it eats the nibs faster?

While the buttons along the side are configurable, I don't mess with them. I do use the scroll ring though and it works well. It is sensitive to light touch and so far has given me no trouble at all.

For a good graphics test I brought up Corel Painter and did a little doodling. The tablet and Painter work together quite well. Painter was able to determine at what angle I held the pen and it allowed me to make nice strokes and then reverse the pen to erase without any hassle. I really have not tried to push the tablet through all of Painter's features (which would do a great job of showcasing what the tablet can do) but I did enough to convince myself that the Intuos5 is a strong tool for the really artistic individual.

The Intuos4 has a small, no-frills 3-button mouse where the Intuos5 has touch features that make it work like a giant laptop touchpad. This comes down to personal preference. I never use the mouse on my Intuos4 but the touch features on the Intuos5 are very handy and convenient. Others may find the removal of the mouse to be a deal-breaker.

So far, the handwriting recognition seems to be about equivalent to that with the Intuos4. I have had to adjust my writing habits because of my using tablets for this, so a lot of the retraining took place long before the Intuos5 came. The recognition software does a reasonable job of reading my handwriting but it still makes mistakes and requires more patience.

The Intuos5 is a really nice pen tablet. It is comfortable, it is sensitive and it has two modes for accepting input. I question why Wacom placed the USB port on the outside edge of the tablet, and I also wonder why the surface is more rough than the Intuos4, but of all the current tablet offerings on the market right now this one is the best. It's not perfect, but it does try hard. I'm satisfied.

I have never been a big fan of earbuds but I do use active noise canceling (ANC) headphones on a daily basis. I have a pair of Bose QC 15s and a pair of Sennheiser PXC-450s (both over-the-ear types of headphones) that I use every day in a noisy lab and they have been a blessing at cutting out the noise. I was interested in comparing these earbuds with both of these. Considering the cost, Creative's earbuds are great. I found only minor shortcomings with them.

One of the most important considerations when using earbuds is comfort. Typically they either "hook" to the ear (like Apple's earbuds) or stick into the ear canal a little bit. Creative's earbuds are the latter and I usually find these types of earbuds to be very uncomfortable. THat said, these are the most comfortable earbuds I have ever used, mainly because of the very soft rubber pads that fit into the opening of the ear canal. I was very pleased that these were actually not uncomfortable to me, a big plus right out of the gate.

With the battery in I turned on the power. In a very quiet room, there is a very faint hiss when the noise canceling engages, and I have heard others say that this is unacceptable. Personally, it is so soft that I don't regard it as an issue. In a noisy computer lab, however, the noise canceling takes on a new dimension. In my tests, it is every bit as good as the Sennheiser set and definitely knocks out a very large majority of ambient noise. For the most rigorous test I stood between two large air handlers and swapped back and forth between the Creative earbuds and the Sennheiser headset, and the differences were small.

I loaded up some music and gave the earbuds a sound test, using some club tracks. Very unusual for earbuds, these have great bass. The highs are also strong, which is normal for earbuds. The weak spot is the midrange which is slightly flat but not to the point of being hollow and lifeless. These earbuds outperform other earbuds I have tried in the past and actually compete strongly with good over-the-ear phones.

A couple of miscellaneous points: These buds work like normal earbuds when there is no power, so the battery is not a requirement unless you want ANC. Also, they come with a "Monitor" button which is a temporary mute button so there's no need to take them out when carrying on a conversation. The mute button alone is a great feature and I wish more earphone makers implemented this (the Sennheiser set has something similar, but that's the only other place I have seen this feature).

One thing I wish Creative had added to these was volume control. There is certainly room for a volume slider but it's not there. Instead, volume is controlled from the source. This is a disappointing design choice.

Overall, these are great earbuds. The price is high for earbuds but then again getting ANC in the deal with much better than average sound quality is well worth that expense. If you like earbuds, and if you want active noise canceling too, these need to be on the short list of options.

The Philips GoGear Raga is the first exposure I have had to Philips' line of mp3 players and I was unsure of what I should expect of it. The price is comparable to other mp3 players of similar capacity so I expected it to be in the ballpark with them. For the most part I was correct, though there are a few things about which one should be aware when using this particular offering. It's a good product, but it has its quirks.

Setting up the Raga is easy. In the package is a USB cable that allows one to connect to a PC (packaging does not indicate if MacOS supports the Raga), and upon connecting Philips Songbird downloads and installs automatically. The installation is painless and does not take long, and a few clicks of the mouse along the way and the software loads up.

The first thing I tried to do was load music into the Raga, and once I got the music into Songbird the Raga disappeared from the available devices list. I am not sure what happened. I unplugged it and shut down Songbird, plugged the Raga back in and everything was as it should be, so I dragged 67 songs to the Raga for transfer. I saw two problems. First, the user has to know to drag and drop - there is no "transfer to..." option that I could find in any of the menus. The bigger problem, though, is that the transfer speed is abysmal and it took close to 2 minutes to transfer 67 songs that average 5MB in size. With my old iPod and with my ZuneHD, transfer speeds are appreciably faster. This doesn't make the Raga a piece of junk, of course, as the problem may be Songbird itself, but the transfer speed is something of which to be aware, especially if transferring large amounts of music.

Navigating to the newly transferred music is simple. For that matter, navigating the Raga is simple, period. Anyone with even slight familiarity with music players will have no problem finding and playing music on the Raga.

For comparison, I matched the Raga against my ZuneHD for playback. Of course, the Zune HD produced a more natural and clear sound, but only slightly. For the difference in price, I would have expected the ZuneHD to REALLY outperform the Raga, but this was not the case. In fact, when playing with the built in equalizers in both, I was able to get the Raga to get very close to the ZuneHD for sound quality. The difference was more pronounced with higher end ANC headphones, but this is unlikely to matter to the large majority of users.

The Raga has a tiny screen (the package says it's 1" diagonally) so this is not the kind of player one would want if frequently messing with settings and searching through. That said, the Raga is designed as a player to be worn with the included arm band, suitable for using at the gym. The ear buds that come with it have over-the-ear hooks to help keep them in place.

Considering the price and size, Philips has put together a very nice music player that will suit active users very well. It has some idiosyncrasies, in particular the transfer speeds, but it really is a capable player.

I will preface this review by stating that I am not a graphic artist and I have the artistic ability of a common garden rock. I did not get this tablet for doing artwork. As such, I have a different perspective on this product than the majority of people who buy an Intuos4.

I am very new to working with tablets and I started with a basic Bamboo small. This was a great little tablet, but the important word there was "little". I upgraded to an Intuos4 Medium because I wanted a bigger tablet, and I have been delighted with it. I do not use this tablet in the way a true artists would use it, but I have gained a deep appreciation for it nevertheless.

Because of the work I do, I use computers very frequently. I use them at home too, which is where I've attached my Intuos4. I am always looking for ways to make computing more comfortable, and on a whim I tried tablets. I discovered that, for me, tablet pens are more pleasant with which to work than mice.

The Intuos, in particular, is a good fit with an excellent digital pen that is designed well and fits my hand comfortably. The feel is right, and when writing the nib/tablet contact feels very much like writing on paper with a pencil. There are multiple nibs too, as well as additional pens for purchase, that make finding the right combination easy. So far, I have used only the default nib that was in the pen when I opened the box, and I am satisfied.

There is also a mouse in the package that works for most generic purposes but I rarely touch it. It is a no-frills, three-button scrolling mouse that is actually not bad, but it is only used on the writing surface of the tablet.

My primary use of this tablet is for writing, not drawing, and I have found the handwriting recognition software that is activated with the driver install to be mostly reasonable with translating my chicken scratches. It does have a bad tendency, however, to translate my lowercase letter "b" to "6" or sometimes even "d". As a result of this and other minor quirks I have changed my writing mannerisms to give the software better accuracy, and these new mannerisms are so habitual that I find that when I am writing on paper I have carried these new habits with me to that medium.

The tablet is much more pressure sensitive than my Bamboo was and when I make an effort to either bear down or lighten up with the pressure I can see the difference. This is especially true when using artistry software like Corel Painter. For serious artists, the Intuos4 offers 2048 pressure levels which should suffice for most.

I've made no use of the buttons on my Intuos4 but I use the Touch Ring frequently for scrolling. This is an excellent substitute for a scroll wheel, though it is not critical for my uses.

The pen and tablet are NOT useful for everything. For example, it's a bad choice for playing FPS games like Unreal Tournament. For chess, sudoku, working in MS Word or even grunching numbers in a spreadsheet, it is very workable.

Ok, so why do I prefer this higher-end tablet over a Bamboo Fun? I tried a Bamboo Fun Pen and Touch, which is a tablet that is more in line with people of my skill level (rank beginner and home user). That said, I could not get comfortable with the Pen and Touch, and I feel the Intuos4 pen is a much better for for my hands. Also, the Touch portion was awkward for me. The Intuos4 just works better for me, plain and simple.

For a non-artist, the Intuos4 Medium Tablet is a high-dollar item that can possibly be looked at as an unnecessary expense. For me, though, it is a blessing in that it makes most tasks on the computer more comfortable and easy. I am hooked on this tablet and recommend it to anyone who is either a serious artist looking for a good digital tablet or someone like me who just wants to be comfortable while working on the computer. It is a serious input device and will change the way you interact with the computer.

The Flip is a pint-sized camcorder with a surprising feature set given its compactness. Though is it not a full-featured camcorder and I would not recommend it for serious recording (special events or production material), it is excellent for on-the-go shots and for spontaneous recording when opportunities present themselves.

The Flip is small - a little smaller than an ice cream sandwich. It may be little, but there's tremendous convenience in being able to drop your camcorder in your shirt pocket or your purse and have it at the ready. This compact size holds everything you need to start recording - batteries, flash RAM and all. Without tapes or DVD media on which to record, there's little reason for this device to be any bigger.

It is a solid little thing and feels durable. That doesn't mean it would do well if dropped or stepped on, but it likely will be ok if jostled a little.

Recording is simple. No, I should be more clear - recording with the Flip is trivial. There is no real science to using it: turn it on, point and press record. Press the record button again to stop recording. Even technological novices, or people afraid of electronics will have no trouble using the Flip to record. Playing back is equally simple - once the recording is finished, press the Play button.

There are + and - buttons, used for Zoom. The Flip doesn't have a particularly capable zoom, so shooting from a distance will not yield especially great results.

I tested this camcorder in my basement on a bright, sunny day, and I wandered about recording and chattering to myself. When I played back what I had recorded, I made a pleasant discovery - it does some light balancing and deals with changes in light levels so that the video is still clear. The sound is also good, better than I expected. When I walked down a dark hallway and into an unlit room, it had tried very hard to accommodate for the lack of light but it was unable to completely overcome the darkness. As there is no light on the camcorder to come on when it is dark, this is understandable, but it did surprisingly well in spite of that.

I attached the Flip to my computer to pull the video to my hard drive. FlipShare installed itself and started up, seeing the video I had made. It allowed me to pull it over and even gave me the option to delete it from the camera. Once finished, I was able to play the video through FlipShare. Instead, I decided to hunt it down and use a different application to play it.

I found the file and tried to open it with Windows Media Player. I got audio, but not video. When I switched to QuickTime, my video came up and filled my screen. This is the point at which I made an unfortunate discovery. Every minute move I had made while recording was now plainly obvious, as there is no anti-jitter built into the device.

The video, on a 1440x900 resolution screen, looked clear. It records at 1280x720, which is not that much smaller, so I was a little surprised. I would have expected a little pixelation, but this actually was not an issue.

There are few settings that can be adjusted on the Flip - language, date, time and recording light.

The Flip is a nice camcorder that provides tremendous convenience and fun. It is very easy to use and very compact. It is important to remember that it has some limitations which make it a less-than-ideal choice for more serious application, but if those limitations are not an issue for you then the Flip is a fun and affordable way to capture things on video.

review_text:
We bought this Netgear WGR614 router back in March 2006. It installed somewhat easily and except for a little problem with the wireless PC card for the laptop (wouldn't be recognized at first but easily corrected) we had pretty stable use for about a year. Then we began to have connection problems. The connection would get slower and slower until internet pages would just not load, resulting in repeated "page cannot be displayed" errors. Powering down and restarting the router, modem and computer seemed to correct the issue. But as of this morning the router appears to have completely died. Powering down and restarting does nothing, the internet connection cannot be re-established. We can connect the desktop directly to the cable modem but for now the laptop is without connection, making for some unhappy family members here.

As of right now I don't know if we'll be buying another Netgear router & wireless PC card. The life expectancy of Netgear products does not appear to be all that great. Looking at some of the reviews we appear to be quite lucky that we got as much time out of the router as we did. Still I'm not in the mood to be shopping for a new router every 1.5 years or less. Hopefully there is a good router out there that can last at least two years.

review_text:
I bought this EVGA CLC 280/280mm AIO a few months ago but I wanted to try it out for a while before I left a review to really get a chance to see how it performs over a longer period of time.

Firstly, I am running this AIO on an i7 8700K WITH an overclock of 5GHz on all cores. With this AIO my idle temperatures are in the mid to high 20C range and under full load it warms up to the low to mid 80s C. This is great performance for such a high overclock. With stock clock speeds this AIO should perform much better and shouldn’t go above 65C during full loads.

Secondly, I want to share my experience with EVGA’s superb customer service. When I installed this AIO I had a problem with the RGB not working. I tried reinstalling it, using different motherboard plugins for the cables, but nothing seemed to fix it. Finally I contacted EVGA by email. They mentioned that the USB cable could be defective. Here is what amazes me: EVGA sent me a brand new USB cable at no cost to myself and they didn’t even make me go through the hoops and hassle of sending my product back, paying for shipping, waiting for processing, etc., they just sent me a brand new cable and THEY paid to have it shipped. I got it 2 days later.

That is the kind of customer service I love and is the reason I try to buy EVGA products when possible. Most companies will not do that. They’ll put you through the hassle of many steps and lots of waiting around and processing which discourages a lot of customers, such as myself, from even bothering to contact them when something goes wrong.

All in all, a great product with even better customer service!

Thank you EVGA!

I’ve had this SSD for a few days and I also have a 1TB 970 Evo Plus and 1TB 860 Evo and all of them are great! But they do have their drawbacks too.

This drive does really well with SMALL (under 15Gb) workloads. The speeds are right up there (~500MB/s R/W) with my 860 Evo until it gets to about ~14GB at which point it slows down drastically. This is fine for things like boot, games, apps, and most programs.

However, if you do heavy workloads like video editing, file transfers, etc,. where you are regularly moving large (15GB+) files around this is NOT the drive for you. If you are a “heavy” user I highly recommend the 860 Pro. It can keep up those high R/W speeds without slowing down after ~15GB. It will maintain full speed throughout the duration of whatever you are doing.

With that said this is a great drive for light/moderate workloads (gaming, web browsing, small work files, etc.,) and it is at a price that gives you excellent value and quality for your money.

I also really love the Samsung Magician software. It’s basically the main reason why 3/5 of my drives are Samsung. Samsung is also known for making reliable, high quality products. Yes there is a premium compared to cheaper drives but you’re paying that little bit extra for quality & reliability.

I took off 1 Star on this review though because Samsung doesn’t include any of the cables or mounting screws which just doesn’t make sense to me. C’mon Samsung start adding that stuff! I would’ve happily paid a couple dollars more for it and it wouldn’t have cost Samsung that much so they could’ve made a little bit of extra profit by adding it.

I still recommend this drive though and would buy it or the 860 Evo again if I needed more storage.

Samsung is NOT falsely advertising. The drive DOES in fact come with the advertised space it’s just that in order for it to work properly and perform optimally it requires approximately 10% of the capacity to be overprovisioned free space.

This is a really great SATA SSD for the price. It's perfect for storing games that have long load times without paying a fortune for an NVMe SSD of equal capacity. I highly recommend it for people like me who need more space for games, projects, and other things like that who want them to load quickly. You can get an HDD like a WD Black for cheaper but the loading times will be much longer and for those who dont like to wait for long load screens this is a perfect choice.

Also don't forget to enable RAPID mode. It uses RAM to speed up the programs & applications that you have been using recently. My CrystalDisk benchmark shows how fast it is with RAPID mode enabled.

review_text:
UPDATE (4 -> 5 stars)/ 9/20/2013 - This thing is $28 now! You'd be nuts NOT to get this case! I'm pretty sure they're taking a loss selling it at that price, maybe they're overstocked and trying to get rid of them? If you're going to buy this case BUY IT NOW!

Firstly, I just want to say if you want to SEE my PC check out the last 3 customer uploaded images, they are of my newly built PC in this case. If you can't find customer images, go to the main product page for this case, and click "See all 5 customer images", it's right under the picture of the case.

My current specs:
CPU: AMD FX 8320 (3.5GHZ stock) Overclocked @ 4.22 GHZ
CPU Cooling: Corsair H80 High Performance Liquid Cooling System
Motherboard: Gigabyte FX 990 UD3 AM3+
Power Supply: Rosewill Capstone 750W 80+ Gold certified.
SSD: Sandisk 32GB (I just use it for my operating system for quick bootups, nothing else.)
HD: Seagate Barracuda 1TB 64MB cache 7200 RPM SATA III
Graphics: Geforce 760 GTX 4GB 256bit GDDR5 (When I was deciding whether or not to order this case, this was my biggest concern, "Will one of the new big geforce graphics cards fit?" - YES it will! I MIGHT be able to fit another one in, but I really don't need another one, the 760 is a beast!)
Ram: 16GB Gskill Sniper Series DDR3 2400

Whew, now having said all that, EVERYTHING fits in this case. Is it a little bit snug? See for yourself, I don't think so, but some might. I also got a non-modular power supply so that adds alot of unnecessary cables.

The fact is though, my computer does NOT overheat. I monitor temps whenever my computer is on (with CPUID, free program!) and as an example, under a full load my CPU temp stays ~20C and my GPU can get up to ~60C on a warm day. Keep in mind though for the CPU I'm using a $104 liquid cooling system (I just happened to get a GREAT deal on it).

The see-through case is pretty cool too, I like being able to see the components plus with a liquid cooling system if any liquid starts leaking I can immediately take care of it, although I highly doubt it will leak.

Anyway, I hope this review helps, keep in mind I put alot of stuff in here with the 4 ram modules, and the pretty large graphics card (the Geforce 760 GTX is about 11.5" long, it's pretty big), but it does all fit!

Keep in mind this is a ~$50 case. For $50 it is a good deal, if you want a "better" case, you're going to have to spend more money it's as simple as that. People nitpick things like a flimsy backplate, or not having the best cable management, well the more you expect from a product the more you're going to end up paying for it. So take it easy on a $50 case.

I can say for sure it's better than my old HP desktop PC computer case. It actually FEELS like a gamer's case.

So all-in-all, if you're on a budget and looking for a nice computer case for $50 I recommend this case. It's got everything I needed and it's got everything 90% of people will need or care about. I'd buy it again.

review_title: Without question this is one of my new favorite things
review_text:
These earbuds combine incredible sound in a stylish and functional package. I would give these more than 5 stars if I could. I had high expectations before trying these, especially in view of the price, and these earbuds blew those away.

Bang & Olufsen's engineers magically crammed a high-end sound system into a lightweight, wireless earbud. You have to hear them to believe how amazing these sound - clean, clear music across an impressively wide range. I noticed details for the first time in songs that I have heard many times before.

Beyond the sound, the craftsmanship and overall product design are outstanding. I don't know about the electronics as only time will tell, but the earbuds and the case themselves look like they will hold up to regular use without any issues. The leather and brushed aluminum on the case adds an extra-premium feel to the product.

Also, at first I thought the charging capability of the case was a bit gimmicky, but I quickly realized my error. It is so convenient to know that the earbuds are fully charged whenever I want to use them. I don't have a Qi charger, so I haven't taken advantage of the full wireless capability. But for me, it is not a big deal to use the USB cord when I need to occasionally charge the case.

To give some context, this is not a product I would have considered purchasing on my own. I've always thought of earbuds as cheap, portable ways to listen to music while working out or on the go - situations where the background noise means that you can't appreciate high-quality sound. However, after jumping at the chance to try these, they have completely changed my perspective on what earbuds can do. Excellent sound quality is available in a highly portable, convenient product.

The only downside I have experienced is that the touch controls take some time to get used to. I had trouble figuring it out at first, but after a few days I can usually get them to do what I intend to do on the first try. I prefer the minimalistic design, so this learning curve is not a significant issue for me.

I also like the Bang & Olufsen music app that allows selection of different listening modes that vary between - "warm", "excited", "relaxed", or "bright" sound profiles. Switching between the modes really gives the sound a different character. My favorite feature on the app, however, is the ability to select "transparency" of the music. A higher level of transparency amplifies your surroundings so you can hear what is going on around you. This does not give you spy-gadget levels of hearing, but it noticeably amplifies background sounds. I've been using these headphones at work, and I can easily hear when my phone rings or when someone knocks on my office door.

Last, the excellent sound quality carries over to phone calls. I have no trouble hearing the other person on the line, which is not always the case with the built-in speaker on my iPhone. Also the people I have talked to have had heard me clearly. This was an unexpected bonus, and I actually prefer to use the earbuds for calls now.

TL;DR: If you can afford these, you won't regret it.

I learned this the hard way. I hope this saves you some time and hassle.

review_title: Very easy to assemble. A few quibbles.
review_text:
This is our first projection screen, and we used it quite a bit this summer. It's very easy to assemble on the metal frame. It comes with legs, but we never used them; instead, we posted the screen on the back of the house.
The instructions are straight-forward; after the second assembly and disassembly, we got the hang of it very quickly and didn't need the instructions. The bag it comes with fits everything snugly, and there's even a pouch just for the screen so that it doesn't mix with the metal.
There is a very strong odor when we opened the box. Definitely has a marine smell, but it did go away after the third use.

The screen latches onto the metal frame by buttons. However, the corners are very difficult to snap on, so much so that we decided to leave them unbuttoned. Thankfully there is a surplus of buttons, so the screen stayed straight and wrinkle-free. Even with the screen folded during storage, we didn't notice any creases while watching movies in the backyard. A great investment, especially during the quarantine.

review_title: Stays cool. Slow at boot, but speeds up.
review_text:
I'm currently using this with my NextcloudPi setup to store my own data over the network. The Raspberry Pi4 supports USB 3.0, which this SSD also does. That's one of the main things I look for when hounding an SSD: fast transfer rates, as well as large capacity.
I know Samsung has a good reputation for SSD storage; I was very excited when this came in the mail. After re-installing NextcloudPi, I let the setup wizard reformat the Samsung T7 into Btrfs. The T7 formated flawlessly, and the storage shows up completely on both my web panel and my web settings.

I had to restart my Pi4 a few times, and each time I shot some items to my SSD for testing. I noticed it was pretty slow on boot, but after a few hours it seemed to read and write almost as fast as my previous SSD. I supposed, over time, it will adjust to the Pi4. My previous drive was a Verbatim USB SSD, also 3.0. That thing got HOT. It was also made of aluminum on the outside, and I was afraid this T7 would be the same. So far so good; it remains much cooler than the Verbatim.

I knew right away that these would be my office headphones. I have a mechanical keyboard that I use at work, and the office I work in is semi-open. There's a *lot* of noise coming every-which-way. These are a much-needed accessory to my work productivity, as I'm easily distracted by things in my periphery, whether visually or auditory.

The presentation is great. The box is very high quality, reminiscent of the recent Samsung Galaxy device boxes. A smooth matte feel with gloss--weirdly pristine. The box slides out of the slipcover and you get the headphones already in the case. What I like is that they're folded, and there's even a little sheet underneath the phones that always reminds you how to put them back in. Also included is a 3.5mm cable in case you don't want to use Bluetooth, a charging cable, and an adapter. The case is nice, but as I keep mine at work I can't testify to its durability. There's a thin mesh net on the backside in case anyone needs to store one or two thin headphone accessory/-ies along. The accent colors are a nice light copper/rose gold color. I love that color; I'm glad it's getting more attention in recent years.

It didn't take long to charge the headphones, so they come with a little bit of juice. As soon as you turn them on, you get a soft beep along with a voice indicating they're turned on. Nice responsive feedback. Once I put them on I could hear the headphones working to drown out the sound; there was a thick veil of soundproofing that was draped over my ears as soon as the earpads touched them.

The first thing I did was listen to podcasts through the Pocket Casts app and .flac music through Poweramp v3. With podcasts, the difference was phenomenal. Listening to "Wait, wait... Don't tell me!" made me feel as though I were in the audience. The music was fantastic...until I tried on my other headphones which I use for music only.
I thought the bass might've been too strong with the Sony headphones, and I was right. After using even "cheaper" headphones like the Audio-Technica M50x, I could tell the Sony had too much bass. I'm not sure if that's partly because of the noise-canceling technology or what, but the bass can be toned down a bit, methinks.

I then proceeded to download the supplementary app to get the fullest suite of attributes the headphones can get. The app works well, and I didn't experience any hiccups while actually using the app. The only hiccup was when I was trying to download the update. It took *forever*. Almost an hour and it was just halfway through. I decided to bring them to work the next day and let the app sit there while updating. Thankfully, it remembers the progress, even though the app kept crashing during the update process.

There are some optimization tweaks in the app, some sound profiles to let you configure the noise cancelation level (yes, level; the noise cancelation is pure software; you can set it to drown out the most noise as possible or have no noise cancellation at all), and even a little snippet of what is currently playing through the headphones. A simple UI with all the features you need.

The first few days I used it I was active, and I kept noticing that my ears sometimes would pop depending on whether I sat down or arose quickly. Another weird thing is that when I take the headphones off, my ears sometimes need a minute or two to adjust. There's so much noise in the world! After taking the headphones off I can hear HVAC activity and my loud work neighbor who's otherwise not that loud.

I had some headphones with some touch controls before and always found them tacky. I used them once when I first got them and never again. But with these headphones, I'm always using the tap gesture to play/pause and the swipe gesture to raise or lower the volume. There are also swipe gestures to skip or go back a track, but since I never do that anyway I never use those gestures. You have to be careful with the tap; when it works, it works. But the whole surface isn't the active portion and you have to hit it right in the center. Sometimes I'm hitting my finger against my ears trying to find the spot and hurting myself in the process. I tested the gesture where you put your entire palm on the cup to turn off the noise canceling feature and let the mic allow incoming conversation, but not after the third try. I could hear the other people just fine, but I found the right hand over my ear felt awkward, and one person didn't realize I could even hear them. Putting your hand over your headphones isn't a gesture people immediately see as you paying attention to them.

The headphones are extremely lightweight and comfortable to use; I left them on for about two hours once before having to take them off. I actually was surprised with how light they were; when I got the Amazon box I didn't believe it was my headphones. It was much lighter than expected.

For my first noise-canceling headphones I'm pleased. The sound balance can be better (less bass), but they make for fantastic headphones to use at work. I wasn't sure what I was expecting with noise-canceling technology. I thought it would drown out all noises, but you still can hear the occasional mutter; it just won't be distinct.

Oh, forgot to mention the battery life. I charged it only once and have been using it for a week, at about an hour or two each day. Still going well. If you press the power button once it will tell you the battery level. AFter the initial update the voice indicator might give the wrong battery level (it did for me), but give it about ten or fifteen minutes to adjust and it will go back to normal.

review_title: Swell briefcase. Works fine with my 13" MBP.
review_text:
Now that I'm transitioning to a more corporate world I figured it's about time I get a more "professional"-looking carrying satchel than my Osprey backpack. The only laptops I possess range around thirteen inches, as I find carrying anything heavier than that is far too large to be considered portable.

This briefcase has it all. There are pockets galore; at times I feel there are too many as I keep unzipping the wrong pocket or can't remember in which pocket I put something, so I wish the tags would've been different somehow. Maybe have some lanyards on some or another.

But inside the pockets you get even more pockets and sashes to separate compartments. The material is sturdy and has held up just fine in this insane Chicago spring weather. We've had temperatures ranging from 40-80 in just two weeks, as well as rainy and dry weathers. Chicago, I tell ya!
My 2010 13" MBP fits fine in the main laptop sleeve without sliding around much, and I'm not able to feel much wait on my shoulder from carrying it around all day, along with a couple of books, a Hobonichi planner, and my pencil case.

The main flaw I will say this has is the shoulder strap. It's not easily adjustable, and I still haven't fully figured it out. There is a buckle in the middle on either side--one static, and the other adjustable. But the adjustable buckle doesn't allow the strap easy give, and so I can't for the life of me get it to a comfortable length.
The removable strap is sturdy otherwise.

The other issue is the clasp holding the two handles together. It's not long enough, so instead of closing it with one hand I'm having to use both hands to squeeze the handles together before being able to snap the button together.

All in all, it's a great briefcase usable even with 13" laptops, but the shoulder strap and the handle clasp need better, user-friendly improvements.

review_title: Extremely sturdy; threads could be tighter, though.
review_text:
Nice lanyard to have on the backpack. Perfect for charging most mobile devices as we transition to USB-C as the standard. The plug ends are inserted into a cap with a thin lanyard. That then gets screwed in so the plugs don't fall out.
I found that the thin lanyard attached to the cap was a bit too thin; not sure how it will be in the long run, but compared to the very thick strand at the bottom it seemed odd to have such a thin one at the top.
Also, I cannot get the screw to tighten all the way; there's always a bit of looseness at the end, and I'm afraid it will defeat the purpose of having such a rugged lanyard when the screw will come undone and the plugs pop out.

Great to have on a backpack, though. I just have it strapped to my backpack with the thicker lanyard.

review_title: Basic mount. Tilt is very minimal. No instructions included.
review_text:
Got this to mount a 42" Samsung TV onto our bedroom wall. It is very basic and doesn't require too much knowledge if you've mounted TVs before, but mine didn't come with instructions. I looked online and there are no available instructions, so I had to figure it out from similar mounts and reviews online. The only biggest problem I had was with the screws; I didn't know what width I needed to drill a pilot hole as many PDFs online had different numbers, but I found the right size and drilled away.
Unfortunately, the drill I have wasn't strong enough to drill these all way, but I was able to use a socket wrench to finish putting them in by hand.

The mount is decent, but, again, instructions would've been helpful. For instance, I couldn't tell if the spring-loaded bolts at the bottom of the mount, once the TV is hoisted up, were to be tightened after positioning the TV or left alone. I tried tightening them only to realize they were to be left alone. About five minutes wasted.
I tilting the mount more but really you get about a half-inch's worth of movement.

Otherwise, fine. Fantastic for the price, and more of a fixed mount if you need it.
