review_text:
I'm a burgeoning audiophile and I'm always eager to try new cans to add to my listening experience. A while back, say 2007 or so, I jumped into the deeper waters and decided to upgrade my stock Apple ear buds (why I didn't sooner is beyond me). I haven't looked back since, and continue to look forward this very day.

But do these headphones do my ears and music justice?

Right now my arsenal consists of some Sound Blasters I use for my computer and my trusty ol' Sennheisers which I've had since 2007 (the selfsame headphones with which I used to help me jump from Apple), along with Monoprice ear buds I keep at work. I'm not the most professional audiophile, but I sure as heck can tell some differences in quality, especially if the sound source is in FLAC.
Unfortunately, I'm not the most ecstatic about SMS Audio's STREET by 50, especially at the higher premium for Star Wars branding.

I've always been wary of celebrity-endorsed products; never trying Beats, I've been bombarded by them on the streets of Chicago by the candy-colored headbands on people's heads. I've always wondered about their integrity, until a fellow flesh-and-blood audiophile renounced them after she had used her ATH -M50s for some time. I took her word for it and never considered using Beats.
But me, being the Star Wars fanatic, had to try the SMS Audio. When they arrived I admit I was impressed by the fancy packaging. For $200, the headphones arrived looking like it.
They came in a slipcased box that was a little difficult to remove as the vacuum-sealed enclosure proved a tough fit, but they open up sweetly after that.

There are some nice manuals that come with, along with some neat little Star Wars stickers and papers. There's even a cleaning cloth and nice soft zippered case. The headphones came folded inside the case.
When I opened 'em up and took out the included removable cable and tried them on, I was a bit dumbfounded and how uncomfortable they felt around my head with such soft ear pads. I'm not sure if I need to break them in longer, but I've been using them steadily for a month and so far I haven't noticed a difference. My ears ache after just 20 minutes.

The sound was very disappointing at first, though I admit it did warm up (or down?) after a few weeks. But are they a large improvement over my $30 Sennheisers? A little, but not considerable. I can hear more background noise--that is, in the music--but there's not much balance as I have to turn up the volume to notice any huge improvement. There's a bit more bass than I'd like, but not enough to drown my ears in it.

I like the fact that the cable is detachable, but the ones they included feel a bit cheap and they tangle easily. I HATE the fact that they have the buttons, something which I've always hated since the iPhone came standard with them. But that they are removable altogether makes up for the buttons, as I'm able to change them out with custom, and higher quality, gold-plated cables.

The colors are fantastic; honestly, they were the reason I was drawn to them, but they look metallic in the press shots whereas, when you get them, the material is actually plastic, forcing the colors to be a lot lighter, more matte, and cheaper in feel. I'm all for matte, but I had hoped the headphone band was metallic; alas, it's plastic.

So that's my take on the cans. Take them or leave them. They're nice headphones, and I've gotten plenty of complements on them both from friends and at work, but at the steep price tag I can't recommend them, especially when you can get far superior headphones for much less (like the revered Audio-Technicas).

review_title: Five stars for the audio. The video: meh.
review_text:
Sorry for the lengthy review.

I love this sound bar. Five stars for the audio. No doubt about it.
I consider myself relatively gadget-savvy, but certainly not tech-savvy. I love gadgets, but I'm an idiot when it comes to sound and sound-related technology. I only recently stopped using ear buds altogether and switched to my Sennheisers as my primary listening `phones.

My family and I live on the third floor of a three-apartment house, and not once did I ever consider getting surround sound. I have the speakers for it, as they were hand-me-downs, but I don't want to set them up lest I receive the wrath of my neighbors. That, and I don't even have the connections necessary on my TV (my TV is two years old; the speakers are far older than that). I recently heard about sound bars (though the PS3 one that came out a while ago caught my eye before), and thought that might be a better fit for me.

I don't normally track Vine orders, as they usually get delivered on Tuesdays. But I was so excited about this one I kept looking on UPS's website, only to be disappointed to read that it had not been delivered on Tuesday; when I got home, my hopes were ultimately crushed when I found the "undelivered" sticky on my mailbox. What's one more day? I signed the note and left it for the UPS man.
When I finally got the package the next day, I realized why they needed a signature: the box was huge! And there's no outer box, so all that's delivered is the product in its factory packaging, as if you bought it from the store yourself. Everybody and they momma are going to know what you ordered. But, thankfully, I don't have to worry about theft in my neighborhood too much.
So when I unboxed it, I was surprised to see how little real estate the actual sound bar took. Initially, I was surprised to see how big the box was, as I didn't think the bar itself was too big. But then I realized the box was oversized to accommodate the subwoofer.

Instructions were easy enough, but the HDMI set-up was a pain. There's a disc with the manual, but I would prefer if LG's website lets you download it (as of this review, they still don't have it up). Out of three HDMI cables I had lying around (two from the same brand), only one worked. I have two Mediabridge cables, one six- and the other nine-feet, and a cheapo one which came with my Comcast DVR. Only the Mediabridge six-foot cable worked, for some odd reason, so that's the one currently connecting the sound bar.
Nevertheless, the Internet capabilities are going to be wasted on me, I'm assuming, as I already have services such as Netflix on my PS3, and I don't see myself switching to the sound bar any time soon.

review_title: Best Wear OS for true Android users, but not perfect
review_text:
I will avoid the facts that this watch is outdated at launch by its hardware (processor). That, coupled with retail and even discounted price also are out of step with the competition. These two big gripes aside. The watch is good and likely the best choice going into 2023 for pure Android Wear OS users (not looking at Apple or Tizen overlay users.)

Its not perfect and Pixel users will benefit the most when paired to this watch. Its lost most of the lag recent watches from other Wear OS brands. Has all the sensors the majority of buyers could want based on watch tech right now. It swipes, it plays well with the apps made for it. It gives you the info you ask of it. There are even a few nice 3rd part accessories now to avoid Google Gouging for proprietary bands. And there are few quirks I hope they iron out soon. Mainly, when the phone is in Bedtime Mode. Make the watch do it too, or add that Zen Mode feature to the watch also. It sucks to have animals tripping the security cameras outside dinging on my wrist and killing my sleep score. The snooze/do not disturb button on watch fails too easily and you have turn it on/off manually everytime.

As many claim, the battery sucks. Sort of. I can go up to 36+ hours on a slow day, and many others can too. It will depend on too many factors to list. But basically your popularity with notifications and thinking you need the screen always on are the biggest battery hurdles. Most can get use to touch to wake. And maybe only having text, phone, front door doorbell and one email be allowed to bother your watch with notifications. Do you really need to know what cousin Billy had at Dairy Queen when he posts the same pic/vid on Facebook, Instagram, Tic Toc and YouTube, etc. Find a nice balance of wrist information along with what sensors you need checking if you are still alive. You can start the day and track everything till the next morning when you charge it again while you shower and get the next day started. It charges quickly. And most other Wear OS watches have the same daily charge requirements. Nobody on Wear OS is winning on battery. Or Turn every setting all the way up and have a spare charger puck ready for a mid day juice. If you go that route. I suggest a quick release band to ease the removal of the watch.

So, its not up to the level or price of the Ultra Apple Watch. And if you don't care for Samsung. Your love for stock Android will eventually lead you back to this watch. Unless you forgo ECG sensors. The price will drop soon. Cases are minimizing the fragility of an ALL glass jelly bean design. But when comes to keeping your phone pocketed and yet still have info relayed in a useful way. Pixel Watch is the best current albeit not perfect solution for now.

Overall I think these are decent walkies. If you want basic push button to talk and small lightweight with adequate range. This is a decent choice. Choosing this model for the Secret Service earpiece can be hit and miss. Guess some earpieces can be just as bad as the black over the ear units the other companies use. In all but a library, the earpiece audio is too low to hear in outdoor conditions. ***see update***

The RT22 cost the same as other models with displays and buttons (thicker and heavier walkies) to control functions this model has to do with button combos, but it does talk to you as you change settings and channels. Sadly as with many other models I tried. VOX is near useless. VOX works as bad as any sub $100 walkie I've tried. It lags and maybe sends half the message at best. You won't know how good/bad VOX is for you till you try it yourself.

Get these for size, lightweight, basic, rechargeable walkie needs. Try to catch it on sale...if possible. I paid a fair amount.

Btw, my wife and I use these for trail rides on our e-bikes. The true two-way communication devices did not fit our non-helmet style and will cost substantially more.

***UPDATED***
Company did reach out to offer a refund because they thought I was unhappy. And only the earpiece was a bit of let down for me. They told me about another similar earpiece that seems to be working a bit better and now I can actually hear outdoors with the earpiece. It is still a Secret Service style, but somehow it is a bit louder. Maybe my original earpieces were faulty.

Let me be clear. I still paid the retail price, kept the walkies and did not take any money/refund for my review. The walkie has so far been a great trail ride walkie. I might have received a bad earpiece. The company seems to care about their ratings and customers use of their products. And we all need to keep what we buy if it works to avoid landfill waste. I just came back to add a star and let others know. Good walkie. And maybe consider one of Retevis's many other earpieces or handset mics. Some of their other walkies include better headsets.

review_title: Sheer Perfection! I Have Not One Negative Thing To Say About This Gorgeous Messenger Bag!
review_text:
In the instant I saw this vintage handmade leather messenger bag on the Amazon page, I knew I had to have it. I loved it...I loved everything about it. When it arrived, I realized the photos on the Amazon page hadn't done it justice. Because as much as I loved it in the photos, it was a whole different ballgame when I actually had the bag in my hands right in front of me and took a good, close look at it. Its simply exquisite. The bag is handcrafted. Everything about it is so precise and detailed. The leather is perfect all around. The stitching is incredibly even and strong. The bag itself is durable and sturdy, yet comfortable. The vintage design is is what attracted me to this bag in the first place and up close, in person, it didn't disappoint. The inside of the bag has 2 large pockets for the laptop as well as smaller pockets for cords, cell phone, pens. The bag is flexible, but NOT floppy and loose. The bag has 2 security straps to protect your laptop and both straps have very secure locks on them which provide exceptional protection. The bag comes with a removable shoulder strap and it is very secure. I prefer to carry my bag by the handle. That will likely change if/when I travel and need to keep my hands free to carry suitcases or my kids. lol. For now, I prefer the handle.

This laptop leather messenger bag is the third item I own made of buffalo leather. review_title: The perfect cord and charger wrangler (with NO LOGO!!)
review_text:
Like everyone else on the planet, I have a drawer full of miscellaneous chargers and cords that you have to poke like snakes to get to stay in the drawer so you can close it.. not to mention that fact that when you need a specific cord, you have to visually inspect the end of every one to find the one you need, only to pull out the whole lot as they have somehow entwined themselves completely into a ball of indiscernible mayhem.

• 23 x USB charging cords of varying lengths (from 6" to 6' long)
• 10 x USB charging bricks (Samsung and Motorola brands.. AKA "the fat boys")
• and a couple of SanDisk microSD cards and adapters

All in all, a great solution, and at a very reasonable price, for organizing your cord chaos.

review_title: USPS LLV Comparison: OontZ Angle 3 Plus vs Anker SoundCore
review_text:
First off, I am not an audiophile. This is a review from a simple person who wanted music at work.

I am a Rural Carrier for the United Stated Postal Service. I deliver mail in an LLV truck and these vehicles are basically mobile tin cans. Every panel rattles, making for quite an unpleasant environment, audio wise. I tried playing music directly off my phone, but alas my speakerphone is only so loud and is constantly drowned out by the LLV.

So, I researched Bluetooth speakers and, based on the reviews and popularity, recently purchased two:
-[[ASIN:B016XTADG2 Anker SoundCore Bluetooth Speaker with 24-Hour Playtime, 66-Foot Bluetooth Range & Built-in Mic, Dual-Driver Portable Wireless Speaker with Low Harmonic Distortion and Superior Sound - Black]]
-[[ASIN:B01LZV6TYQ OontZ Angle 3 PLUS Splashproof Bluetooth Speaker - Designed & Engineered by Cambridge SoundWorks for Richer Bass, HD Sound, and 30-Hour Playtime, 10W+ Power, Water Resistant, Portable Wireless Speaker]]

The Anker SoundCore is being returned while I am keeping the OontZ Angle 3 Plus and here is why.

I tested both speakers in my home at first. My very first impression, out of the box:
OontZ Angle 3 Plus - was nice to touch and just felt solid and very well built.
Anker SoundCore - just felt like a simple lightweight brick. It really didn't give the impression of longevity or durability.

The set-up guides were quite different from each other.
OontZ Angle 3 Plus - Extremely easy to read, follow and understand (remember, I am not a music nut lol. This was my first time ever using a Bluetooth speaker and was in completely uncharted territory.) It was all in English, and only English and the diagrams were detailed and made the entire set-up process seamless and carefree.
Anker SoundCore - This guide was very hard to follow. It is printed in darn near every language, in tiny print and the diagrams were quite small as well. I ultimately did get the speaker paired with my phone and figured out what buttons did what, but it took nearly 15 minutes to do so.

Bluetooth Pairing
With both speakers and my phone lined up on a table (well within the proximity specified in each set-up guide), both speakers paired, however:
OontZ Angle 3 Plus - MUCH faster in pairing (mere seconds!).
Anker SoundCore - took nearly two minutes to complete the pairing process.

Pause/Play Button
Since I dismount to deliver packages to a customer's door routinely on my route, I really need to have a simply way to pause my music. I really like how both speakers offer this function on directly on the units, saving me from having to handle my phone.
OontZ Angle 3 Plus - I barely press the Play/Pause button and the speaker immediately reacts. There is NO hesitation.
Anker SoundCore - I press the Play/Pause button and there is a delay of about 5 seconds.. just long enough to make me think I didn't press hard enough and reach to do it again only for the speaker to finally react.

Volume/Overall Playback Quality
OontZ Angle 3 Plus - Wow. Just wow. It is truly unbelievable to hear such full sound, and bass(!), coming from such a small unit. I found myself perfectly pleased with the output without ever reaching max volume on the speaker itself. So I am looking forward to how well it will work in my LLV during my first road test. As for now, I am thoroughly impressed!
Anker SoundCore - I maxed out the volume on my phone and the speaker and was just not impressed. If I could guess, I'd say the max output this speaker achieved was only about 25% more than my speakerphone alone (while the OontZ Angle 3 Plus blew it out of the water with close to double, if not more, output than my speakerphone alone).
I also noted some kind of distortion or interference type background sound with the Anker SoundCore at mid volume and above.

Speakerphone/Mic
I was able to answer an incoming phone call on both units as described in each set-up guide. The quality of in-call sound on each speaker differed:
OontZ Angle 3 Plus - My husband's (the caller) voice was crisp and clear, as if he was sitting talking right next to me. There was no distortion or feedback out of the speaker. Husband reported nothing but a clear voice on his phone.
Anker SoundCore - Husband's voice was clear, but echoed horribly. No matter what volume level I used. There was no distortion (I was expecting this given the distortion with the music playback) bu the continuous echoing is a major issue for me. Husband reported a slight "faded" type of echo on his phone.

Road Test (in my LLV)
OontZ Angle 3 Plus - The sound is amazing in the truck! Thinking I would need it, I maxed the volume on both the speaker and my phone then pressed play on my music. Well, I certainly don't need max volume. I reduced the volume on both the speaker and my phone and found a very happy medium output. This speaker performs perfectly in the loud, rattling setting of a USPS LLV.. even while bouncing down rural dirt two tracks and washboard gravel roads. I am extremely pleased with this tiny speaker.
Anker Soundcore - Even with maxed volume settings, I could not get this speaker to perform anywhere near as well as the OontZ Angle 3 Plus. It had volume and was loud enough to hear over the vehicle's own noise, however the distortion/interference mentioned earlier was still present and in the truck during the road test it had what I would describe as an echoing effect on the music, specifically the singers' voices. It just wasn't clear. (I hope that makes sense.)

Battery Life/Listen While Charging
OontZ Angle 3 Plus - So far, the battery life is impressive. After receiving it, I charged it overnight (as recommended). I then had it connected to my phone for about an hour of home testing. Turned it off and I next used it at work on a Saturday.. had it powered on and connected to my phone and actively playing music for about 5.5 hours. I then used it again on Monday (much longer and busier days in the USPS, FYI).. had it on, connected and active continuously for nearly 9 hours. I have yet to see the low battery light come on. I plan to see just how many days of work I can get out of a single charge.
Anker Soundcore - I have no information for this section on this speaker since I am returning it.

Exterior/Cleaning
At first, I had the OontZ Angle 3 Plus setting on the dashboard of the LLV. This didn't last more than two stops. Despite having the four rubber "feet", the speaker still slid around causing more of a distraction than I would like. I ended up setting it on top of my personal bag, in a bin by my feet with the speaker facing up. This move really helped my piece of mind, knowing it will not go anywhere. This speaker has a soft rubber exterior. It is quite nice and feels luxurious, however... this exterior attracts all dust particles within 50 feet! USPS LLVs are *not* known for being the cleanest and even though I moved the speaker from the dust-ridden dashboard to a bin, it was still slathered with dust and dirt by the end of my route. I figured it was a fair trade, sacrificing the appearance for the gain of having decent music. But.. I got home and went to clean it. I will tell you, my expectations of this working were very low. I didn't think the dust would come off that supple rubber. But with a wet paper towel and a few slow wipes, it did. So, it can be cleaned up!

Case
I did purchase the case for this speaker ([[ASIN:B01NBDY6VP [Official] OontZ Angle 3 Plus Bluetooth Portable Speaker Carry Case, Neoprene with Aluminum Carabiner, reinforced zipper, by Cambridge SoundWorks [NOT FOR OontZ Angle 3]]]). I was mainly wanting a safe way to transport and store the speaker, but after reading the other reviews I was hoping I would be able to keep it clean in the case and still enjoy my music on my route. I received the case and used it yesterday. The case is extremely nice and I appreciate the interior mesh pocket. I have no need for it now, but I'm sure it will come in handy if I ever take this speaker on vacation and need to take the charging cables along. As for playback while in the case? Yeah, it was terribly muffled. It didn't work for me as it apparently has for others. Yet, the case itself is exactly what I was wanting for taking it to and from work. It is not as thickly padded as I would have expected, however it does protect the speaker.

Overall, for my specific purpose and intended use for a Bluetooth speaker, the Anker SoundCore simply won't cut it. However, it is still a nice speaker and will perhaps fit your needs perfectly. After all, most people don't drive LLVs and have the same high demands that go along with that. For me, the OontZ Angle 3 Plus is what I'll be bopping down the road to, mailbox to mailbox.

Happy hunting! Hope this review helps you out!

review_text: My husband and I bought two sets of these three years ago from Circuit City during their going out of business sale. We both travel quite a bit and were in need of decent headphones for longer flights (let's face it, the ear buds provided by the airlines just don't cut it). My husband accidentally left his set, in their pouch, in the seat back pocket on a flight last year and was in need of a replacement set for our trip to Germany last week. I was amazed by the price when I came onto Amazon to check - $29.99 was a steal compared to the $80 we spent a few years back! This headset is not the top of the line, but it is effective in canceling out the low aircraft drawl while in-flight. (They are also quite nice when you need to drown out the crying child in 23F. ;)) The battery life is remarkable. I have had to change the battery on my set only twice in the three years I've owned it. The only complaint that I have, which results in the four star rating instead of five, is that after wearing the set for a few hours (i.e., Amsterdam to Houston, TX), my ears begin to ache on the outside. It is almost like the headset becomes to tight over longer periods of time. I tend not to wear earrings on airplanes, so I can rule out the possibility of pinching. Other than that slight achy feeling, these are wonderful for the casual traveler and the price simply cannot be beat!

review_text:
Do not buy this if you're looking for the fastest tablet. That's not what it is, though it's by no means slow. It will take a lot more abuse than the fastest tablets available for the same price. You can stand outside in the rain or snow and use the touchscreen when it's wet. You can drop it in the mud, pick it up, wipe it off, and keep using it. I wouldn't take it scuba diving though. I will take it off-roading. This one has enough storage to preload maps for off-road hiking/biking/riding/driving for when there's no signal at all.

I've seen several questions about whether this works with Verizon, and several people answer that it doesn't. Those people are wrong. The Enterprise/LTE/4G/WiFi version does work with Verizon. It should work with others. Find this model number (SM-T577UZKGN14) on the Samsung site to check. Samsung knows. Those other people don't.

This is the third tablet I've used my Verizon SIM card in. The first was a tablet I bought through Verizon. The second was a TabActive2, and now I'm using the same SIM card in this TabActive3. This does not apply to the WiFi-only version. Don't confuse the two.

I pulled the SIM card out of the TabActive2, inserted it in the TabActive3, restarted the device as requested, and a few minutes later the line was active on the new device. I ignored Verizon's emailed instructions, because they don't appear to apply to swapping a current SIM card into a new device. I even restored a Google backup from the 2 to the 3 and saved a lot of time installing apps.

So, why this tablet? It's rugged. It's Samsung. I really like having an 8" tablet. It works with Verizon.

Why 4G/LTE? It's not 5G. I drive a truck through at least 5 states on a regular basis, and in some areas the signal constantly switches between 4G and 5G and the data connection is interrupted. When I can't access online banking, credit cards, and apps relating to business with my 5G phone, I often can with a 4G tablet. I have unlimited data on a second plan for only $10/mth, since I already have a smartphone plan. No hotspot/WiFi needed.

Why upgrade? My TabActive2 only had 16GB of internal storage. The TabActive3 I bought has 128GB. The TabActive3 has DEX. The TabActive2 didn't. I didn't manage to hurt the 2, and the 3 is physically very similar. The 3 has a faster CPU, and a faster GPU.

From the beginning, everything about the TabActive2 as a usable tablet simply wasn't enough. It wasn't fast enough. It didn't have enough storage. But it was rugged. It still is. This is the first time I've upgraded when the old tablet still worked as well as it did when I bought it. It appears that the TabActive3 is just as rugged.

Con: The biggest downside to these is that there's no external charger that I can find for the replaceable battery. At least I can't find one. Maybe one exists. I have no evidence of that. It is possible to buy another compatible battery, but I can't find any way to charge said battery other than to charge it in the tablet, and it's a pain to get to, because of the lengths Samsung went to to seal the battery compartment. The battery life is substantial, partly due to the less-than-premium performance, but it would really be nice to be able to easily carry a fully-charged spare.

review_title: Great watch, much better than my old "smart" watch
review_text:
I got Moto 360 several years ago when smart watches first came out and it was nice, but annoying. It was tied into everything and kept giving me alerts and so eventually I got tired of it. My wife also had a first generation Samsung Gear watch and that was about the same as the Moto.
Well, fast forward a few years and now my wife, daughter, son and daughter-in-law all have newer smart watches (Apple Watches and Fitbit) and they all love them. It was time to get a new phone, so I got a Samsung S20 FE and then decided to get the Samsung watch. I saw on the reviews that it really works well with Samsung phones and so I decided to get the Watch 3. I was looking at the Watch 2, which had a few less features and then I found the Watch 3 in the 41mm size and then found a refurbished one so I ended up paying about the same for the Watch 3 as I would have for the Watch 2.
I'm very impressed with the watch and really love it. I didn't get the one with a cell phone, it just connects to my phone with bluetooth and/or wifi, but it's really amazing. I get my messages, and can turn off the ones that I don't want and then I also get all the health apps. So, now it tells me to get off my chair and walk around and does EKG and stress tesing and Oxygen levels..
I was concerned that the 41 mm might be too small, but it is a great size for me as you can see from the pic. I have had a Citizen Echo Drive for more than 10 years and it is a little larger, but I like the size of the Watch 3 better.
If you are thinking about getting a watch, this one is a good deal right now and I believe it does work best if you use it with a Samsung phone.

review_title: Minor complaints, but generally a decent buy
review_text: I’m not a DIY kind of guy, so I went with the cheapest, simplest mount I could find. It’s okay, but be prepared for some minor adjustments. The Pros: price. It’s much less expensive than most of the others. It’s also quite minimalist - no thick bezels. It’s made of a flexible silicone material - that’s both a pro and a con - the pro - it’s soft on your tablet - no scratches. It’s also somewhat flexible - I installed mine vertically in a tight space and there’s no room to slide the tablet in from the side. They're very comfortable - I wear them for hours at a time on a daily basis. I don't get the uneven cord length, but it really isn't a big deal. Headphones are like operating systems - there is no such thing as one size fits all. Get the ones that work for you (and your audio device!) and don't start a holy war with someone who prefers something different.

I'm not an audio expert by any means, but I know what I like and I have owned many, many pairs of headphones in the past. Noise-cancelling, non-noise-cancelling, earbuds, headphones, in-ear, out-of-ear, surround-ear, you name it. It seems like headphones and headsets are kind of an obsession of mine.

I use larger headhpones such as these Sennheisers primarily for playing video games on my computer after my toddler has gone to bed, and occasionally for listening to music (also on one of my computers). (When it comes to my iPod, I generally use something smaller and more portable, such as earbuds.)

When I took the HD201 headphones out of the box, I was first amazed at light they are. They seem to weigh almost nothing, though they don't feel flimsy by any means. I tried them on, and they were immediately very comfortable. They surrounded my ears comfortably, and the adjustable length on each side allowed for a perfect fit. I also noticed that the cord on these is nice and long, which is a plus. So far, so good. So I plugged them in for the real test.

WOW.

These sound GREAT! It's really kind of amazing to me that Amazon can offer these for under $20. I read the other reviews and paid attention when some reviewers said that they weren't loud enough, or sounded funny on "s" sounds. I did not find that to be the case for me. They sound just fine on all types of sounds and music, at various levels, and the volume is not a problem.

Pros: light-weight, comfortable, great sound, amazing price
Cons: too big for my taste to travel with, since they don't fold

I kind of wish they had an attached microphone, because then I'd never need another headset for gaming! However, for listening only, these are top-notch and I was very pleasantly surprised by the terrific quality at such a low price.

review_text:
Most of the places I have lived have been reasonably safe, so I have never felt any pressing need to add a camera security system to my home. I already have an alarm system, which is useful, but no camera system. I decided that it would be good to be able to see people at the main entrances to my home/property and this convinced me to add the Arlo Ultra - 4K UHD Wire-Free Security 2 Camera System to my house.

Setting this security system up is simple enough. You have to mount the included 2 cameras and it doesn’t take much time to complete this step. I placed one of them by my front door and the other one just outside my garage, facing the driveway. The gated entrance to my backyard is right there, and I usually leave my car in the driveway and not the garage, so this seemed like a good place.

There are many things to like about this security camera system, like the wide angle of view that is good for seeing from my backyard gate to the end of my driveway. You can even speak back and forth with someone at your front door and this can prove useful when you want to avoid talking directly, face to face, with solicitors.

With the image quality, although it isn’t as sharp as I expected, it seems sufficient to me. I haven’t experienced any intruders thus far- knock on wood- so I haven’t necessarily needed to get crystal clear details. One limitation I have is that I haven’t owned a camera security system before. This is a first for me, so I don’t have any point of comparison. Still, the picture quality seems good. And I like the notification system. Any motion detection is set up to record, so you can see what is going on and you know quickly.

The app itself is user- friendly enough but one thing to keep in mind is that the Arlo Smart Servive and cloud recording are free for only the first year. After that, you have to pay for a subscription. I will wait to see if the system is worth my while, then decide whether to subscribe. A year of free usage time should be sufficient to make the call.

Security is important and the Arlo Ultra - 4K UHD Wire-Free Security 2 Camera System is a good way to keep safe. Two cameras are definitely better than one because I am able to secure the two areas of my property where an unwanted individual is most likely to show up. I find the app and picture quality good and the system as a whole has enough positive points to recommend.

In the age of electronics, we all need more ways to plug ourselves in and manufacturers know this. They have responded by added usb ports and regular outlets to everyday appliances and this added convenience was enough to convince me to get the Seealle Bedside Desk Lamp with USB Fast Charging Port and Outlets Power Strip.

This lamp requires a small amount of assembly out of the box. The assembly is simple, but it takes longer than it should due to the way they pack everything into the box. I know they do this to require as little space and as small of a box as possible, but the way the shade is inverted with the base stuck inside it takes effort to get loose. I was extra careful and avoided damage, but many people will not be so lucky.

Once assembled, you just need to screw in a light bulb, screw the shade in place, and set the lamp on your desired table. My wife needed a night light for evening book reading, so I placed the lamp on her night stand. She likes having two places to plug in her phone, and the added light is nice for reading. There is a master switch on the cord and this provides another way to turn everything on and off, including the outlets. Another switch on the side of the base also controls the outlet. This is why, when you plug something in, you need to check to make sure it is charging. If it isn’t, then there is a good chance that one of the switches is in the off position. The light can be turned on/off using either the switch on the cord or by pulling the vertical, hanging metal cord underneath the light bulb.

This small light looks good on a night stand, but it is slightly smaller than expected. It also seems rather delicate and due to the darkness of the shade, it may not produce the level of light you need. I find it fine as a bedroom nightlight because we don’t want it to be bright in this type of setting anyway, but other people might find that the shade makes everything too dark.

It’s always good to have extra outlets and lamps with added outlets are commonplace nowadays as manufacturers answer customer needs. I like that this light has two added outlets, but the lamp is small and I still cannot get over the effort it took to dislodge the inverted shade from the base when I pulled the lamp out of the box for the first time. So, when all factors are taken into account, this lamp rates as average overall.

review_title: Much More than Your Standard Power Strip
review_text:
Electronics have become a regular part of life. There is really no sense in resisting- electronics are here to stay and most would agree, even if they have slight reservations, that electronics have improved our lives overall. These electronic devices need to be continuously recharged and an excellent tool for the job is this Kasa Smart Wifi Power Strip.

This power strip is intended to charge lots of electronics at once. It has six standard outlets and three USB outlets. That means you can charge up to nine devices at once, making this a very useful and popular item to take with you at your next conference. You will find that people around you will ask to plug themselves in and you will have no trouble obliging. It has surge protection, too, so that your electronics stay safe.

What sets this power strip apart, however, is its high tech personality. It can be controlled remotely using the Kasa app and you can see exactly how much power each item is using, then shut off individual outlets if you like, all from the app! And if you have Google Assistant, Alexa, or Microsoft Cortana, you can use voice commands to control the outlets. That means being able to turn on and off, say, a light that is plugged into the strip with a simple utterance. It’s a geek’s power strip dream come true. I plan to use it on my holiday lights when the season comes around- it will be much easier then climbing behind the tree to manually turn the lights on and off.

Kasa Smart Wifi Power Strip is a heavy- duty power strip that seems like it was made to last. The plug on the strip does require a three prong outlet to plug it in, so make sure you can accommodate before you buy. It has all of the things you would want in an app controlled, voice activated power strip and it receives my highest recommendation.

review_title: Good Protective Cover and Stand for your Apple iPad2
review_text:
The Targus VuScape Protective cover and stand is a pretty good, helpful aid for those who own an Apple Ipad2. It features a thin, lightweight design that is meant to hold the iPad2 snugly in place while you work.

Having a stand for your iPad is certainly a good idea and I like that this stand can be used to position your iPad in different ways. There are multiple grooves so that you can display your iPad at different angles. The cover can also be folded back completely, allowing the consumer to hold the iPad in the hands without the stand.

This protective cover/stand does have some nice features to offer, but after using it for a while, it is more than apparent that the stand is not perfect. Probably the greatest issue is that the stand isn't as sturdy as I would prefer. If you use the stand on a solid, flat surface, you shouldn't have too many problems, but place it on other surfaces and it tends to bend just a little bit. The slightest bend will cause the grooves to give way just a little, and the iPad will no longer be securely held in place.

I generally like the thin, lightweight design of this stand, but the thinness possibly goes a tad far. If the manufacturer had made this stand just a little bit thicker, it would be stronger and more likely to hold the iPad in place without any problems. I suppose this is the trade- off one must make when selecting a stand such as this. Lightweight is nice, especially for something like an iPad, but lightweight means the stand is lacking in strength.

All in all, this is a good stand and certainly worth considering, but not a deluxe stand like I expected. Again, as long as you are willing to sacrifice sturdiness for lightweight design, you should be fine. And try to use only on the flattest surfaces for the best results. Follow these guidelines and you should find yourself reasonably happy with this protective cover and stand from Targus.

I use it about once a month for a week at a time when I go RV camping to power my laptop. On its own, the laptop’s battery would only last at most 2 hours. But with the laptop plugged into the power bank, after I’ve used my laptop for 2-3 hours, the power bank charge has only dropped from 100% to as low as 77%--that extrapolates to 8-13 hours which is way more than I would usually need. So I no longer have to worry about my laptop running out of power. When I’m done, I plug the power bank into my RV’s 12V outlet and it recharges back to 100% in about 4-8 hours depending on how low its charge is. Between my monthly camping trips, when the power bank sits idle, it maintains its full charge without my having to recharge it.

review_text:
I have had several water resistant shower speakers and none, not one, my $600 Samsung Galaxy phone isn't. . . nothing is waterPROOF. It's a lie. Many advertisers and sellers like to claim waterproof status but what they mean is water RESISTANT. IPX7 means a device can survive immersion, up to 1 meter (3 ft 3 in) depth for up to 30 minutes. Let's also be clear here; those tests were with pure, likely purified, filtered water not highly chlorinated pool water. Not salty sea water. Not brackish lake/pond/river water. And also not water containing soaps, shampoos and conditioners. All that. . . stuff in every day water is going to reduce the effectiveness of the water resistance of any device.
So, I unbox this and it's light. Lighter than just about any speaker I've used. I look at the specs. . . 3 watts. THREE watts of power? Okay it's supposed to be primarily used in a small enclosed indoor space but it also says it's great for camping, hiking and general outdoors stuff (please, don't blast music when you're hiking, wear headphones, show some respect and restraint). I've never seen a non-novelty speaker that was less than 5 watts. It feels light and cheap and thin. The suction cups; they send two likely expecting one to fail. Neither worked. The best I could get with the cup wet with soapy water, alone, no speaker, stuck to a mirror for maybe five minutes. I can't get these suction cups to stick to my desk. No worries, my shower has a shelf. I turned off my oontz Angle 3 and connected this to my phone using Samsung Music as a player to take advantage of the Dolby Atmos and excellent sound (only PowerAmp sounded better of the half dozen players I tested and PowerAmp is a paid app only) quality it offers. I guess if you wanted noise in the shower this would work. Sound quality was about as bad as you'd expect. Distorted bass, harsh highs, muddy midrange. No EQ settings I tried made this sound good. It's just not worth it. You can for just a little more money get far better sounding water resistant speakers. You should enjoy the music in your shower or bath not suffer with it.

I had a Galaxy S4 for several years. It was suitable and did the job. . . mostly. I was having some battery issues and my phone wouldn't update past Android 4.4. I was running into apps that needed a newer version of Android. I could have bought something cheap but I decided to treat myself and found the blue Galaxy S9 on sale for a decent price. I have to say I'm loving this phone.
The 5.8" Quad HD+ Super AMOLED screen is GLORIOUS! I run this is high performance mode with the brightness cranked up. Games, movies, even YouTube and TikTok videos look amazing. The curved edge I worried might be distracting but honestly I only notice in a couple games.
Sound is really good for a cell phone it has stereo speakers. Volume is more than enough.
Performance from the Octa-Core processor and 4GB of ram have not struggled to run anything I've thrown at it.
The camera is great. Maybe struggling a little in very bright light with a light colored subject. Otherwise, night mode gives great low light results. Video shooting is very nice with great slow motion results and a nearly unique super slow-motion recording mode at a mind boggling 960 frames per second is a lot of fun to mess around with.
Battery life is good, I got most of a day is high performance mode and could easily extend it by cutting things back to save battery.
The fingerprint sensor is quick to unlock and easy to use. A trick I found online to improve performance of the fingerprint sensor is to register the same finger more than once. It really works like a charm.
The look is sleek and sophisticated though I'm protecting that glass body with a nice Otterbox Symmetry case. The only real minor negative to the whole thing is this weighs more and is larger than my S4, a little hard on my hands and pocket but really, it's worth it.
I can't express how happy I am with this phone. I'm even buying props and things to use in creative videos and photo shoots.

I like the size. It's small enough that I was able to put it on the far side of the mirror and I really have to crane my neck to see the body. That being said I didn't pull the trim and conceal the cable so that runs down almost in the center of the car. But after a few weeks I completely stopped noticing it. The screen shuts down to be less of a distraction and the status indicator lights aren't bright enough to be annoying, even at night. Installation was fairly easy. Hardest part for me was getting the static disc that goes on the windshield and is what the mount glues to (this is done so you're not putting super strong glue directly on the glass) off its backing paper. I ended up needing an Xacto knife to get it free. Clean the glass then the clear plastic disk applies to the glass with static cling. The mount sticks to this and the camera easily attaches to the ball socket and can be swiveled into optimal position before being tightened down.
There are many settings you can use to configure your camera, I suggest going over them carefully and making the changes you want before mounting the camera. It's small and the buttons are fiddly. Some options include recording audio or not (I've got a foul mouth and tend to sing horribly off key so I turned my audio off), video resolution I set it to highest for best possible details, clip recording length; the camera will film for X number of minutes before saving a clip and starting the next (once the memory card is full the oldest video is deleted to make room for new video) I have mine set to 3 minute intervals. There's a G force sensitivity setting that once triggered (by impact or even extreme braking) it locks the current recording so it can't be deleted, recommended is medium to avoid over sensitivity. Night recording can be set to color or black and white. It does a good job with color in most situations. There's a ton of other options so make sure you explore and see what there is you may want to change. I'm quite happy with this unit and feel safer knowing it has my back. . . by watching out the front.

Cheaply made feels like it will easily break. I do like the grey and blue color. Cable is proprietary, would using a micro-USB plug to charge instead of an old style round plug-jack add that much to the cost? With a universal cable for power I could use my 10' cable and put the fan nearly anywhere without worrying about wasting batteries. I'd only use batteries during a power outage. I can still use one of my large battery packs but I honestly find it ridiculous not to use a standardized cable.
The fan had two speeds, I guess we didn't need the option of three. On low it moves a fair amount of air and is nearly silent. On high, with no batteries inside, it tends to creep across the desk. Use care or it will end up on the floor. It's somewhat noisier on high but surprisingly more quiet than similar portable desk fans. It moves quite a bit of air on high.
Pros: USB powerable. Quiet. Can be run off battery packs. Moves air well.
Cons: Cheap, thin plastic, proprietary cord. 'Walks' across desk on high.
I honestly don't have much faith in the hinge for adjusting air direction. The high/low/off switch. Or the very thin power cable lasting a year but we're heading into hurricane season so an extra battery powered fan isn't a bad thing to have around. I'll update the review should durability become an issue.

review_title: So Far So Good. Decent Tablet For the Money.
review_text:
This tablet was purchased to replace my 85 year old mother's Big Lots special that she used for years and which was starting to have more problems than it was worth. The biggest problem my mother had was adjusting to the wide-screen 16:9 format of the Fire tablet compared to the old fashioned 4:3 format of her old tablet. This also had a faster processor with two more cores and four more megs of ram augmented by an 8gb memory card to expand storage. The blue color is quite attractive. The tablet so far runs everything she wants and I've even taught her to use the appstore to download her favorite games. The colors are sharp and clear. Video is smooth and while we watched only one half hour show so far there was no pausing or buffering.
I think the only thing I honestly dislike and it's my fault for not seeing it when this was a Prime Day special. I can forgive the tablet going out of stock and not being alerted to that fact when we placed the order. What I find somewhat insulting is this is the ONLY Fire tabled that comes with a limited 90 day warranty while every other Fire tablet has a minimum of one year warranty. I think there's something wrong with that. I probably would have bought this anyhow. My mom can't stand the weight of my 10" tablet (an ounce heavier than the 10" Fire) and the 8" was (and still is) available in one configuration (color, memory, special offers, etc.) which wasn't attractive and appeared to be fairly heavy.
So far so good. The tablet is functioning properly with a couple glitches here and there but every touch screen tablet and computer has similar issues. Other than what should have been a year warranty like every other Fire, Kindle, TV stick/device and Echo/tap has. That's just wrong and unfair to people buying a specific size of tablet.

The zippers operate smoothly and feel sturdy. The shoulder strap has an okay pad, it's better than nothing. The strap hardware is hard plastic and somewhat cheap feeling. The inner material is a bit thin and chintzy feeling but it will keep papers and your laptop separated well enough. I have two portable hard drives in a soft case and two USB cables in the outer pocket and there's plenty of room with the laptop inside. This is more than enough for what I need and the price can't be beat for what you get.

review_text: So far so good. I've had this laptop for just about a month now and it's done everything I expected of it. I'm not a gamer. I needed a machine to maintain my ebook collection, edit and manage my photography as well as general email and web browsing. As another reviewer has mentioned the keyboard is a bit flimsy feeling but I'm getting used to typing lighter and that seems to work. Everything on the laptop works the USB 3.0 port is screaming fast. The memory card reader reads the cards from three of my cameras. The touch screen is very responsive. The only thing I found lacking was no support for playing DVD movies. When I contacted Asus about it they first pointed me towards an uninstalled CD/DVD authoring utility that isn't installed but was put on the drive. When asked again about playing DVD movies they shrugged and suggested I go download something. I'm quite happy with my choice and for the money this does everything I really need.

review_text:
This is just an adequate cover for the Kindle PaperWhite. I'm not really fond of the pebbled leather texture and would much have preferred a smooth leather cover. Though the pebbling does give a bit of texture to aid in holding onto the thing.

The magnetic clasp does an okay job of turning the Kindle on and off with only occasional flubs which require you to open and close it again or push the power button. I've painted the clasp on mine black to match the case as I really didn't care for the silver color that it comes as.

The case holds the Kindle INCREDIBLY tight. I've taken my PaperWhite out of the case twice since I received it and both times I was scared to death I was going to damage the Kindle getting it out of the case. So, yeah, it securely holds onto your Kindle... with a death grip.

The rubber edges provide adequate protection against bumps and bangs and the back of the case is rock hard.

The cover itself is where this fails to be a four or five star item. It's flimsy. You can easily press on the cover and make it tap on the screen. It should have been made as stiff as the material on the back of the case. With the way the hinge is made and the case is put together a very stiff cover would have had little impact on holding and reading your Kindle but would have offered much better protection to the most easily damaged part of any Kindle, the screen.

The opening at the bottom provides easy access to the power button and micro-USB connector.

I'm going to keep mine, I'm very careful with my devices so I'm not too worried about damaging the screen but if you toss your Kindle in your purse or backpack you might want to think twice about which cover to get to protect your Kindle.

review_text:
This is a reasonably attractive leather case. About a third of the cover on the spine side has a pebbled texture while the rest of the cover is smooth.

The Good:
I really like Belkin's four corner mounting system. It's very secure and doesn't interfere at all with using the tablet.

The inner material is a soft micro-fiber that's gentle on your screen.

It doesn't add a lot of weight to an already heavy tablet.

There are a plethora of positions the tablet can be stood in.
But...(see below)

A stylus loop is included.

The Not-So Good:
If mounted in the case so you can use the rear camera through the camera cut-out all the controls as well as the 3.5mm headphone jack are exposed.

This also means that to charge your tablet you have to leave the cover open or pull your tablet out and mount it backwards to access the charging port and protect the screen at the same time.

The front cover has 20 very shallow grooves pressed into the micro-fiber material of the lining. These catch the bottom edge of the back cover and hold it in place for viewing. These actually hold the tablet in place reasonably well but because of the soft folding 'hinge' design the table is very bouncy at any angle. Good for viewing not so good for typing or playing games.

The case material is thin, 4mm on the front cover and thicker on the back because the stand system. There's also a grooved 'hinge' as part of the front cover which lets the cover flex. This reduces the protection already marginal case material can provide for the screen.

Because of the Cinema design the front cover can't be folded over flat against the back for comfortable use while off a table.

The elasticized strap that holds the cover closed is flimsy and will certainly stretch out over time.

Cover 'creep' happens very easily on this model. When strapped closed the cover can, because it's 'hinged', slide up exposing the screen.

There's a notch cut into the back cover that allows you to flip the cover around and stand the tablet up at a high angle. This position is very unstable and I would never use it.

I wouldn't recommend this cover. It just doesn't offer enough protection for an expensive tablet.

review_text:
Horribly Uncomfortable.

What's the one thing that makes a good neck strap comfortable for long term wearing? Padding. What's the one thing this strap is completely lacking? Padding!

The part of the strap that's supposed to go around your neck is a two inch wide very rough textured bit of nylon webbing. Seat belts are softer than this material. The first time I tried the Joby UltraFit Sling Strap I carried my Kodak Z990 around for about an hour and it was so uncomfortable. Who designs a neck strap with NO padding?

This strap attaches to your camera via the ¼" tripod screw mount on the bottom of the camera. It's odd that your camera hangs upside down and I don't like the single point of failure mounting. Also, because of the way it's designed it puts angular force on the mounting threads when hanging and even more when releasing or engaging the quick release latch. Since the threads in my Kodak are plastic I have even more dislike for this mounting system. Additionally, you have to dismount your strap any time you want to use a tripod or monopod.

I found in the time I used this that the only time the (non) padded portion of the strap is on your neck is when the rig is retracted when you use the 'Speed Cinch' to bring the camera up for shooting, at least on my extra large frame, the whole strap rotates forward and puts the even more uncomfortable thinner strap around your neck and the 'padded' section down on your chest.

To sum it up... it's uncomfortable. It completely lacks any padding. It has an odd mounting system that puts lever like force on your tripod socket and you have to take the strap off to use a tripod or monopod. The only good point to this system is that it is rather well made. Unfortunately it's just well made junk. I wouldn't recommend this to anyone for any application.

review_text:
What I Like:

* It's HUGE! You can fit so much gear in this thing it's crazy. I've got my AE-1 with a 300mm tele/zoom mounted on it and there's more than enough width for it. I have an extra AE-1 body a 55mm lens, two point and shoot digital cameras, a flash for the AE-1 bodies, assorted cables and the kitchen sink in this pack and I think there's still some room left over.
* The interior is orange which makes finding things in low light situations much easier than in a dark colored bag.
* It comes with a rain cover.
* The shoulder straps and backpack are seriously padded. Even fully loaded this thing is comfortable to carry.
* It has a chest strap and a waist belt.
* Did I mention it's huge?

What I Don't Like:
*The camera quick-access patch. While it almost certainly won't dump your camera out (it secures at the top with a plastic latch & velcro) the zippers 1) don't completely close off the opening. Dirt, bugs, moisture can easily get inside your backpack. 2) the zippers are attached to each other with a loop of nylon. This is going to catch on things (branches, chairs, doors, etc.) and open. Again, you probably won't lose your camera but if you don't notice the zippers opening and they open VERY easily, you're going to have even bigger openings for problems to get in. You can remedy this somewhat by putting the loop under the latch it still allows the zippers to slide down several inches.
* The rain cover comes in a small pouch kept in one of the back pockets. It could easily be lost.
* There are only two compression straps on the top 1/3'rd of the backpack. None lower 2/3'rds.
* The waist belt has no padding.
* There is a pocket for up to a 14" laptop but it's right up against the wearer's back.
* The bottom is heavy duty but it should have had feet/rubber runners so it doesn't sit flat on the floor, dirt, puddle, etc.

All in all it's an okay backpack but not a great one. There's room for everything you could want to carry but the quick-access patch... that just ruins the backpack for me. My camera gear is expensive and dear to me, I want to protect it the best I can. Having an opening that doesn't seal completely and can easily be opened wider by accident is a poor design.
This might work as carry on luggage or getting to and from the car or hotel but I would not recommend using this in the field.
I can honestly only give this three stars. I'd love to see them redesign the quick-access patch. That would greatly improve this backpack.

review_text:
I picked this up in a GoldBox sale from Amazon after I became unhappy with the ultra cheap tripod I had been using. The difference in quality compared to the small difference in price is amazing. The ball head is smooth. The center shaft turns easily for panning when the head is locked. The amazingly adjustable legs are a delight. The lack of a center brace that many tripods have (and which initially worried me) means you can position your camera is SO many ways that a conventional braced tripod would not allow.

The camera mount has a safety lock. You cannot accidentally disconnect the camera from the tripod. You need to squeeze the release lever while swinging the mounting arm out of the way.

One word of warning. The center shaft can be reversed to place the head closer to the ground for macro photography etc. reversing the shaft is easy, you remove the counter-weight hook and slide the shaft out. Reversing this operation however can be time consuming. There are plastic tabs that ring the opening that go one way they're a bit hard to push out of the way to return the shaft to normal operating position.

The ball head is also removable. With the correct adapter you can fit most other tripod heads to this base.

In conclusion: You just cannot go wrong with this tripod. From entry level photographers to serious hobbyists this will suit your needs for many years.

review_text:
The Tivax 3.5-Inch Digital TV is also a multimedia device supporting multiple image, video and audio formats. Audio through the unit's single speaker is a bit tinny and slightly underpowered. At full or nearly full volume it's not all that loud. The unit does have a headphone jack and the addition of a set of decent buds or headphones will improve audio quality quite a bit although there are no bass or treble controls. It comes with a clear plastic screen protector and be warned, if you remove it getting it to lay perfectly flat again is nearly impossible.

Along with the headphone connector the TV also has a single Micro-SD memory card slot. I purchased a 2-GIG card to test this device with. I do not know, and the manual does not say, if the TV supports the newer, larger SDHC style cards. The device has NO user accessible internal memory.

All input and control are accomplished via two buttons on the face and a four way directional button set. The buttons are stiff and I found, with my thick fingers, that manipulating the directional arrow buttons was a bit hard to do with accuracy.

My unit, which is white as opposed to the stated black, arrived with a USB cable (which I have not used) an AC adapter/charger, an external antenna and a peg/tab stand on a lanyard. I found attaching the lanyard to the unit (you'll likely lose the stand otherwise) to be a complete pain and required a bent pin to accomplish.

Television Reception:
The Tivax 3.5-Inch Digital TV has a built in rod antenna which feels very fragile and easy to bend. The antenna also has a swivel base so care must be exercised when pushing it back into the unit. The included external antenna has a nicely long cord so it can be positioned easily for optimal reception. For the sake of reference I live approximately 80 miles South East of Orlando Florida on the coast. Using the built-in antenna, indoors, upon initial setup the channel scan was unable to find any stations. Plugging the external antenna in resulted in around a dozen channels being found during the setup scan. The 320x240 LCD screen images are crisp and sharp. Colors are vibrant and clear and I was pleasantly surprised at the adjustability of the picture including brightness, contrast, tint and color mode. Moving the television while watching TV should be avoided as the picture will often freeze and breakup. I was quite happy to find that one of the stations I do get is a 24/7 local area weather channel. During Florida's frequent power outages due to severe weather and hurricanes this will be invaluable.

Video Playback:
I loaded over a GIG of video files onto my Micro-SD card to test the Tivax's ability to playback video files. I chose a mixed batch of AVI, MPG, WMV and MOV file formats. WMV files are not supported at all (oddly the unit DOES support WMA audio files, go figure) and the support for the other formats was hit or miss. Approximately 60% of the fifty or so video clips I've tried to play were supported, but the rest just returned an error. Those that did play did so quite well. Picture quality was good (dependant, of course, on the quality of the videos) as was the audio playback. Perhaps they'll release a firmware update for the unit to add further CODEC support.

Audio Playback:
As I previously mentioned, the system's speaker is quite tinny. Don't expect great quality sound from it. It's not horrible but it could be better. I tested several dozen MP3 files on my Tivax including low (80 kbps) and very high (320 kbps) bit rate files as well as variable-bit rate encoded files and it played all of them without a problem.

Image Playback/Slide show:
The Tivax 3.5-Inch Digital TV supports JPEG, PNG, GIF and BMP image formats. Images display crisp and clean with bright and true colors. Landscape oriented images display best and while you can rotate images that are portrait oriented there is a distinct quality loss during rotation. Images can be zoomed in on with multiple levels of zoom.
The slide show feature is nicely configurable. The delay between images can be set or turned off for manual page turning. The transition effect done while changing images also has many options. The Tivax will also play any MP3 files in the same location as the images as background music during the slide show. I actually couldn't find a way NOT to have this happen if the audio and video files were mixed together on the memory card although the volume can be set to zero this will surely use more battery power even with the volume down.
One feature which I liked, but was not mentioned in the manual, is the ability to set one of your own images as the startup `logo'.

Power:
The Tivax 3.5-Inch Digital TV comes with a built in Lithium Ion battery which they state can be recharged approximately 500 times.
I found that their claimed charge durations were quite accurate. Watching Digital TV with the volume set to around 75% I was twice able to watch for a bit more than three hours before the unit turned off. I loaded several hundred large image files onto the memory card and set the unit to running them as a slide show (silent) and was able to achieve just over six hours of playback before the battery died. MP3 playback resulted in similar results of around five and a half hours of continuous play.
When charging there are NO indicator lights showing that the unit is charging nor any way, short of turning it on, to tell if it has fully charged. There is also no on screen low battery warning. When my battery was depleted the unit simply shut itself off.

Finally:
This is a nice unit and far more than just a digital TV set. A padded case would be a nice option. I'm going to try some of the smartphone cases to see if any fit. I really don't want to scratch or damage the screen. The external antenna while mildly magnetic really needs to be weighted and/or have a clip attached to it as it is rather light and hard to keep in place.

Images can be zoomed in on with multiple levels of zoom. The slide show feature is nicely configurable. The delay between images can be set or turned off for manual page turning. The transition effect done while changing images also has many options. The Tivax will also play any MP3 files in the same location as the images as background music during the slide show. I actually couldn't find a way NOT to have this happen if the audio and video files were mixed together on the memory card although the volume can be set to zero this will surely use more battery power even with the volume down. One feature which I liked, but was not mentioned in the manual, is the ability to set one of your own images as the startup `logo'. Power: The Tivax 3.5-Inch Digital TV comes with a built in Lithium Ion battery which they state can be recharged approximately 500 times. I found that their claimed charge durations were quite accurate. Watching Digital TV with the volume set to around 75% I was twice able to watch for a bit more than three hours before the unit turned off. I loaded several hundred large image files onto the memory card and set the unit to running them as a slide show (silent) and was able to achieve just over six hours of playback before the battery died. MP3 playback resulted in similar results of around five and a half hours of continuous play. When charging there are NO indicator lights showing that the unit is charging nor any way, short of turning it on, to tell if it has fully charged. There is also no on screen low battery warning. When my battery was depleted the unit simply shut itself off. Finally: This is a nice unit and far more than just a digital TV set. A padded case would be a nice option. I'm going to try some of the smartphone cases to see if any fit. I really don't want to scratch or damage the screen. The external antenna while mildly magnetic really needs to be weighted and/or have a clip attached to it as it is rather light and hard to keep in place.

review_title: Went with a cheaper Brand to see if it worked and It does
review_text:
I decided to go cheap after seeing some online YouTube reviews because one of them compared a $3.99 antenna with a range of price point antennas and said it pulled in most of the stations with a few fuzzy channels. Couldn't see spending $50 on a Leaf or other models cause I tend to be cheap. If it didn't work I could always buy another.

I read that the limit for reception is 80 miles because of the curvature of the earth and Amazon features a lot of Antennas that claim 100-200 miles, which is impossible. Also impossible, 4-K. Free view stretches the 80 mile limit too., claiming 130 miles. New ATSC technology is supposed to be coming out that can extend ranges, etc., , but you can bet it won't be in the $50 and under price range.

I hung the Freeview near a window in our bedroom and it pulled in all the channels in our area including UHF, and most of them were crystal clear. The Freeview comes with an amplifier, which I think helps.

I don't like draping the cords along the wall, but I draped it above the bedrooms patio door and to a window.
It is sensitive to location and I found it didn't pull in behind the TV, when I wanted to see if I could hide it. .
Depending on where you need to put the antenna, you may have better or worse results than me, but what the heck. For $16 bucks you can't go too wrong.

My only suggestion: Offer it in white, please. All of these antennas seem to come in black. I don't want a black antenna hanging on a white or beige wall.

review_title: Good concept, not so good device
review_text:
I bought and installed the Pogoplug on my LAN for the purpose of sharing photos over the Internet.

Right out of the box I had misgivings. There is no documentation or technical specifications. That immediately raised serious questions in my mind about it being vulnerable to hacking or opening access to my computer and personal information. You have to attach it to your modem/router and allow it to go out on the Internet without knowing what it is doing. I decided to take it on faith that the company was legitimate and not going to install a backdoor into my system.

I attached a Seagate USB external hard drive as my main memory device. I have also used USB memory sticks for temporary storage. All are USB 2.0.

Initially I had issues with people accessing my files. The Web access used by outsiders does not show any indication of activity. If you have a couple of hundred photos like me, it can take a couple of minutes for anything to appear. I have also had people report 404 and other errors fairly frequently. My workaround was to create more folders to compartmentalize everything. They load quickly enough for people to see something happening and know that they are connected.

Once you get inside the folders, people see a filmstrip and a large image like they would see in Windows. It is a serviceable but not glamorous interface. It is also not customizable.

Once I established that people could access my photos over the Internet, the next step was to fill up the hard drive. To do so, my plan was to push the files over my 10/100 MBps LAN. The Pogoplug shows up as a drive, so all I have to do is drag-and-drop. The problem is that it is incredibly slow. I normally get about 30 kBps. That is dial-up modem slow.

This exposed the second big problem. Remember the total lack of documentation? I had no FAQ, troubleshooting guide, technical specifications or other information to go on. I had to contact technical support via the Pogoplug web site. The Web site is slow and not always working, but I did get to someone, and they gave me the obvious suggestions like turning everything off and back on, dismounting and remounting the drive, trying a different drive, etc. After several iterations, I still had a slow connection that was now unreliable, a bunch of tech talk gibberish on ports and processes to open and close, and a closed out support ticket.

Doing more research, this appears to be a known and frequent problem. It is a deal breaker for me. I am going to be looking for a replacement. As an interim solution, I will attach the USB HD directly and transfer my files on an as-needed basis. However, I am looking for an alternative now.

So, to summarize, the concept is great, the implementation is okay, but the tech support and the LAN connection are not good. If you are serious about file sharing, this is not the device for you.

review_title: *UPDATED REVIEW* Will not automatically pair, on-board microphone disables the mics in my phone, and charges phone VERY slowly
review_text:
*UPDATED REVIEW*

A seller replaced a different defective FM transmitter unit with this one for me (mine has the Kollea brand name on it, but this is the identical unit, private-labeled). This is a better product than what it replaced, but is not without it's flaws. I have three (*UPDATE: now four, and the fourth one is a deal-breaker--see below) complaints with this unit:

1) It will not automatically reconnect to my phone about 75% of the time. I have to manually shut Bluetooth off and turn it back on on the phone, sometimes a few times before it pairs successfully. This is a hassle--a PITA. Every time I get in the car, I have to go through this process--every time power is cut from the transmitter, actually, so if your passenger knocks it and it pops out of the 12V socket, it will have to be re-paired, which is supposed to happen automatically, but does not, and you then have to go through the process. Frustrating.

2) Charge output is only 1.0A. this is why I returned the first one--phone gives a "slow charging" warning when charging from this unit, regardless of what USB cable I use (I tried four different cables, all of which I know for certain can carry 2.1A).

3) Callers have occasionally complained they cannot hear me well when using this unit, and I occasionally (but not often) encounter FM interference. I believe Bluetooth itself is part of the problem, and anyone who has used a few Bluetooth headsets or units like this knows audio quality is terrible. Period. We just deal with it. Add to that the burden of having to transmit your signal via FM to a car stereo and the user-side audio (what you will hear in your car) is always going to be craptastic.

4) (*UPDATE) When paired, voice recognition on my phone, which is usually quite good, becomes severely impaired. This is also likely the culprit for complaint #3, above. I suspect this is because when paired, it tries to use the built-in microphone for voice recognition instead of the microphones on my phone (of which there are 4). It is disabling the extremely good microphones in my phone (Nokia lumia Icon which is well known for having incredible audio input) and using the unit's crappy microphone instead. This microphone is located in the unit, which is attached to the center console of my car near the shifter, and thus picks up all the vibrations and related road and engine noise transmitted through the structure of the car as I drive. This approach is terrible. I have stopped using the unit for anything requiring voice input, including telephone calls. In other words, this is just a big awkward charger now, and one that charges painfully slowly (see complaint #2). If it were possible to disable the onboard mic, and use the mics in my phone instead for calls and voice recognition, this would be a much more serviceable unit As it is now, it is just a piece of junk.

Cannot recommend this item. There are definitely worse products out there. I have not tried them all, but of those I have used, this is the best one so far. I will likely keep using it until the lack of automatic pairing pushes me over the edge with it one day and I get something else. (*UPDATE: this thing just does not work well, and I am now looking for something else.)

This is going to be quick--I only have a minute. However, as an avid point & shoot hobbyist, I wanted to contribute my $0.02 worth in on this magnificent little gem. Small, simple, and almost goof-proof, this is an ideal inexpensive camera for anyone just getting started. No optical viewfinder, managable file sizes, and the typical unbeatable Nikon lens mean you get serious bang for your buck with this camera. Full auto works well, and easy access to simple manual control over the basic parameters of the capture process mean it is easy for anyone to make minor adjustments. Also, there are (I think) 16 or 20 custom auto modes, including fireworks, black & white, etc.

HUGE plus: this camera runs on AA batteries. Spend about $25 once on a charger and two sets of high-capacity rechargables (2600miAh), and you will be all set. Regular Energizers are good for 100+ shots with the flash. The rechargables I bought are good for easily 250+ on a charge. MOney VERY well spent.

For your dollar, this is a hard camera to beat--and what makes it great is that it's a Nikon--these people know lenses... and TRUST ME, it's all about the optics. Nikon simply rules in that dept, IMHO.

We picked up this camera because we were getting a new puppy and needed to keep an eye on him during the day.

The clarity is pretty solid overall given the cost and can be seen in the photo above (which includes our little pup).

The camera can take snapshots which I am not able to save to my phone (or haven’t quite figured out how to save to my iPhone but they do save in the app).

I don’t really need this for motion detection but have tested that feature out as a just in case measure if we used in the future. The sensitivity can be adjusted but overall a very nice feature.

The camera does have a micro sd slot that would allow storage of footage (like movements) but we use the live footage as our means of checking the feed.

The connection to the device was fairly smooth but we did have to refresh our router when completing the process. It could’ve been a bandwidth issue given we have more Smart items than ever.

The app is fairly user friendly and my wife and I can both view the live feed at the same time. The feed itself is about .5 -1 second slow which we haven’t found as a problem.

The audio in/out is also quite clear which was fantastic. We try not to talk to our pup too much but it definitely was a nice feature for the first 2-3 days of him being in the crate (and being able to hear him as well as talk to him if he got frustrated).

Highly recommend this one!
