review_text:
I'm a big fan of the Mi Band series of trackers, and this is the first device that finally got me to switch to something else. If you aren't familiar, Xiaomi and Huami aren't big brands in the US compared to other countries, but these are solid high quality products and not your standard fare Chinese junk. I've tried a LOT of different fitness trackers and smart watches- Everything from Google WearOS, Fitbit, Apple, and all the way down to the cheap trackers from Chinese throwaway brands with obscure apps. For a long time I've said I liked the features and quality of the expensive brands, but found they all had major flaws (battery life being a major one- I don't want another thing to charge as often as a phone!). The Mi band from Xiaomi was super affordable and high quality compared to others in that price range, and had a battery that only required being charged once a month.
This is basically the smarter older brother of that band. It is compatible with Mi Fit, so all my data transferred right over, but it is so much nicer than the band. For starters, the notification system is easier to read and keep up with messages, but the benefits go far beyond a larger screen. The music control is a nice touch, I like being able to pause and adjust the volume without taking my phone out of my pocket if playing on a BT speaker while I'm doing dishes, for example. The tracking is pretty accurate compared to other expensive brands, and while it doesn't support apps like Wear OS and Apple Watches, it has all the fitness functions you'd need built in already, including some fun widgets beyond the expected ones like a stopwatch, phone finder and even a compass! And unlike cheap brands, the UI is responsive and smooth. Not the smoothest out there for sure, but more than acceptably smooth considering how much a flagship smartwatch costs compared to this.
It has support for voice commands, but I honestly found that feature kind of gimmicky more than useful. The higher end version of this includes a speaker which might make the command function more useful as sort of a digital assistant, not to mention the ability to take phone calls from your wrist. But the model I got to try out lacks the speaker, which is a fine compromise for a cheaper price tag all things considered. The battery life at first was just OK, a few days on a charge if using lift-to-wake functions, but just as on my Mi Band tracker of old, I found if I turn off auto-wake and rely on using the button to wake the display, the battery life goes from counting in days to counting in weeks. That's the killer feature of this device- the ability to leave it on to track fitness and sleep habits without having to charge it so often. I'll have to charge it more than my old Mi Band's monthly top up for sure, probably at least 2x a month, but that's still very manageable.
So that's it, after years of loving my Mi Bands and considering it the standard by which all practical fitness trackers should be judged, I'm finally moving on to an Amazfit watch. This is a difficult value to beat.

I listen to lectures on headphones when doing chores around the house and often can't hear people trying to get my attention. I've seen neck speakers before, and I thought it would be a very cool option for me as my family gets kind of annoyed that I can't hear them and they can't tell if I'm currently listening to something.
But I'll be honest, after trying these, I'm not really loving them. I had a pair of sunglasses speakers that aimed sound towards my ears, but this sort of blasts sound out and around me. Like, not even towards my ears. Basically, it seems just as loud to someone else in the room with me as it does to me, which then begs the question of why not just use an external speaker at that point? The call quality was just OK as well. The one thing I can say is that the build quality seems quite good. It feels really durable and made with premium feeling materials. But I just can't shake the feeling that for the asking price, I'm missing the point of these. Shouldn't the speakers be facing upwards towards my ears instead of blasting at each other in front of my Adam's Apple? Seems like a weird design that might be missing the mark.

review_title: Good FOV with very little distortion
review_text:
A lot of these cheap webcams use very small sensors and rely on super wide optics to see the room. They also tend to overstate their resolving power, claiming to send a 1080 sized image that looks more like an upscaled 480. I'm happy to say this is a degree better than those!
The sensor is still small, as expected, but the optics aren't super wide to the point that edges distort. In fact, it seems pretty rectilinear (straight lines stay relatively straight in the background). The resolution seems decent as well. I'm not sure if it's actually resolved a full HD image like it claims, but it is definitely more resolution than a lot of the cheaper webcams I've tried. It looks pretty good and I'd argue that any live web call, skype, zoom, etc, will look perfectly fine with this camera and play at whatever resolution that protocol is capable of clearly.
The thing that sorta disappointed me, however, was the "ring light" built in. I mean, I have a REAL ring light so I get what that should do, but this sorta does... nothing. It doesn't create soft shadows or a circular catch light in my eyes- in fact, it's very hard to discern the difference between capture with the light on versus off. In a dark room, it can add a bit of illumination to the subject to make you a little easier to see, but it really isn't all that bright and under normal lighting conditions in my office, it makes zero difference at all. It also seems to get kind of warm as long as it is plugged in, even if not currently active, so I'm going to be in the habit of disconnecting it when not using, and only plugging it in when I need to make a video call at my desk.
For what it is, it is definitely a better webcam than most of the cheap ones, but it definitely is not perfect!

review_text:
I'm a fan of Panasonic's electronics, and have been since I first used their GH camera line for work, and the DVX prosumer cameras before that. I was excited for a chance to replace my working headphones with ones from Panasonic, however I found it interesting that the plug type was NOT MENTIONED on this listing! The last pair of headphones + mic that I ordered came with a USB plug. It worked fine on my laptop, but not on my phone or tablet, obviously. I want a regular headphone jack, as in 1/8" or 3.5mm (whatever you want to call it!) to be compatible with all my things, and not rely on the limitations of bluetooth.
I was a little bit nervous about buying this one since it doesn't say anywhere that it is, in fact, a standard TRRS headphone-jack sized plug, but I'm happy to report that it IS! And the sound quality is what I expected from Panasonic, a good value for the price. One thing to note, however, is that this requires both sides have a wire going to the plug. This is a seriously old-school design that I almost forgot existed. Modern headphones have a single point of cable that splits to the other side in the band, however this is more like earbuds in that there's a wire going to each side.
It's not a deal breaker, it works fine and some people may actually prefer that look, but personally I'm worried about it being another point of contact that could get snagged/rip/break/go wrong, and actually prefer the more modern single-side cable style. But this is still a great pair of traditional tried-and-true headphones!

review_text:
This is a great little capture device for streaming and recording content from HDMI sources! I've been asked to stream a lot of live events (graduations, benefit concerts, etc) since Covid19 started. With this, I can take the feed out of my camera directly into the box, and stream or record using something like OBS software on my laptop. The input is considered like a USB webcam to the system, so really anything, including Zoom or Skype, can utilize the content coming from a camera or other HDMI source.
I have a Magewell HDMI to USB box that I was using before this one, and while the quality of the stream was professional (excellent color and stream clarity), it actually would often overheat and drop frames. I actually had to put a cooling fan on it to prevent that from happening on a long event outdoors. But so far, this adapter seems to be better at handling heat- likely because the overall box is bigger so the heat can dissipate. Crazy because the Magewell cost a lot more than this. Also this one has an HDMI pass through, which the magewell did not! That means you can split this with another ouput, for example run it out to a TV, a camera monitor, projector, or external recorder like a Atmos Ninja. The magewell couldn't do any of that without a separate splitter sitting before it to copy the signal to multiple outputs.
Yes, there are cheaper capture card adapters out there, but in my experience they are a mixed bag of mostly unreliable performance and subpar coloring, and lack the features this offers. The Magewell might still be the most pro version of this I've used as far as color and clarity, but it is more expensive and only offers a single input with no passthrough, not to mention overheats easily. I'd definitely recommend giving this one a try!

review_title: Manual focus, but decent quality + surprise macro function!
review_text:
So, let me start off by saying, this isn't the best quality webcam on the market. But for the price, no one is expecting it to be. And it is FAR from the worst! During the Covid Pandemic, all the regular brand name webcams were sold out so I found myself trying out a bunch of these no-name brands from Amazon. The last one I tried actually had a much harsher fisheye effect in the corners, as well as over-saturated color. This one seems far less cartoony and more realistic in color reproduction, as well as being somewhat more rectilinear (photo speak for straight lines being straight, not as much curved distortion). There is a bit of fisheye curve on the edges, but it is very usable and didn't make my ceiling look concave like my last one I tried. See attached images for examples of the room's wall distortion. It's there if you are looking for it, but not terrible when you're looking at a subject. The microphone is just meh. I have a desktop mic and the sound out of that was MUCH better, especially because you can get it closer to your face than the camera. But the fact that this HAS a mic is a good option in a pinch. I would just strongly recommend an external mic if you want people to hear you clearly. Also something I didn't know before trying this:
It is MANUAL focus! That means it won't follow and focus on you automatically, you have to twist the lens until you're sharp in the view. It actually isn't that hard to nail focus, the depth of focus is pretty deep so once you've set it for your standard sitting distance, you likely won't have to change it ever again unless you walk away from the camera. A fun side effect, however is that the focus lens gear lets you push it to EXTREME MACRO distances! So you can do insane closeups of things if you want to, for example, put a webcam on an ant farm maybe? I tried it out on my desktop speaker, and in one picture you can see the relative size of it compared to my desk and then the closeup you can see the detail of the scratched plastic where it says Harmon / Kardon. Ha, if nothing else this shows me I should probably get new desktop speakers too! These are beat up when up close! A fun and versatile camera for a good price. If you need autofocus tracking, this might not be for you though.

review_title: A cool concept, not quite what I expected- Read to understand
review_text:
Let's get one thing straight right away: THESE ARE NOT SUNGLASSES. They are blue-light blocking at best, or just mildly tinted most likely. I took them out of the box and thought "Oh cool! These are the kinds of glasses that get dark outside and transparent when you are inside!", but nope- I wore them for a full hour outside and they didn't get any darker or exhibit any sun blocking properties AT ALL. So that's false advertising right there. They aren't for use in the sun. They don't darken anything.
As far as audio quality... they are a cool concept, but again, falls short of expectations. The open ear design means the speakers have to work harder to be audible. That means they often make those tin-sounding rattles that tiny speakers make when cranked up too high. This is definitely NOT cool for music as most of the fidelity is lost right off the bat, and adding insult to injury is that they often don't get loud enough to use outside. I'm not saying using it in a crowded subway terminal (that you can just forget about completely), I'm talking about even just going for a stroll around my suburban block with some birds chirping and the wind blowing lightly, maybe a car driving in the distance. I tried listening to a recorded lecture (since music was a lost cause), and they couldn't get loud enough to hear clearly. The microphone for calls was OK in my test, so I guess they are cool as a way to take a phone call without wearing a headset, but that only works if you're wearing these anyway as sunglasses. They aren't sunglasses, so you wouldn't be wearing them anyway, and you wouldn't be wearing them for music, and you wouldn't be wearing them to make a phone call either because they rarely get loud enough unless you are home alone... in which case you can put your phone on speaker and avoid this whole mess.
In conclusion- its a good idea but executed poorly and does NOT live up to expectations. I'm surprised there are so many good reviews on this product. I can't think of a time I would use it.

review_text:
It's so good to find more wired TRRS headsets hitting the market. For a while it seemed like only wireless ones were selling and the wired models were all low-end earbud styles or the kind that have the mic embedded by your ears instead of your mouth.
This is a good over-the-ear style set, with decent bass response and sound quality, as well as a mic on the wire. I really like the placement of a microphone on the wire, it is second only to the telescoping mic style you see receptionists and gamers using. It keeps the mic relatively close to your mouth (rather than headsets that put the mic by your ears) so you pick up your voice more than ambient noise in the room. Just keep in mind, it is a TRRS set which means it has the extra pin on the plug for a mic. It may not work properly in standard TRS headphone plugs (stereo only, designed for use with headsets without a mic), although some can work with both.
Most modern laptops support TRRS, as well as tablets and phones (if you're lucky enough to still have a 3.5mm headset jack!).

review_title: A great kit, cool LEDs and plenty fast
review_text:
These sticks are a hair faster than my previous DIMMs, which were also rated with a 3200mhz XMP profile. I actually really like the LEDs on them because I happen to have an MSI motherboard that recognized them instantly and let me control the lights via their Mystic Light setup. The glow adds a cool look to the case, and can also be used to keep an eye on CPU temp (you can have the colors change as the CPU temp rises). The ones I got were 16-18-18-36 timings, which actually were close enough to my G.Skill ram that I could combine them and get pretty good performance out of both kits together.
The only thing I didn't like, however, is how the height was difficult to work around my heat sync. I had to switch which DIMM slots I used because the one closest to my cooling system didn't have enough height clearance to fit. Thankfully my other RAM could slide in there and I now have these LED ones in the other 2 slots. So, just keep that in mind if you have a tight space and a large heat pipe system, you might need shorter DIMMs that forgo the LED.
I'm actually quite happy that I was able to make this work, there was a moment in which I was almost going to give up. If they'll fit in your setup, I'd say they are pretty cool looking and plenty fast for a modern Mobo.

review_text:
This is a good card if you're on a budget and want some CUDA acceleration for your desktop. Personally, I have some applications that require CUDA cores for proper operation (Photogrammetry and Adobe's Mercury Playback Engine), and it's not so much that I need the fastest performance out there as it is that I need some CUDA cores to merely EXIST at all for certain features to work!
This card is a great because much like the 1550 ti before it, it offers a decent entry-level gpu without costing significantly more than other components in your desktop. It is faster than the 1550ti, so that's nice, and does a decent job pumping out fps in light gaming if that's your thing.
One thing I didn't know beforehand and wish I did: This card does NOT support the Nevnc Turing engine. It only supports the (somewhat inferior) Volta one, which isn't as efficient in hardware accelerated video encoding. Since I bought this card primarily to compliment a home video editing setup, I wanted that feature. The new 1650 SUPER, which is a slightly more expensive card, DOES have the Turing engine, and when that showed up in a Google search I assumed this card had it as well.
Its a shame, I was looking forward to that but I'll have to wait until the next time I upgrade my GPU.

review_title: An excellent first generation product from Nikon
review_text:
Full disclosure: I'm a Sony E camera fan and use them for work, so giving this Nikon 5 stars means a LOT from me.
I was skeptical about Nikon's entry into the mirrorless camera world, since in the past they saved their higher end specs for DSLRs, and didn't take the mirrorless market seriously (*cough* Nikon 1 *cough*). However the full frame Z cameras got a lot of positive acclaim, and this Z50, their first APSC crop sized mirrorless, is a heck of a lot better than any first generation product has any business being!
First let's talk about ergonomics- the camera feels great, not point-and-shoot tiny in your hands. Definitely smaller and lighter than a DSLR, but more substantial than a phone, as a camera should be. It has a touch screen, which is AWESOME for touch-focus and really helps avoid the "how to I change that setting" learning curve- generally, just press on the icon and you can change the setting. Yet it doesn't RELY on the touch screen, there are plenty of physical buttons and dials, many of which are customizable and can be assigned to functions you need more often. Essentially, this is a camera that's got more than one way to do most things and therefore will adapt to YOUR workflow rather than force you to learn its own. The screen can also tilt up or down, and lets you flip it around on the bottom to see selfie-style if desired. This is one area that seems a little odd for me- other cameras like the Sony A5100 flip UPWARDS, so you can see over the camera if taking a self portrait. Or the Panasonic GH series articulates sideways. This, only flips DOWN. Which means if mounted to a tripod, you can't see the display at all. That is alright since honestly most of the higher end full frame cameras don't even let you flip the display around at all these days. The fact that you can, even if in a silly orientation, is better than nothing and a welcome feature.
Image quality seems pretty great, the kit lenses are adequate. I really liked the 50-250, as 16-50 with variable aperture feels very limited in creativity (however this lens is necessary as a "walkaround" standard zoom length). To be fair, I'm spoiled by my pro constant f-stop lenses that I use on my other cameras, so I'm rarely impressed by the performance of budget friendly kit options. I'll admit that for kit lenses these really perform remarkably well, but I'm hoping Nikon rolls out some awesome affordable Z-mount DX lenses soon. Cropping in to view pixels at 100% zoom size, the image holds up and seems reasonably sharp. Nikon colors are there as well, which are admittedly excellent. As with any new system, there aren't a lot of lenses available yet unless you adapt from other mounts. Nikon has F-mount adapters for native adaption, and I've read good things about third party adapters for other camera types as well (Canon, etc... I've even seen a Sony EF adapter for sale!). Sadly, I don't have access to any adapters at the moment, so I'm stuck judging imaging quality by the included kits for now.
Now for video, this gets even more interesting. Nikon has done a bang-up job supporting popular frame rates and resolutions (4k at 24p? Hello filmmakers!). In my tests, the quality of the video was very clean and sharp. I haven't noticed much in the way of moire or aliasing yet, and it has a clean HDMI out option as well if you want to record externally or view on a bigger monitor while filming. Unlike certain other cameras (like the Sony a6300), it is able to keep the rear display ON while also using the external monitor / recorder, and also recording internally at 4k. Other prosumer crop cameras have turned off the internal display when doing all of those things at once. It does support a microphone jack which means you can use this for recording interviews, however it is missing a headphone jack to monitor the audio levels. That's a huge omission if you wanted to use this as a semi-pro video making tool.
Thankfully, I found a workaround: If you get a cheap HDMI monitor (they have for around $100 that can attach to the hotshoe mount), they often have audio jacks. I happen to have a couple by Feelworld that do exactly that, and I was able to plug headphones in and hear the audio while in recording mode live. Well, semi-live at least. When recording 4k, there was a brief delay in the A/V playback, I'm guessing because the throughput required for 4K creates some latency. But the point is that you COULD hear it, and therefore make sure the volumes are appropriate and audible, and thereby making it possible to use the Z50 as a more pro level tool.
All in all, this is an excellent entry into the market by Nikon. Whether you are a beginner looking to eventually start using semi-pro tools or a seasoned pro looking for a budget friendly walkaround or B-cam, this is a very impressive value.

review_title: Great for hauling my gear around!
review_text:
Let me start off by saying I work in freelance video and I love how much I can fit inside this case! I've been using a Pelican 1510 as my go-to travel carrier, so that's mostly what I'm comparing this to. For starters, this is a longer case so in addition to my cameras, lenses, batteries and other accessories, it has a long open sleeve that can even fit a light stand or small tripod! For extra versatility, the whole interior can actually be pulled out (it has its own handle straps if you want to use it as its own carrier), which then frees up the ample storage space inside the case as a separate giant unit (see pictures to illustrate). There are also plenty of pockets on the inside, as well as the outside and front of the case. Of course, for a case this size there is the requisite wheels and carrying handle.
The only things I like better about my Pelican case, however, are the toughness and waterproofing. This bag comes with a rain cover which you can keep inside the case, however I don't like the idea of having to carry around a cover inside the bag, then take it out and put it on if it starts raining. The Pelican cases are air tight by simply closing them, no rain cover needed. The Pelican cases also are tough enough that they can be stacked under other equipment, thrown into a corner, sat on, stood on, etc, and 99% of the time come out unscathed. That's more than I can say for this bag. I bring this bag on gigs that I'm not worried about those things happening, because I can fit what I normally take in 3 separate bags into just this one. You could get a Pelican style case in this size, however it would cost quite a bit more than the asking price of this one. I think for the price this is a great tool to keep your stuff organized and ready to go whenever you are!

review_title: Works well as a way to get analog out of your HDMI
review_text:
I'm running a 1080p projector for our home entertainment system, and have a high quality decades-old analog stereo system for sound. Without this Audio Extractor device, I used to be limited to source devices that let me separate the video from the audio (Fire TV box and other devices that offer both analog stereo and HDMI video simultaneously) since the sound has to go one way and the video feed another.
This device opens up possibilities such as more modern equipment that does away with analog connections entirely. A Fire TV Stick 4k for example, or Raspberry Pi board (yes, technically the Pi has analog outputs, but they are subpar and not recommended for high quality audio). I'm very happy with this device and the opportunities it opens for me. It works well for me with the 2ch setting and my equipment. I can't vouch for 5.1 as my system doesn't support that, nor can I vouch for 4k as my system doesn't handle that either. But so far it has worked well sending a stereo analog audio feed somewhere other than my projector when needed.

review_title: Good if you like wear OS watches - but not a pedometer?
review_text:
This is a smartwatch running Google's Wear OS. My wife does love it, but we have some reservations with recommending it. Before we go any further, I'd like to point out that most of our qualms have to do with Wear OS itself, so it would be true of any smartwatch running that system.
Let me start off by saying this watch is really very pretty and my wife LOVES the styling of it. Before this she was using more utility-looking fitness bands like those from Xiaomi and FitBit. Her last band, a Mi Band 3, was great for functionality, but she found it ugly. This one she actually really likes, and features like apps, the full color touch screen, custom watch faces, programmable buttons, and dial to control menus really showcases the difference between a proper "smartwatch" and the cheaper activity trackers she is used to. It feels and looks undeniably cool.
But after a week or two of using it, there are some things that we really wish were different about it. For starters, the battery life is pretty terrible. On days that she uses it a lot (like when we first got it), it seems to need to be charged before the day is over. After settling into a routine and changing to a very basic watch face, and also turning off features like wake on wrist detection, we are able to last at least 24 hours to maybe a day-and-a-half on a charge. In other words, even with pretty conservative battery usage, you can easily make it the entire day but still need to charge it daily because it definitely won't make it through that second day. That means when we go away for a weekend, its another charger that has to come with us. I see that this is unfortunately normal for Wear OS devices, as 1-2 days of battery is the average even from other brands running Google's smartwatch OS. To contrast, my wife's Mi Band 3 went for nearly 3 weeks on a charge, which meant she could wear it 24-7 and get the benefits of things like sleep tracking with it. This can't really do that well. To be fair, my friends with other smartwatches (Apple, Samsung, etc) say they have to charge it daily as well, so perhaps this is an expected compromise for users preferring smartwatches to bands and other trackers.
The next thing, and this is sort of a recent sore point it seems, the pedometer and step goals have been replaced with "heart points" thanks to a very new partnership between Google and the American Heart Association. They decided that counting steps isn't good enough, and came up with a different calculation for activity and setting goals for it. This is all fine and good, except that they DON'T HAVE THE OPTION TO SET STEP GOALS. I guess in an effort to get everyone interested in the new system, they are almost trying to hide the pedometer functions of Google Fit. In order to get your steps you have to find them buried in a menu, and there's no current watch face that will show you real-time steps that I could find. Oh, and did I mention you can't set it as a goal anymore? This is very frustrating as my wife and I use steps competitively as do many work place initiatives and similar programs... this is a basic function that EVERY activity tracker lets you do! Everything from the cheapo Chinese trackers to the name brands, to the Apple watches, to even Google Fit as of a few months ago! I looked up ways to bring the pedometer functions back into front and center and found many tirades on the internet from disgruntled users who also wanted the feature back. I get it, the heart points is probably better, but at least let US, as users, choose!
At the end of the day, my wife and I find it very awkward that this higher priced smartwatch, with all of its high end features and wow factors, can't handle the simple things that her cheaper Mi Band did great- the old band showed us her steps on the main display with the time, in real time, and would need to be charged about once monthly. But to be fair, now that she's been spoiled by the style and ability to respond to text messages from the watch (the band only showed them, you couldn't respond to them), she's not planning on going back. I'm hoping that Google's Wear OS addresses some of these issues in the future and/or Fossil themselves address it. They could, for example, design a device with better battery and a custom Fossil watch face that still does step counting. But this doesn't. So for us, the experience doesn't seem to match the price point. IF you like Wear OS and are already aware of its limitations in battery and pedometer, this is a very nice option.

review_text:
This is a good product, but perhaps not exactly what I was expecting it to be. I was hoping to conceal two different things- a floor lamp cord, and a cat5 cable along a wall. In both cases, this cover is far wider than it needs to be. This is better suited for multiple cables, such as all the power/hdmi/composite/etc connections running down the back of a wall-mounted TV. For a single cable run like a power plug or a measly cat5 cable, it seems absurdly wider than the cable it is concealing.
That other thing I found interesting is that one of the walls I wanted to use it on isn't completely straight. A handyman had helped me repair a wall and paint it, and now I see it has a slight curve to it which I wasn't able to notice before. The covers don't sit entirely flat against the wall, which just sort of looks awkward around the ever-so-slightly-curved portion unless I fill it in with spackle. I could overlook all these things and say perhaps my test usage are uncommon scenarios, except for one final thing: the adhesive is TOO good!
If you decide you don't like it / want it, and used the adhesive instead of the screws, you are going to rip a lot of the wall off with the cover when you remove it. I wasn't sure if this was just me, but I see from other reviews that they claim pieces of the drywall were coming off with the paint, which is quite frankly somewhat horrifying if you didn't know it would do that. I still have the paint for this wall so I'm not concerned, but I'd strongly recommend using the screws if you have the option and don't want this to be a permanent fixture in your home.

review_title: Works great to send video feed across the room
review_text:
UPDATE: I noticed that my setup would start displaying an incorrectly sized and formatted hdmi feed (instead of 1920x1080, it was a squashed 960x1080 with incorrect colors). If I turned the whole system off and wait a few minutes before turning back on, it would sometimes go away but it is very strange. I thought it was either the player or projector connected to it for months now, but I just did some testing and realized it has been this HDMI extender! A monitor plugged into the source displayed fine, and plugged into this receiver had the same 960x1080 w/ mixed up colors that my projector did. The good news is that the transmitter has a reset button and that seems to fix it when it happens. But it sometimes comes back when I reboot or start up from everything being off. It is annoying that I have to go find the little reset button because the transmitter is hidden in a cabinet, and it seems like a completely unnecessary step to take every time I boot up. Hoping Sabrent can offer a solution- if so I'll update my review back to 5 stars because otherwise this is excellent.
These things are a great way to reliably reach farther than an HDMI cable, but you need to still understand the limitations. Video requires a lot of bandwidth, so the quality and length of your cable is directly related to how realistic it is to reach the maximum resolution and frame rate.
I already have an older one of these from a different brand, which I bought a couple of years ago for a projector in the back of the room (switch between TV and projector, but entertainment system is in front of room and projector is in back, hence the need for a long run of cable). That older one claimed to work at 1080/60p, and in my initial tests it did. But once I ran the long cable, I was able to only get 720/60p or 1080 at only 24p. 1080 at 60 was just too much bandwidth and the adapter just couldn't handle it over a longer cable run.
This adapter, however, is rated at a higher spec for 4K. Swapping my old one out with this one, I'm happy to report that now I can get 1080 even at 60p from point to point. Could I get 4k at that length? I don't know, my projector doesn't handle 4k, but I'm guessing as the length of cable increases, it will limit what spec you can reliably expect. But I am very pleased with finally getting 1080p at this length of cable, so 5 stars!

If instant gratification is your thing or you just have a nostalgia for old Polaroid concepts, this camera is for you!

NOTE: Does not come with film/paper. You'll need that, and/or a Micro SD card. The camera can work with either or both, but not with none.

review_title: Incredible bang for buck and AMAZING parental controls!
review_text:
I bought this during a mother's day promotion for ten dollars less than normal. We had our iPad mini stolen almost a year ago, and figured it would be nice to have a small tablet around again.
I've seen the cheap tablets and wasn't expecting much for the price. They're usually laggy and have poor displays and cameras. Man, was I surprised to see how solid of a product this is! Don't get me wrong, it comes in basically minimalist packaging and doesn't look like much at first. But the UI is surprisingly smooth, screen has great viewing angles for both reading and landscape movie watching (more than I can say about other cheap tablets), and the Amazon software is pretty nifty.
Ok, the camera on this thing isn't very good, I must admit that- but I have a cell phone for pocket shooting and a DSLR for real shooting, so what do I really need a camera on a tablet for? Skype? Its good enough for video calls.

What really impressed me is the software for creating kid profiles. I love it that I can set up usernames for my kids that they can log into and are only allowed to access the things that I decide are appropriate for them- including movies and books from the marketplace! Also I can set up time restrictions to give them only specific amounts of time for play before locking them out. Another cool feature I haven't tried yet is one that seems to not let them play any games until they have spent a designated amount of time reading. I love that!

All in all, I was impressed enough with the parental controls and the price that I decided to buy 2 more to give my kids!

review_title: GREAT upgrade from tablet for my kids, first Chromebook
review_text:
I did a lot of research as to what to get for my kids to replace their aging and damaged Samsung Tab A's. We decided that it was time to go to a Chromebook so that they could get more repetition with a standard keyboard and GoogleOS. They are still able to download all the PlayStore apps that they had on their tablets, but now with better hardware and longer support.
This model has 64GB of storage (with SD card option), so thats a huge upgrade. The RAM is 4GB, which is more than most cheap tablets these days, and you can tell. Its a LOT snappier than the Galaxys.
The 2in1 flip with the screen is my kids favorite part! They can use it like a "real computer" and then flip it to make a huge tablet screen instead. Much bigger than the 8" screen they had before.
For an entry level chromebook, these are sturdy, snappy, and cheap! I dare you to find something better for preteens at this price point!
NOTE: some of the reviews here complain about the speaker quality/power. This was one of the only things I was weary about when I finally committed to this unit. Those reviews are DEAD WRONG. The speakers are GREAT on these Chromebooks. The quality is clear, and they are louder than both of my other laptops and tablets. Playing videos through YouTube at 1/2 volume is much louder than the max of my other units. Don't let the "terrible speaker" reviews sway you.

review_title: I'd probably pick something else honestly
review_text:
I have had several Netgear products in the past, and like those, this is functional and not bad, but not great.
Setting up was easy, fairly standard for anyone with some IT experience. The WiFi coverage and strength is great, it was a noticeable upgrade from my Google Home in that area. The hardware is quality
The issues are in the supporting software. Everything has to be setup through the Orbi app, which is clunky. As others have mentioned, there is no way to turn off the 5ghz range, and some devices need that option to connect. I did have issues connecting my smart thermostat and some of my older devices. I also had a couple instances where it would lose my connection to my devices and I basically had to start from scratch with setup again. Netgear's customer service is frustrating at best, completely unhelpful at worst.
I would likely stay away from this, and either get something cheaper that does the same things, or something better that doesn't give so many headaches.

review_title: Powerhouse Sony Moves into Corner with Its Own Future
review_text:
Unlike Coke Cola company, which continues to produce exceptional products, Sony has thrown in the towel when it comes to it WALKMAN market share, and loyal customers. While millions of hard working adults and millions of dillegent students have turned to Sony Walkman for their music while at the gym or out in the sports field, Sony has turned its back on them. This D-NF340 will be one of the last walkmans, as its quality has continuously diminished, and Sony has lost its willpower to make leading edge MUSIC.

First, the FM Tuner does a poor job in getting a good reception. I mostly get static on my machine. So, what happened SONY? Where is the quality?

Second, the CD Style is outdated, as so many are moving into SD cards, micro SD cards, and internal memory to play the music. Sony should have continued with their ATRAC-3 technology, and onto memory stick, rather than throw in the towel to just MP3. Yet, something could be said about going MP3, which makes sense. But, not providing a SPORTS walkman, now that is bad news. It is like Coke Cola saying to Pepsi, "ok, you win." Now, wait a minute. Both Coke Cola and Pepsi continue to make advancements, and both continue to make sales and keep business going. So, what happened Sony. Is this the end for Sony? The CD style is also very bulky. There is no need to carry such a bulky physical CD anymore. But, another version of the Walkman should have been created. Shame on you, Sony.

Third, the knobs and controls are good, yet they could be better served on a digital walkman. There is something nice by having knobs and buttons, controls and sliding switches. The controls of such nature blend well with humans who are sweating, running, exercising, stretching, pulling, pushing, bumping, etc. The digital up/down arrows, push etc. just are not controling enough for this person. Maybe it is the same with driving a car. Manual transmission, putting the hand on the stick shift knob, feeling the car going from first to second, from second to third, and so on. That feel is part of being human. Not sure why a sports version of a digital mp3 player by the GREATEST CREATOR of WALKMAN cannot put together such a product. Knobs, oh how they provide controlable pleasure.

Fourth, the sports thing. This CD player, along with its many many prior versions failed the drop test. Oh, so many start loosing a function, like the loss of one side audio, or loss of display, etc. after one drop on the ground. And, because they are heavy, what can you expect. Ahh Punka, Bash, Blop, Clunk!, Dah Pinga, Dah Dong, Blip, Ding, Dong, Crash, Kaput. Even the sports version was heavy. Eh. So, yeah SONY WALKMAN designers, make the MP3 version with digital memory, in the light weight version, please. Sweat resistant, slightly water resistant (for the rain,) unlike this one. Dah? Where have you been Sony? And, call it the Walkman, MAN!!

Now, for all the poor people who just do not want to hurt their eyes, make the display FONT size a good bit larger. Give your loyal customers a break. Large enough so it can be seen in various environments - lighted room, darken street, etc. Some of us JOG at night, and can use the larger font size.

Until then, this product is a "don't buy." It is not a sports version, It is not supported by Sony software, it is not MP3 and ATRAC3, it is not light weight, it is not water resistant, ... what it is ... OLD FASHION.

review_title: First Time MP3 User - Having Difficulty Here
review_text:
Because I am a First Time MP3 User, please ignore this review (if you are an expert.) I am having difficulty with this MP3 player because the manual does not have references in each paragraph as to "more readings." For example, Sandisk does not offer its own MP3 burner and/or Music Management Software. This would have been a great advantage, even if the software was at cost, say $10. It would mean the equipment would be integrated with mp3 music burning. I had difficulty transfering mp3 music to the sansa clip +8. First, it seems that the PROPERTIES data in each song was important. With 100 of songs having a song title as "track 1" and "track 2" the music had some chaos creating a playlist. So, a warning about this on the manual, for novice mp3 users would have been nice. (Do you agree?) Maybe I should have looked harder on the sandisk website. (Maybe?) At least a reference to help beginners in the manual would have been appropriate. Ok, second, the internal memory saves music more true to original names than the extended memory. Some of my files says "DN30000101 Journey - Love is Everything" where the DN330000101 tag was added by Sandisk. Not sure why, but this just adds to the chaos. (OK, stick a pencil in my ear.) I am a beginner, so music management means everything to me. Chaos with this Sandisk is life right now. If my collection was just two or three CDs, then I could say ok. (Life is beautiful.) But so many readers, I assume, have a collection of 100 CDs that have been existing on their library for a few years. So, the SANSA CLIP must meet integrating with old files in mid stream. (Old, old file systems, maybe?) It appears not enough testing my Sandisk has been done to make the product user friendly for first time MP3 users. If they did enough testing, they would have built their own music management software I am tired. I called Sandisk, and they suggest to change ALL of my ID3 tags on the PROPERTIES of each song. Well, there goes my summer vacation. If I can manually change 100 songs each weekend, in about 10 weekends I will have make sense out of chaos. Right now, I have so many songs saying "track 1." Yeah, etc, track 2, track 3.

Bottom line is that Sandisk is not creating a product like the iPOD which takes responsibility for all experiences the user has: managing albums, burning mp3, transfering data, creating playlist, and teaching novice people about the equipment. Instead, Sandisk just makes the equipment, and assumes "sink or swim" to the users. So, all the good reviews, I assume, come from experienced users, and not first time idiots, like me. Maybe I should go back to my old music player? (Tell me.)

I must be tired, because I am having a hard time with this Sansa Clip. Ok, give me about two years, and I'll catch up. So, I give it a 4-star.

review_title: Nice keyboard - but not for Mac OS
review_text:
I purchased this keyboard from another vendor as Amazon and Logitech were out of stock of white ones.
My wife has used her beloved Logitech K811 keyboard for years with her iMacs - and that is the perfect keyboard but sadly is no longer made by Logitech.
Instead they sell this K380 keyboard which is a total disaster.
For a start, it uses batteries instead of being rechargeable and doesn't have the beautiful illuminated keys that light up the K811 at night, and it has user-unfriendly round keys.
The K380 doesn't even have a Caps Lock light to show that you are in that mode.
There is no 'repeat' function when you hold a key down - for multiple characters you have to keep clicking the key.
But the worst thing is that there is NO FORWARD DELETE function on this keyboard - just a backward delete. This is pathetic.
I wasted 2 hours going through Logitech's web site, downloaded drivers and software etc - there is NO mention of this missing and important feature in their technical or marketing bulletins.
I had to go on Amazon's K380 feedback to learn that other purchasers have this problem. There is NO FIX for this.
Fortunately the Vendor accepted the return of my K380 - so I am back to using Apple keyboards.
Very disappointing, frustrating and time wasting. Shame on Logitech!

review_title: Quality product, but XP-Pen is better for the $$
review_text:
First off I am not an artist. I do a little of everything Adobe AI, photoshop, writing, drawing, signatures, annotating documents, basic coding, scripts, etc. I recently changed companies and went from Apple to Windows and have been missing some of the peripherals. I was originally looking for a keyboard/trackpad combo that would allow me to kickback(feet on desk), stand up, or be upright and take my interface with me, something different. I landed on drawing tablets and found many reviews of people who switched from a mouse and I was intrigued. I have a 34" monitor & 2 22" monitors(the basics.) The bigger the screen you have the bigger the tablet you need and they quickly get expensive. I ordered the XP-Pen Star05v2 & the Wacom Intuos Wireless Medium.

Unboxing:
The Wacom is much like opening an new iPhone. You get nice packaging, the device, and a charging cable. The texture and quality of the device is lovely. You find yourself liking it before you have even used it.
Setup:
Setup was super easy, I downloaded the software, and connected the device within a couple of minutes.
First impression:
At first it feels really weird at first…when you hover & move the pen over the tablet it moves the mouse. Tapping the tablet is like a mouse click. The pen/tablet is mapped 1:1 to your screen(s). If you go to the top right of the tablet the mouse goes directly to the top right of your screen. You can map the tablet to a specific screen so you have more space to draw on the tablet. You can also turn off the 1:1 mapping by putting the tablet in mouse mode. This is what I did to make the transition easier. However if you want to draw, sign documents, etc you really need to be in drawing/tablet mode. Otherwise your writing looks just like it would using a mouse. I setup some of the shortcuts in the software. I put the tablet back in tablet mode and tried Adobe AI and doing some of my work, diagrams, and did some drawings/writing.
Usability:
The tablet is superb for drawing, writing, design, & precision. I also liked that I could put it in my lap and scroll through web pages, applications, etc. However it just isn't quick enough for me. Perhaps one of the models with the dial and additional buttons would work.
Conclusion:
This unit is nice and if drawing & design were my primary function I would love it. I think I will try one of the other models with the dial. Probably the XP-Pen Pro as the Wacom Intuos Pro is just too expensive for my needs. I think a magic keyboard, magic trackpad, with the bridge would work perfectly for my needs, but I'm still using Windows primarily and not willing to pay for yearly software to make everything work.

The touch screen is very uncooperative compared with the tablet. You have to poke and poke to get things to work, even turning the pages. I wish there was a volume control on this one which you could use to turn pages instead. It's also not very intuitive where everything is. For instance, once I finish a book and wish to go back to the front to collect information for a review--the copyright date, for instance, or the name of a character--I have to mess around trying to get back to the first page.

I gave it four stars because the battery life is incredible and it doesn't bother my eyes as much, but for the touch screen it might get closer to three stars.

review_title: Lightweight and Comfortable, Perfect for Work or Play
review_text:
I was hesitant to order these headphones because they had no boom mike. My husband's previous headphones, from Turtle Bay, had a plastic headband, and several weeks ago the plastic headband on the side of the phones that had the boom mike snapped in half. We had to tape the outside shell of the headband shut with electrical tape so that he could still use them to work with or play music on, so that the headphones sat cockeyed on his head. Luckily these Sony headphones turned up so we could try them out, but he was wary about the lack of external mike because their most important use was his taking phone calls when he teleworked. He needed to be understood by his callers.

All his fears have been unfounded. He uses them for his work, 10 hours a day. The people he speaks to over the phone can hear him perfectly, despite the lack of a boom mike, and he can hear them clearly as well. He charges it overnight and they last through the entire ten hours of his shift. Even better, these headphones do what his Turtle Bay phones did not: he can use them via bluetooth without the bluetooth shutting off when he doesn't use it. He was using the Turtle Bay headphones with a wired connection because if he didn't use them for over 20 minutes the bluetooth would shut itself off.

The noise cancellation function is excellent. When it is off, he can still hear external noises, but once on he can't hear much of anything. I shouted at him at one point and he did not hear me. If you were working, especially in a noisy office, these would be ideal, and they should be useful on a long airline flight as well. (Having no crying baby to test this with, he can't vouch for these covering a whiny child.)

As for the music, he said it sounded perfect right out of the box, without using the Extra Bass, better than his old Sony wired headphones. He listened to a favorite Moody Blues song and said he could hear when the riff changed channels from one guitar to the other, and the sound effects changing from ear to ear. Next he engaged the Extra Bass and listened to a Moody Blues selection with a heavy bass portion and loved the results.

At this moment we are totally satisfied with these headphones. Time will tell if they will stand up to weeks of work calls and listening to music. However, my husband says there is definitely one thing wrong with them: THE SIX INCH LONG CHARGE CORD. Really, who makes these things? Luckily we had a multipack of USB C charge cords we got here on Amazon.

review_title: When Your Second Pair is as Important as the First
review_text: I try to take a mile to mile-and-a-half walk each morning with our dog, to keep both our weights down, and since I walk the same route every day, after a while it gets a bit monotonous. Sure I can watch the weeds at the side of the road as they progress through the seasons--presently the privet and the honeysuckle are in sweet bloom, later on I want to see if the thistle plant blooms this year, in the fall the leaves make a carpet of color--but most of the time, dull, dull, dull. So I've taken to listening to a podcast while I walk, and was using the nice set of Jabra earphones I have, but they are too heavy to walk with; they work fine if I'm sitting still but if I move they fall out of my ear (I do mean my ear, because the traffic is so bad and I have to cross a busy street, I only keep one in). So I wanted a light pair to walk the dog in. These are great! The sound is nice and clear and very full even if I only have one in, and I love the fact that three sizes of earpads are included. I am using the largest ones and they are a nice tight fit. No having to push them back into my ear every three minutes. Very happy with these.

review_title: Very Nice Case/Stand for Galaxy Tab 2 10.1 Tablet
review_text:
After purchasing my tablet, I had found a case for it at Walmart, very sturdy, adequately padded, and with the ability to tilt the screen. However, the mechanism to tilt the screen was established with velcro, which after a while did not hold as well as it did in the beginning. In addition, at least one of the little elastic straps that held the tablet in the case pressed on the power button, sometimes with bizarre results. I therefore considered this Belkin case with interest.

Upon receiving, I immediately fitted the tablet into the case, and was delighted when it was held snugly and kept from slipping out by a flap which tucks under the tablet. All the buttons except the charging button were close to a cutout so that button could be accessed easily. In addition, the cover of the case has little grooves at intervals so that the tablet can be propped up to be viewed at various angles.

As other reviewers have mentioned, it's a very sturdy and thick case, which does increase the weight of the featherlight Galaxy Tab somewhat. And as I have been careful not to drop it, I do not know how well it protects and from various heights...and nor am I likely to test! But it appears very solid, and the elastic cord sewn into the case cover keeps it closed well.

Drawbacks: there's no hole for the charger, so you must charge with the case open. Nor can you charge when using the tablet propped up. And you can only prop horizontally, not vertically, although I doubt if that is much of an issue for most of the things you would want to do with the tablet propped up.

In short, it's not perfect because of the case having to be open to charge, and I also wish there was some way to keep my stylus inside; the case is so tight that I have to hang it outside, exposing the tip to dirt and damage. But otherwise it works well for me. Your mileage may vary!

review_text:

Still it smells, not AS intensely, but enough that I won’t use it. I threw both sleeves away.

I realized quicky as soon as I started packing for my next trip that this purchase was a mistake. If you're looking for a bag to carry your laptop around, this bag will serve you just fine. But if you're looking for a bag specifically for business travel you should move up a few price brackets.

This bag is tight. And I don't mean that in the slang good way - you put a few things in it and it's almost busting at the seams, even after releasing the bag compression clips. The bottle pockets on the side have zero stretch to them and it's virtually impossible to fit a water bottle in them! I had to turn the bag on its side and wiggle it so the contents would shift enough for me to get my water bottle in the side pocket. Needless to say, this was not convenient.

As far as the rest of the bag, the zippers don't go all the way down (due to the useless water bottle pockets on the side) so it's pretty difficult to remove anything from the backpack that's more than a few inches down. The two compartments aren't adequately self-contained, so as soon as you put stuff in one side of the division it becomes almost impossible to put stuff in the other side. And even if you magically manage to get it all in perfectly, as soon as you remove one item - good luck getting it back in there because all the contents have now shifted and you'll never get that item back in the bag.

Oh and the lock on the top won't snap shut if you've got the bag full up to the top. You need a bit of empty space at the top of the bag or the lock is completely useless.

I'm going to return this bag because it didn't meet my travel needs. This bag will definitely serve you for simple tasks, but if you're a serious business traveler you should keep looking.

I'm not going to take a star off for any of the cons I have cause this tv mount works just as good if not better then the way over priced ones at more then over half the cost. If you read the comments on NIMH rechargeable batteries you will see that they do not work with Blink cameras. I think that changing batteries, even on an annual basis, is better than running power/communication cabling to other cameras systems. I can relocate cameras as needed to meet changing needs without hassling with wires. I do have one camera mounted where it it will be exposed to sun, wind, rain, snow, whatever mother nature has in store. I will update on how that survives. I signed up for the annual blink service. I'll see if it was worth it in a year. For now it was a simple setup solution to check video capture and storage.

review_text: This is the third tablet I've tried recently. On the plus side, it has some nice accessories that didn't come with the other two tablets. It turned out that the stylus was, for some unknown reason, entering a symbol I had never seen before instead of an s. When I used my fingers, instead of the stylus, to enter the code, it worked perfectly and I was finally able to connect the tablet to the internet. I don't know if the stylus and the charging glitches are something I am doing wrong or some problem with this tablet, so I'm giving it a neutral three star rating. Check the other reviews. If I am the only one having these issues, then it's likely just me. If, on the other hand, others are reporting similar problems, you may want to hesitate about buying this product.

review_title: Pretty Lights, Nice Sound, No Effect On My Gameplay
review_text:
Somewhere there is an ancient marketing survey that identifies teen-age boys as a prime segment of the gaming market and that says they really like bright, flashing lights. So manufacturers who want to sell to the gaming market still think they have to add flashy lighting to all their products. Well, the gaming universe is much larger than teen boys these days and bright, flashing lights have nothing to do with playing a game. With that pet peeve off my chest let me add a couple of things to give this review some context. First, I do spend a lot of time online playing an MMO but I'm very much a casual player, not a hardcore competitive one. Second, I am not an audiophile. High end stereo gear is wasted on me as the music coming from most any clock radio is good enough for me.

To my non-audiophile ears, the sound from this speaker is fine. It provides a nice range without being too heavy on the bass end or too shrill on the high end. Whether gaming, streaming videos, or listening to music and audiobooks, this speaker holds its own nicely. Though, like the flashy lighting, the sound quality really doesn't make any significant difference while I'm playing in my MMO world. The ambient noise, NPC chatter, battle music and such, all come through nicely but that's a perk, not something that particularly improves my game play.

The under the monitor design of this speaker really doesn't save me any desk space. The mini speakers I was using before were much smaller and were out of the way on the side of the monitor. This space bar basically sits in front of my monitor and takes up more room than other speakers. One strong plus to me for this speaker is the fact that it really is plug and play. I had it up and running in just a few minutes. Other "gaming" gear I've tried with flashy lighting systems require software to control the lighting and sometimes getting that software to install and run properly can be a major, frustrating effort. So I really, really like that this product lives up to its "plug and play" claim.

There is one last negative point to mention. a minor one. The volume and other controls are flat buttons on the side of the soundbar. So to adjust the volume, change the lighting, etc, you need to move the soundbar to look at the side of it so you can see what you are doing. I call that a minor issue because my keyboard has mute and volume control buttons on it and I can just use those to adjust the sound as needed.

The bottom line of all this for me is that I wouldn't buy this speaker as a "gaming speaker" but simply as a nice mid-range speaker who's sound quality I like, one that is easy to set up and use. Oh, and lest I sound too much like a Grinch, the lights really are pretty, the way Christmas lights are. It's just that they have nothing to do with gaming. :)

review_title: Okay For Light Computer Use But Not For Gaming, Extensive Typing Or Other Serious Work
review_text:
As an old, retired guy I spend a lot of time online gaming, streaming videos, and dabbling on social media. Over the last few months I've tried out a variety of keyboards and mice, some of them high end gaming gear. As soon as you take this keyboard and mouse out of the box it's clear that this is a low end rig. It just doesn't have the solid heft of more expensive equipment. That's not necessarily a bad thing though as I've used some excellent, inexpensive keyboards and mice. Sadly, this product is not of that caliber either.

The compact size makes the keyboard feel cramped when typing. Even as I'm writing this, my fingers are feeling strained from the cramped tightness. The manufacturer makes the 12 function/F key combos seem like a big deal. To me those combos just seem like an unnecessary complication. There are other, more standard ways of doing all those things without having to learn a whole new set of keys. The six "hot keys" seem to be just a set of video controls that duplicate functionality already available on any computer with a standard video player.

The mouse is particularly disappointing for anyone who does gaming. Now I'm just a casual gamer, by no means a hard core one, and even I find this mouse to be a handicap. In my main game you move your character forward by holding down both the left and right mouse buttons simultaneously. With other mice that is no big deal. With this mouse there is a perceptible hesitation or stutter before moving when holding down the buttons like that. That may not sound like a big deal to a non-gamer but that kind of stuttering can quickly get your character killed in a gaming battle. Also, it seems to take some effort to hold those buttons down. My fingers feel a strain in holding these mouse buttons down, a strain I haven't felt with other mice. And yes, I did try the suggested solutions for mouse problems offered in the "Manual" that came with this product (one tiny sheet printed on both sides). They didn't help.

So if you are mostly watching videos and reading Facebook on your computer, you will probably be okay with this gear. Any more serious use than that and you will want to pass on this stuff.

review_title: Too High Maintence For Me To Bother With
review_text:
The need for an uninterruptible power source is obvious to anyone with a computer or other expensive electronic equipment. The very day this product arrived, before I even opened the box, a severe thunderstorm knocked out power in my neighborhood. My two computers immediately went down and the screen on one kept flashing on and off even after all the power was dead. So yes, a UPS seems like an important piece of equipment these days. Sadly, this one is not for me. To be fair to the manufacturer though I need to give you a bit of context to help you evaluate if my reaction and this review would be applicable to you or not.

At age 70 I have a pretty low tolerance for muss and fuss. If it requires special handling, if it is a hassle to use, I don't want it. If it's not plug and play, I won't bother with it. For example, I do all my laundry in one load throwing everything in together without any sorting of any kind. It all gets washed and dried on the hot cycle. Anything that can't handle that gets tossed out. I treat everything like that. This UPS looks like an industrial strength product but acts like a delicate little snowflake. Coming out of the box it has 20 pages of instructions they want you to read before using. I didn't bother, just plugged it in, turned it on, and starting using the USB charger to juice up a battery run children's night light. A little while later I noticed a burnt plastic smell and saw the warping on the case that you can see in the attached photos. So this thing is not for me. More detail oriented and careful folks might have better luck with it. Thus I'm giving it a neutral 3 star rating and suggest you read through all the reviews here before deciding whether you want to try it yourself or not.

review_title: The Speaker Itself Is Good But Bluetooth...
review_text:
Bottom Line - The speaker itself is excellent but Bluetooth can be an irritating technology.

The speaker is lightweight and even has an attached carrying strap. Unlike a lot of lightweight products though, it doesn't feel flimsy or fragile at all. Instead it has a nice, solid, durable feel to it. While I am not an audiophile, the speaker has a deep, rich sound that I really like. It does well with audiobooks, music, and videos.

The problems seem to be with Bluetooth. One major issue is that the sound stutters while using Bluetooth. It's very noticeable when playing music and very irritating when listening to audiobooks. That's happened with every Bluetooth speaker I've ever tried. A google search indicates that it's a common problem related to the amount of information the computer is trying to pump out to the speaker. There's a checklist of possible issues to go through to try to fix the problem but the stuttering seems all too common with this technology.

Another issue involves changing modes on a Bluetooth speaker. To sidestep the stuttering I plugged this speaker into my computer with a standard jack. It worked fine and the sound was good. When I unplugged it to bring the speaker into another room with me, I had to redo my audio settings. When I plugged it back in with the jack, an audiobook played just fine but there was no sound while playing videos. Again, I had to go into the audio settings and fiddle with them to be able to watch a movie. I've had similar issues with other Bluetooth speakers.

If you are a techie you may be able to resolve such things quickly and easily. The less tech adept you are, the more hassle they will be though. Myself, I'm just going to leave the speaker connected to my pc via a good old fashioned jack because I like its sound. Bluetooth? Bah, I haven't got time to bother with it.

review_title: Works great for a mobile printer bag
review_text: I bought this for an HP OfficeJet 200 mobile printer. I do not take my printer on planes, but rather in my car as I travel to clients. I mention this because the cases sold specifically for mobile printers are very well padded or hard-sided. This is a laptop bag, but opens completely flat and has a strap that holds the printer. It also can hold both replacement BW & Color ink cartridges at once, plus power cord. There is a full pocket inside that holds the booklet and half a ream of paper without distorting paper. The specific mobile printer cases are at least $80 - this was under $20, and besides the heavier padding of the specific cases, there is not much difference. The printer itself is hard and folds completely, so unless you are worried about it getting crushed (like in a plane overhead bin), this works great. I figure if it is ok for a laptop, the printer should be no difference. The printer is 4'1/4" H, and this bag is about 3-1/2", but since it is not a hard-sided case, it fits well. I checked what it would be like if you used it for a laptop (it's intended use) just to see how it fit, and there is plenty of room for cords, accessories, and also an outside pocket for pens, etc. Very substantial bag for $20. Recommend.

review_title: Perfect for amateur or beginning photographers/videographers!
review_text:
If you are a budding photographer or videographer, the Wikico 4K camera is for you. Society has moved away from printing out photos, and instead turns to using their smart phones. I on the other hand love scrapbooking and assembling photo albums. Sometimes, I even print those that I take on my phone. This camera is a nice alternative. I like that it is not overly expensive and yet gives you the feel of holding a camera. For those who are beginning photographers or who want to do this as a hobby, it is perfect. It is a small investment for an easy to use camera. We own several high end cameras, both film and digital, that I could use if I wanted to go on a serious photo shoot.

In terms of value for your money, this is the perfect set. Teens and young adults can enjoy it. Of course, once you are serious about the hobby you will invest in a more expensive device. It comes with everything you need: a wide angle lens, SD card, charger, batteries, USB cable and an adapter, with the exception of a bag. The picture quality is decent. It can produce videos and photos. So if you are into YouTubing or posting videos, you’ll enjoy this too. It is pretty easy to set up, the battery life is decent and it is extremely light weight. I give it 4 stars.

I used option 1 (the tabs) and have had no problem with it staying put. From the side, no one can see what is on your screen (or what you are working on), but as you move to the front of the monitor it becomes more visible. And finally it does minimize some of the harsh blue light. I’d recommend this.

This plastic case appears to be well made and is attractive. There is a latch that closes securely.  I really like the colors, grey and teal. [This case does come in other colors (i.e., pink, white, yellow, blue, black and lime green)]. It is watertight and convenient to use while traveling, or engaging in outside activities (i.e., beach, hiking or fishing). You can just place your essentials, like your DL, credit card, cash, some headphones, a USB charger, or SD cards (if you are a photographer) inside. For short activities like walking your dog in the park or doing a short bike ride, you can use this case to secure an ID and some money if needed. Or you can attach it to a backpack or throw inside your bag. Now the issue that I have with this product. In my opinion the designers of this case did not take into account wanting to secure a cell phone. To be honest, that is the main reason that I ordered the Pelican Go, so that I can leave my purse at home and secure my personal items inside of it while doing stuff. For example, we have an annual race in Atlanta known as the Peachtree Road Race. This would have been perfect to secure my items while I participated. I can fit some (flat) items and maybe a lip gloss inside of it, but not a cell phone. I own a One Plus 6T, and it doesn't. Out of curiosity I tried my husband’s work cell (a Samsung) and it does not. I even tried my son's, which is an older model of the iPhone and it doesn't. So unless you have a very tiny cell, this case isn't going to work. However, if having your cell phone isn't an issue, you should be good to go. And finally, Pelican offers a lifetime guarantee on this product, which I assume means that any issues you might have should be resolved by contacting the company.

I have owned/purchased several different types of headphones in the past ….Beats, Koss, Sony, Sennheiser, even wired V-moda’s, and I would say these are in my top two.

These headphones are attractive...I received these in gunmetal black. If you’d like to customize your look, you can order different colored metal shields and ear cushions.

The earmuffs have soft cushions and surround the entire ear. More importantly, these muffs allow for several hours of comfort if worn for extended periods of time. The volume control and mic are integrated on the right side of the headset. And while these can be worn for several activities, I wouldn’t really suggest working out in them, they are too nice (or expensive), but it can be done.

The headset comes with their own case, a USB charging cord, a 3.5mm 45’ degree plug with 24k gold tips and a clip to hang them from your bag or jeans. Bluetooth connection is fairly easy, there is a switch that you push on the back of the right earpiece. Once activated it gives a tone that lets you know it is trying to connect. Once you activate bluetooth on your device, it is ready.That’s right, these headphones provide great sound and are WIRELESS. What a fantastic feature. And you even have the option of not using the wireless feature by connecting to various portable devices (i.e., smartphone, laptop, tablets, etc) with the provided “mic 1 speakeasy cable”.

And finally, when I listened to different genres of music (i.e., jazz, rock, rap, classical) , the sound was clear and the quality is among the best. The frequency response listed is 5Hz-30kHz and that appears to be accurate. The sound wasn’t muted or distorted.

Overall, I would give these headsets 5 stars. These are definitely worth the money.

review_title: Just what you need when you are on the go…a LowePro for your GoPro!
review_text:
Reviewed by my husband, a photography enthusiast.

Over the last 20 years, my husband has purchased several LowePro camera bags/backpacks (i.e., Mini Trekker & Micro-Trekker 100). He has found that they have been some of the best he has ever owned. He prefers backpacks because they are easy to carry and keep up with, especially if you are on the go. Backpacks also allow for easy storage and are super convenient. They give you freedom of movement and your hands are free to capture those special moments that you may not otherwise get if you were holding a bag in your hand. The Viewpoint (LowePro) BP 250 is the perfect addition to his bag collection especially since it is specially designed for small video equipment.

Here’s what he liked:

• This bag is attractive. The design is smart, functional and full of surprises. The Viewpoint BP250 is well-made with plenty of room for your Go Pro and accompanying equipment. There is a ton of storage (inside and out). There are several compartments where you can store your accessories, cords, lenses and other equipment. On the outside of the main bag, there is a zipper pocket (which allows for small items like a memory stick/card or thumbdrive). review_title: I'm officially a hit with my sons! They love these headphones.
review_text:
I was looking for stocking stuffers for my two teenaged boys. Both had expressed an interest in the Beats by Dre. I don't know about you, but I was looking for a reasonable pair of headphones to accompany other high priced gifts (new Xbox, Laptop etc) they were getting for Christmas. BUT paying almost $200 for the Beats seemed unreasonable. So when these (V-Moda, Crossfade LP) were highlighted on Amazon on Black Friday, I seized the opportunity and purchased two pair (which was still cheaper than one pair of Beats), and hoped that I could rely on the reviews that I read. (Please note that I did read reviews for Beats, and found that the V-Moda pair received more positive reviews.) So with both sets of reviews under my belt, I begin to compare the features and was even more convinced that I had made a wise purchase. (Also note that later my sons were able to compare them with the Solo Beats by Dre and they still liked the Crossfades better.)

Features that my sons say make these a standout amongst most headsets:
* The overall sound quality is great and not too bass heavy.
*The over the ear covers (ear piece) have memory cushions. They are very comfortable and you can't hear outside noise (Of course I found this to be true when they could not hear me calling them. Of course, they may be ignoring me). I also can't hear the music that they are listening to.
* The volume or pause feature can be used from a control button on the cord. They even say that besides skipping songs, the rarely have to touch their devices when using these headphones.
* These earphones are versatile and can be used with multiple devices (i.e., the computer, Ipod, cell phones, etc). They are able to even use them in the car by connecting with the stereo.
* These headphones are stylish and attractive. I ordered one pair in Phantom Chrome and the other in Phantom Black.

And finally, what Mom likes about the headphones...well, the price. These headphones were reasonably priced and offered the same features as the Beats. And later when I compared them with the Beats, they appear to be better quality in terms of sound quality and workmanship (the Beats are plastic looking and don't seem to be as well constructed as the Crossfade, which seems sturdy).
Finally, overall for the money I think I got a top notch product. I highly recommend these to anyone on the market for some headphones and give this product five (5) stars.

False advertising is a bad practice, and we're conditioned to expect less all the time. But my time and money is worth every penny, so $350 may be cheaper than other products, but I value my money and expect things to work as expected, as advertised, and nothing less.
