review_title: Solid build quality but with a few quirks.
review_text:
I ordered the ‘adidas RPT-01 Bluetooth Sport On-Ear Headphones - New’ for review as I am a sucker for wireless headphones. My initial thoughts right out of the box were that these are solidly built, lightweight and beautifully designed headphones. They look and feel "high end". I’ve now had these for nearly a month and feel that I am ready to share more.

First I would like to comment on the fact that these are touted as “Sport” headphones and my idea of “Sport” headphones are more of the "in-ear" earbuds, which fit much more securely and do better in the “head-shake” tests. I honestly don’t see these working for anything more extreme than jogging. Don’t get me wrong, they do fit well and are lightweight but just don’t quite pass the “head-shake” test haha. These are IPX4 Water Resistant which is a bonus, and the padded ear cups are removable and washable which is nice (though I have not been able to figure out how).

Pairing was super easy and they sound really good for “On-Ear” headphones which leads me to comfort of “On-Ear” headphones and wearing glasses. I wear glasses and I have issues with “On-Ear” comfort in general. These are no different. Though they are very light and comfortable at first, within only a few minutes of wear they get quite uncomfortable for me. With that said, my Son who does not wear glasses has zero issues with comfort and says that they are really comfortable to him. Also speaking of comfort, personally (after about 30min of wearing) my ears tend to feel like I am wearing Winter Earmuffs as my ears get quite warm. This isn’t a huge deal but I thought it worth mentioning.

Now on to my absolute favorite thing about these headphones. The single Toggle Button on the right earphone. This is so simple to use and can control pretty much everything. Long Press to turn the headphones On or Off. Toggle forward or back to go forward or back a track. Toggle up or down for Volume Up or Down. Short press to Answer and End calls. This innovation is absolutely incredible and makes this the easiest pair of wireless headphones I have ever used. The button on the Left Earphone has the ability to assign three different functions. For example a single click could activate your phones default assistant or double click to play your favorite Spotify playlist and three clicks could play a different Spotify playlist. So basically the left Earphone button can only be used to use your default assistant or play Spotify. My guess is that Adidas could eventually add other apps to this button (with a firmware update) but for now, you only have the two to work with. In my experience so far, this button is a little tricky. First off, the button does not protrude much and can be harder to get it to click, especially if you have large fingers. Once you figure out how to get it to click, the next issue is that you really need to click fast to get the triple click to work. I've gotten to where I can get the triple click to work nearly 80% of the time. It's not a big deal because there's really only two apps it can control. I did notice that if you use this button to start playing Spotify, the Spotify app does not actually open on your phone which kind of freaked me out. This means that the headphones will be all that you need to use to quickly start playing Spotify. If you need to access it for anything else (on Spotify) you'll need to actually launch it from your phone.

USB C charging! More companies need to get on board with USB C and I appreciate the fact that Adidas have included USB C charging which makes for super fast charging of the Adidas RPT-01 Headphones. I have not fully tested the advertised 40 hour runtime but I can say that I have used these a couple hours here and there over my time with them, and I have only had to fully charge them once.

The Adidas app is pretty basic but it does offer some nice eq presets with the option to customize your own. Personally I like to start with the Adidas preset which is "flat" by default. Then if you prefer, you can customize it. The sound is amazing but not quite comparable to some of the other higher end noise cancelling headphones which I won't name.

Overall, I do love the Adidas RPT-01 headphones and they definitely have a place in my collection. Really the only two complaints that I have is, the comfort issue while wearing glasses, and I feel that at this price point they should have come with a nice protective case.

review_title: Love EVERYTHING about these except the soft flimsy case.
review_text:
I ordered the 'New Sennheiser Momentum Wireless Noise Cancelling Headphones with Auto On/Off, Smart Pause Functionality and Smart Control App' to review. So far, and after almost a month of testing and playing with these amazing headphones, I am ready to share my thoughts.

First and foremost I must express that I am really disappointed in the case that Sennheiser has included with these "High End" Headphones. I mean come on Sennheiser. It seems pretty standard these days for higher end headphones to come with a nice clam-shell hard case. The case provided is a soft zipper pouch with little to no padding at all. I would not feel comfortable to stuff these into my backpack or even suitcase for that matter.

Now with that said, these headphones ARE solid. The stainless steel headband is sturdy and not fragile. The headphones themselves are of a very nice quality construction with real leather, both on the headband and ear pads. The physical buttons (which I tend to like much better than the new "touch" buttons on some of the others out there) are nice and solid and function perfectly.

The sound is absolutely AMAZING! I compared them to my wife's Bose QuietComfort 35 II headphones and honestly I love the sound signature on the Momentum's better. And as for the Noise Cancellation, I honestly can't tell much difference between the two. I do think the Bose do a slightly better job but for the sound quality you get out of the Momentum's, I'll stick with the Momentum's.

As for the weight and comfort compared to the Bose, the Bose are lighter but not necessarily more comfortable. The Momentum's just feel SOLID. The Bose feel nice but light and flimsy.

Other thoughts - Others complain about the "auto pause" feature on the Momentum's, but I personally love it. Others complain about the way you have to power these off by folding them up and personally, it doesn't bother me a bit. I would rather that then pressing a button and wondering if you pressed it correctly. This way, you KNOW they are off.

Battery life isn't the greatest compared to many others in this price range but for me it's just fine. I don't travel long distances and for the occasional 5-6 hour flights I rarely take, they will give me what I need. Plus with the much appreciated USB type C charging port, they will charge pretty fast.

Overall I LOVE everything about these, except for the soft flimsy case provided. Sound is fantastic! They are loud with rich thumping Bass, Nice clean Mids and wonderfully crisp Highs and for me the Sound Isolation works great.

review_title: Packs a punch for the size.
review_text:
I ordered the iHome Alexa Built-in Bluetooth Speaker Portable Wireless Waterproof Rechargeable Lights Up to Music, with Speakerphone, Passive Subwoofer, Carry Strap, Durable Shockproof Floatable Design (IBT158) to replace an old sub par portable speaker that I’ve had for years. The iHome is quite the upgrade with the built in Alexa, better sound and being waterproof. I’ve had this product now for several weeks and would like to share my thoughts.

I must say that the sound is pretty good and packs a punch in such a small size. It’s much better than the much smaller and several years old portable wireless speaker that I have been using. In fact there really is no comparison at all. Let’s just say that it is the best sounding portable wireless speaker that I personally have ever owned. My daughter who “borrowed” the older speaker some time ago (and she never gave it back) keeps asking to "borrow" the new iHome as she says, “it’s louder and sounds WAY better”. I absolutely agree with her. Plus the lights on this thing are a nice touch, and there are options (via a button on top) to cycle through and change the color options or turn them off.

Setting up the iHome for Bluetooth and Alexa was easy and very straight forward, and there has been no issues whatsoever. We are mainly an Android household however my oldest daughter uses an iPhone and everyone has had the same great experience. So far my only complaint is that the Bluetooth connectivity distance isn’t the greatest but with that said, none of my Bluetooth devices really have much range in our home so I am not going to knock points off for that. The sound out of this little guy makes up for the Bluetooth short comings and the bonus of Alexa being packed into this as well as the waterproof features make this a great value for the selling price.

One thing worth mentioning is that to use Alexa, you can’t just say “Alexa” to activate her. You do have to physically press a button on the iHome speaker to access her, which isn’t a huge deal breaker, but because of this, you can’t use other Alexa devices to make an announcement and have it broadcast to the iHome speaker. Being fairly new to the Alexa and smart home world, I am not going to hold this shortcoming against the iHome device. It actually makes sense that with this being portable, you wouldn’t want to have Alexa always listening and drain the battery while on the go. Speaking of Battery life, it's decent but not spectacular by any means. This is pretty subjective however as usually when I use the iHome, I'm listening to it at a pretty high volume ;)

Another observation is that this uses micro USB to charge, and I really would like to see more devices using the newer and better USB C charging capabilities.

As far as the “waterproof” capabilities go, I must report that I have yet to float the device in a pool or let the kids play with it outside while running through the sprinklers. I know that it says it’s waterproof and it absolutely looks like it would hold up to getting wet as it is very well built, rugged and quite solid, but I don't want to risk ruining this new toy that the whole family has been enjoying so much.

review_title: This vendor (Selens) delivered what they promised -- a 59x78.7inches Pop Up Green/Blue Screen
review_text:
My order was delivered on time within 2 days. It is the correct material (thick woven material that I cannot see through, and slightly shiny), chromacolor green and blue color, and correct size. It was in its carrying case and the case was sealed in plastic. I knew other seller products were supposedly hard to fold back down and so I tried folding mine right away. It folded down for the most part easily (took me two tries to get the hang of it), but then it popped closed easily. It opens flat. There are a few small wrinkles that should shake themselves out if I hang up the screen, but I think they are fine to use the screen with anyway. And there are straps to hang the screen in portrait or landscape layout, which I like very much.

I really searched for a vendor I could trust. Some of the other sellers had customer reviews saying their screens were nylon and not muslin, had dark colors, wouldn't lay flat, and couldn't be closed. I didn't want to buy from any of those vendors and waited a long time for a seller who might deliver a product that matched their ad. I took a chance on this seller (Selens) even though they had no reviews mainly because they were so very accurate in listing the size of the screen as 59x78.7 inches. I thought that this was a seller who wanted to do a good job for their customer. Thank you for delivering what you promised, Selens.

One comment -- there is a small (oil?) stain/streak about 2 inches on the green side, but you can't see it when looking directly at the background so the manufacturer probably didn't see it. But if you look at the screen from a high angle it is noticeable. I'll have to shoot some video/photos to see if it is a problem. I don't think it will be. I didn't see it on the blue side which is darker, but I just glanced. I'll look to see if it is on both sides later. Again, I don't think there is a problem as on the green side you can't see it if looking directly at the screen. But otherwise I liked what was delivered so far. :-)

I got this headset during the 50% off deal and I am really enjoying it with Battlefield 5. I decided to upgrade from my Logitech G430 headset. I was mainly looking for a wireless headset that had great battery life, great sound and did not cost too much. Even without the deal, the $200 price point is still reasonable compared to other wireless headsets. I was considering the Corsair and Astro's before purchasing this one. I am using this headset for my PC only, to game.

The Headset:
- Customizable buttons to change the Equalizer, play/pause, and many other options to choose from
- Convenient volume dial to change sound on the fly. This is great so you dont have to minimize the game and adjust the volume settings with the mouse
- Headset grips my head. I have an angled forehead which my old headset would easily slide off when moving around
- Comfy ear pieces that does not cram my ears and feel uncomfortable
- Comes with long braided charging cable, AUX cables, and RCA cables
- USB adapter to connect the wireless headset it plug and play. You just need to make sure you install the Logitech dashboard to customize the headset
- The Logitech logo and a line down each ear-cuff lights up. To me this is a pointless feature as I am wearing the headset and cannot see the lighting and only uses up battery life. I disabled the lights and my battery life increased by 3 hours.

Sound:
The sound i will say is significantly better than my G430. There are multiple equalizer profiles to choose from (FPS, Cinema, etc.). Once you turn on surround sound and 7.1, it makes a big difference of sounds. You can change the treble, bass, and customize the sound to your liking.

Battery:
I cannot say too much about the battery life, but after a full charge, and turning off the leds on the headset. It said I have 12 hours of battery left. After wearing the headset playing Battlefield 5 for 4 hours, I still had 93% battery life. Overtime with charges and draining, i would assume the life would degrade a bit and would get around 10 hours of battery. I did not check how long it takes to charge the headset from a full depletion.

The only cons I have are the pointless LED lights if you are not showing off your headset. I do feel the headband part of the headset is not as strong as I would have expected it to be, just do not twist headband much.

Personally, I like this keyboard - I intend to use it when traveling instead of lugging along my oversized laptop. Recommended.

review_title: Nice sounding, versital studio mic - large and solidly constructed
review_text:
This is a USB based studio mic that's mounted on a desktop stand. The mic can be swiveled in the stand to tilt forward or back as needed. The mic itself is solidly constructed... it feels very well made. The stand is similarly constructed and should sit firmly in place. Theres a headphone volume control on the front of the body, along with a mute button, and similarly positioned on the rear of the body is a polar pattern selector switch and a gain control for adjusting the mic's recording output. The pickup patterns available are:stereo, omni, cardioid and figure 8.

I have some typical studio mice, but this is my first USB based mic, so I ran it through some typical trials to see how it fared. First of all, I found the sound to be accurate and with just the slightest "edge" - which seems to give it a slight touch of presence, especially in cardioid mode. Playing with tv he polar patterns, I could tell a bit of change in tone as I moved in close or away from the mic when in cardioid or figure 8 pattern - the effect is expected for these patterns and, though slight, were definitely there. Omni mode (picks up sound from all directions) did not show this effect (you would not expect it to). As for off axis rejection, I tried singing off to one side and then the other. Again, it performed as expected with no rejection whatsoever in omni mode. Rejection was minimal in cardiod and figure eight mode, though. (I would have preferred more). Also, in cardioid mode (signal is picked up directly in front of the mic only), I found the directional pattern a little wide. I like to use this mode specifically to isolate what's directly in front of the mic from the rest of the room. It works as it should, but I would have preferred it to be slightly more "directional". Finally, for stereo mode... this probably had the most impressive sound. It truly delivered a stereo sound... evenly balanced, with no dropout in the center. I even snapped my fingers on either side to see if it would pick up properly... it performed exactly as it should. As for sensitivity, it picked up the central heating unit fans in the background (just like a studio mic should), so some form of noise reduction would be called for (or turn off the hvac). Self noise did not appear to be evident - another specification that would have been nice for them to share (I dont even know if self noise is an issue with USB mics- this one didnt seem to have a problem with it).

Most people that I know would be interested in things like diaphragm size... that kind of detailed technical information is lacking from any of the paperwork that comes with this mic. It makes reference to a three capsule head, which makes me assume theres 3 diaphragms in there with the pickup pattern selector turning them on and off as needed, but no other info is provided.

All in all, I was impressed with this mic... it sounds good and has great versatility. It simply plugs into your computer's USB port and you're good to go (you may have to select the mic through your systems settings page). I think it would be ideal for any desk top application, podcasts, etc. It even has a screw in stand mount on the bottom. The only thing missing is some kind of a shock mount system, like a spider mount, or something), to shield it from noises that may vibrate through the desk to the mic. I suppose, sitting it on some foam would serve to isolate it.

review_text:
I'm somewhat particular about my music and my headphones and have specific things I look for. I'll try to touch on those items in this review.

Sound Quality: obviously most important. I look for solid bass (not boomy or hyped). And clear trebles (not sizzling or hyped). These headphones performed okay on both counts although it did seem the bass was a little hyped. I have some expensive headphones that these did not compare favorably to. I also look for general clarity in vocals... here, they did good... nothing nasally or buried in the mix. The exception came when turning on the noise reduction circuit. More on that later.

Comfort: okay, I have a big head (size xxl hat). So comfort is important to me. These headphones are adequate in that regard. I had to extend them fully, but at full extension they fit me properly and comfortably, sealing off around the ear. They did not completely surround my ears as some studio monitors do, but they did cover my ears. The padding is decent and I was able to listen for a reasonable amount of time before they became uncomfortable pressing on the perimeter of my ear. If your head/ears are smaller, my guess is they'd be plenty comfortable.

Noise reduction: I'm not used to using this feature and wasn't sure how to test it, so I simply sat down next to an air cleaner I have in my home and tried turning noise reduction on and off to see what happened. There was definitely a reduction in the noise... mainly in the lower frequencies. It didnt completely eliminate the sound of the blowing air, but what was left was a thinned out version of the original noise. It was definitely an improvement in the level of noise. The only thing I didnt care for was that there seemed to be an impact on the sound of the music also. Again, the noise reduction thinned the music and left it a little nasally.

Controls: straight forward controls. Theres a slider to turn noise reduction on and off and an adjacent button to activate the phone function. Since the phone button was just below the slider, I kept accidentally turning on the phone when trying to activate the noise reduction. Better button placement would have helped.

Overall, I was reasonably impressed with these headphones. Especially considering the price, they seem to do well. They come with a nice, soft sided carry case and needed cables. I expect I'll get some good use from these.

review_title: Works well and will satisfy even the pickiest reader
review_text:
I love to read but held off buying a Kindle until now because I could not abide the resolution of early generations' screens. The fonts used to look penciled-in, jagged and coarse to my eye. Plus, I travel frequently and would need a backlight for reading on long flights, and the earliest Kindles lacked a backlight option.

Times change, and when I finally succumbed to the Kindle's siren call just ahead of a sun-drenched holiday where there'd be zero hope of reading poolside on my iPad or iPhone, I was happy to see that the Paperwhite model now comes with a high-resolution display and a backlight at a reasonable price.

Reading Experience

The fonts do look pretty nice now. There are about six or eight font choices you can apply, and you can choose their size and weight easily from a menu. I'm still experimenting to find a favorite. I'm a bit of a font snob but have no serious criticisms of the kerning and justification options (I prefer ragged right formatting to fully-justified, and most books allow this).

The backlight works well, is fully adjustable, and is nice and even save for a bit of faint scalloping at the far bottom edge.

Glare has been no problem at all.

Images look pretty terrible, but that's not what this device is for. It's a single-purpose tool for consuming textual books in any environment, and at that it excels.

There are lots of reader tools, such as word lookup and things like that. I haven't explored most of those options.

User Interface

I have a passcode set, and entering the passcode is weirdly slow; you must pause significantly between characters.

The touch interface works well, but there are some drawbacks to it. Mostly, it can be annoying to fumble the device and find you've lost your place in the process of grabbing it. That's less of a problem with the dedicated buttons on some other models.

I do wish the Goodreads option were removable from the menu as I have no interest in it and have accidentally tapped it a few times.

The single ads you see on waking the device don't bother me. They're static and inoffensive and go away with a swipe. I'm unmotivated to spend the $20 to eliminate them, but that option is there if they bug you.

Slightly more concerning is that occasionally the text has lacked contrast. But I've found that going into and out of a menu, which forces a screen refresh, can help that. (I have Page Refresh turned off to minimize the blinking effect that otherwise accompanies most page turns, limiting the blinks to chapter transitions. This may be the cause of the occasional contrast loss. Now that I've found what seems to be a work-around, I'll leave Page Refresh off.)

Connectivity

Both the WiFi and mostly-free 3G connectivity work well. So far I've tested the 3G in five countries with no problem. WiFi has worked well and I've had no problem connecting to hotel WiFi that requires browser input-- the Kindle's "experimental browser" has worked sufficiently well for that.

My understanding is that Amazon-purchased book downloads, syncing and updates are free over 3G even if you are roaming internationally. But, if you're roaming internationally, you will be charged a small amount for downloading documents other than Amazon-sold books. review_title: Surprisingly good functionality for the money
review_text:
UPDATE: Six months in, this router has been flawless. AND I've discovered it has its own dynamic DNS support capability. That's a nice feature if you run any sort of server application. So, I continue to be impressed with this product.

---

I will be keeping a close eye on this router, which I just purchased yesterday, because it seems too good to be true. So far, in my 24 hours of usage since purchasing it for $29 at Walmart (sorry, Amazon, I was in a hurry) I have found it to be flexible and powerful in my unusual application, which is remote and requires 100% uptime with occasional bursts of heavy usage. Mine is a factory-fresh rather than refurb unit, incidentally.

I'll admit I had some trouble believing a router this cheap could be as good as this one turned out to be (assuming it stays reliable-- but, the one I bought trumpets a lifetime guarantee on the box). I expected something dumbed-down, with seriously constrained functionality and annoying firmware. (This model's v3 hardware, although Broadcom BCM5356-based, is not compatible with alternative firmware such as DD-WRT due to its problematic NVRAM size.) It's a single-stream design, with an internalized antenna, potentially suggesting performance limitations. And it's from Netgear, which I've frankly not had great luck with before... but it's been years since I've tried one of their products, and the reviews here are generally good. Most of the negative reviews here relate to support experiences, but my networking knowledge-level is expert, so ...what the heck, did I mention it was $29? An easy roll of the dice.

Though my application requires custom configuration, I initially started the unit using its web-based wizard, which you access by connecting your computer (via cable or WiFi) and pointing your browser to 192.168.1.1. With the unit connected to my cable modem, it set itself up quickly and voila, Internet. For most people this would be good enough and the job would be done. Kudos to Netgear for delivering the product with WPA-2 encryption enabled! They provide a SSID and password on a printed label. So, you're good to go. And its default configuration is just fine for most folks' usage.

For my application, however, I needed to cable several devices including a VoIP adaptor (a la [...] and a server with several ports exposed to the Internet. The unit needed to be set to a specific IP address scheme, SSID and password. And a dynamic-DNS utility on the server needed to communicate with my DNS provider. ...To accomplish these and other advanced tasks, the browser-based configurator at 192.168.1.1 has an Advanced tab. Proceeding through the settings is straightforward and similar to other reasonably-configurable routers. The default settings established earlier by the wizard remain intact in the Advanced panes so you are starting from a known-operable configuration. All good.

So I proceeded through each of my customizations, taking care to click the Apply button after modifying any pane. Usually there's a ten-second delay during which the unit sets up the new settings; a few necessitate that the router reboot itself. Everything went smoothly.

So, for $29 I'd replicated an unusual configuration and everything was working. But how well?

Okay so my wife had to take an important international FaceTime call as I was finishing up. So, for a while there the server was downloading some massive updates, two ssh clients were talking to the server, VoIP was in use, six WiFi clients were doing whatever they were doing, a 3G microcell tower was initializing and downloading firmware updates to itself ...and FaceTime was running smoothly with a high frame-rate on her third-gen iPad. A nice acid test!

In particular, I did not feel the need to mess with the unit's default QoS settings... and additional props to Netgear for including QoS in a router this inexpensive!

So far, I'm impressed. It's hard to imagine a better value in a router. I'll update this review if there are any reliability issues, but so far, so good. So excellent, in fact.

review_title: Was A 1 Star Until I Adjusted It, Makes It 4 Stars
review_text:
I received this mouse on September 17th. It is now December 19th, so I have given it three months of use before writing this review. Before purchasing this 3M mouse, I was using just your average, typical, mouse with a scrolling wheel in the center. For work I am on the computer around 13 hours a day. Recently my right wrist, forearm, and shoulder started to ache and eventually became very painful because of the unnatural position my mouse held my hand/arm in. Also I use the scrolling wheel very often and my middle finger (which I used to scroll with), started to swell and experience pain in the joints, with a hard, painful bone-like spur on the underside.
After using the 3M Ergonomic mouse, the swelling/pain in my finger joint went away immediately, and the bone spur also dissipated.
However, while it did alleviate the pain in my wrist, it actually caused more pain in my forearm and shoulder, and now the bonus of the entire thumb area of the hand - from the wrist up to the tip of my thumb. After a week of looking at the design and messing around with folded towels under my arm, it finally dawned on me why this mouse caused so much pain....

Though I purchased the 'small', the hand shaft is still too long, and with the toggle button at the top of it, it holds the thumb in an unnatural upward position thereby putting strain on that entire bone. When you lay your arm down on a table, with palm facing inward, in the relaxed position a thumb is NOT sticking upwards, but instead it naturally lays level with the index finger. Hence the hand shaft is too tall.

The shaft cannot be cut down obviously, so the 'deck', the part that the hand rests upon, had to be raised. To to do this I took a few sheets of paper towels, folded them to the thickness that would give the best height for my hand, then wrapped sturdy packing tape around it, to keep it folded (and makes it easy to wipe clean). Then I made a 'collar' out of paper towel to go around the base of the hand shaft, to which I taped the front part of the folded paper towels to, it helps keep it from shifting. I then put a large piece of rolled tape on the rest of the 'deck' which holds the rest of the folded towels onto the deck.
Did it work?
Yes, it did. The paper towels have conformed perfectly to the shape of my hand, and is very comfortable. It stays rather clean because of being wrapped in packing tape, which I periodically wipe clean with rubbing alcohol. More importantly, it has elevated all pain in my arm, shoulder, and thumb area. It holds my hand and fingers in a very natural position.

So while it is not perfect, and I shouldn't have to make padding for it, I gave this mouse 4 stars because I do like it, even though I had to make adjustments to make it work. It glides smoothly on a mouse pad. The toggle button is smooth, as is the scroll button. It does take some time getting used to scrolling this way, but once I got the hang of it, it's second nature to me now.

Some tips:
* I found myself 'gripping' the mouse like a joy stick because I was so not used to a mouse of this shape, which makes the four fingers hurt after a while and would make me hit the scroll button inadvertently. I had to keep reminding myself to relax my hand. No need to 'grip' it, it's not going to take you on a 'white knuckle' ride!

* Does not move well on thin or hard surfaces. I had a very, very thin mouse pad and it would not glide well on it. I purchased a thicker pad and now it moves smoothly.

* Because the hand shaft stands so far up, I have knocked this mouse right off my desk a number of times, my arm would hit it, or walking past my desk my sweater would catch it. So when not in use keep it away from the edge of the desk. At least I know that this mouse can take a beating!

review_title: outlandish price for poor optics and flawed alignment
review_text:
I bought these at the same time as a Steiner 7x50 Marine model. The Commander XP's use the same case but for triple the price have better eyepieces, coatings and optical specifications and a few additional or better accessories than the Marine model.

I compared them in terrestrial and celestial viewing but the easiest comparison is done with astronomical subjects since they really define performance clearly. The images in the Marine model merged effortless. In the Commander XP, I have difficulty merging the images. They're obviously badly out of collimation. I don't care to fix this myself on binos in this price range.

I evaluated the real and apparent fields of view as well as the sharpness near the edge of the field.

In the Marine model, the real field of view is reasonably wide but apparent field is quite narrow. It's not bad but it's not a spectacular vista either. In the Commander XP, the real FOV is only barely perceptibly wider. Steiner's website lists the specifications. The apparent field is about the same. The almost indiscernable extra width of real FOV does not contribute much to the value for triple the price.

On the Marine model, I put Sirius and Jupiter in the center of the field. They look nice. Moving the binoculars so that the objects were farther from the center of the field I could see the image degraded about half-way to the edge of the field of view. Near the very edge, the image was appalling. Much more than half-way out of the center of the field of view, the star or planet turns from a bright point to just a smear. Near the very edge it's a dim smudge. I tried the same with the Commander XP. It was every bit as bad.

Are the XP's better on dim objects? The optics are supposed to transmit 96% light compared to the Commander V's 95% and the Marine's 90%. I saw very little difference on dim objects like the Orion nebula or the background of the Pleides or Jupiter's moons. Again, I can't see the justification for triple the price.

Both have generious eye-relief, 20mm for the Marine and 22mm for these XP's. They also have the same weight and dimensions. They're heavy but still reasonable if you're wearing a thick coat to pad your chest and a harness to keep them from swinging all over if you're moving. Also, at 7x they're reasonable for handholding. For me, 7x50 is about the limit for handholding. Heavier or higher power would be too shakey. 6x56 might be nicer if they were more common.

Where the XP is clearly better is with small details like the click-loc strap attachments (for use with Steiner straps and harnesses only), the better eyepiece covers, lens covers, focuser grips, shading eye-cups, and various doo-dads that come in the case. It comes with a flotation strap which the Marine doesn't, but I would still rather prefer a harness which neither comes with.

I bought these Porro prism binos because I thought for the high price they should be outstanding. While roof prism binos might require fifteen hundred dollars or more to achieve optical exellence (or so I've heard), it should be easier with porros. With these, it's possible they lost collimation after leaving the factory but the optical quality is lacking nontheless. To be honest, I have nothing to compare them to. I've never seen better, but I was still totally underwhelmed by the performance which was only slightly better than I would expect from binoculars in the hundred dollar range.

review_title: Returned to Canon for repair for out-of-the-box sensor mis-calibration
review_text:
Tried to write a review of this on DP Review, but their over-the-top, religious zealots banned one post for using the word "gobsmacked" (when describing my experiences with the first 6D) and another post because of the word "pissed," (after calling Canon and finding out I would have to send it to them at my own cost) both banned claiming violation of their "rule 6," for "profanity." So..., I'll make sure my review is somewhere that people can or might see it and be able to use for their determination if this camera is right for them.

For the price, overall, it's NOT a good deal. Uses the same processor as the Rebels (ie; T7i) and the same articulating screen. Also, the focus points are all bunched-up in the center of the sensor, so a FF sensor is kind of meaningless for AF when you only cover 40% of sensor and it's all in the center? Also, the sensor is a step back from the older 6D. It claims more MP's, but really, if it doesn't have the DR of the original camera it's supposed to replace, then I say it's a step back. Yes, it has DPAF, but that's a function of the processor, not the sensor. So it's basically a weather sealed (maybe) FF T7i. Except without the flash...

Honestly, the T7i feels like a toy, but the few weeks I had and tested it, it was rained on, snowed on and I generally beat the camera up. It took the abuse with zero issues and the DPAF worked brilliantly. Photo's rivaled that of this 6D MII.

First day I had the 6D Mark II, something seemed wonky, but an update of the firmware to 1.0.4 fixed the weird switch issue. Nothing could fix the wildly un-calibrated ISO issue though. After talks with Canon repair center, they said to ship it to them. Since it was after the 30-days I have to return something at BB, I had no other choice.

So why did I send it in? The ISO calibration was WAY off from the get go. Orders of magnitude off. The orig 6D had me gobsmacked (oh my..., there's that profanity!) with it's low-noise at very high ISO. That was unbelievable. This camera though couldn't touch a 5D MII, a 70D or the T7i. Same lens, same coverage (making allowance for 1.6CF of the 70D/T7i), same shutter speed, same aperture, the three test subjects were 1200ISO, with the 6D MII, to get the same exposure, I was at 3200 and higher ISO. Kind of the opposite of what you'd expect, especially considering my opposite experiences with the original 6D. Esp from a $1600+ NEW camera/sensor. And sending back to Canon means YOU Pay the shipping to them. And insurance. So roll in $35 more into the price of the camera.

Some will say just a fluke and that these things happen. They do. But with all the issues combined in a camera that is sub-par to a $750 rebel in almost every aspect, well..., I say stay away until the price comes down to a point that it makes sense to buy a FF rebel with (alleged) weather sealing and no flash.

review_text:
I am loving the Logitech Rechargeable Touchpad T650 with its user-friendly ease of use and many great features. The small size of 5 1/4" width x 5" length, smooth surface, rechargeable battery, very responsive with light-touch to activate gestures, on/off switch, place anywhere to use and sturdy design makes this the perfect touchpad for me. I got this touchpad as my computer mouse stopped working. I thought about a touchscreen monitor, but opted for this touchpad instead as it would be so nice to not have to stretch and fatigue my arm with the actions needed with a touchscreen monitor. The touchpad only needs a very light touch of the fingers to click, slide and navigate the gestures to activate the product features, which is most excellent to keep stress off the fingers. I have a desktop computer with Windows 7 right now, but this touchpad supports Windows 8 when I make the change which is another plus for me. Note a gesture not listed on the Logitech site that I just happen to notice worked to activate the right mouse click is a very light tap of two fingers in the middle of the touchpad. Also, note that a two-handed gesture not listed on the Logitech site that I found useful to highlight is to apply pressure to the left-hand bottom corner of the touchpad with the other hand lightly touch the touchpad with a smooth move of the cursor to highlight, then release the pressure on the touchpad to end highlighting-- after you have finished with copy and paste or drag and drop, to release the highlighted text--place the cursor on the highlighted area then lightly tap anywhere on the touchpad with one finger. Make sure to download the latest version of software for this touchpad to avoid possible glitches. It took me less than a day to get used to using this touchpad, and I find this touchpad superior to a mouse. I highly recommend this rechargeable touchpad and hope this review is helpful to others.

Tips for this touchpad's gestures (includes some that I wrote above):

(1.) To activate the right mouse click is a very light tap of two fingers in the middle of the touchpad.

(2.) A two-handed gesture to highlight is to apply pressure to the left-hand bottom corner of the touchpad and with the other hand lightly touch the touchpad with a smooth move of the cursor to highlight, then release the pressure on the touchpad to end highlighting-- after you have finished with copy and paste or drag and drop, to release the highlighted text--place the cursor on the highlighted area then lightly tap anywhere on the touchpad with one finger.

review_title: Very good optical cable for audio connections
review_text:

I played a Scarlatti sonata with this cable and the other cable, and can detect no difference with my ears. (I don't claim this is a lab test, but with optical fiber at these short lengths and this limited frequency range, there really ought to be no measurable difference that would matter to human ears.)

So I'd say these cables are just fine, and they're sufficiently well made that I'd have no qualms about using them. And this heavy braided wrapping makes the cable heavier and less flexible (as well as uglier!), so I'm taking off a point for it, since I can find other such cables that are superior.

review_title: Very nice sound after proper settings, comfortable to wear, great for the price
review_text:
Overall rating 4.5, rounded up to 5. I don't think there's anything better for this price.

I wanted a "better" set of wireless earbuds for casual music listening: I wanted either AptX HD or LDAC, good battery life, and comfortable to wear for at least an hour or two. (I specifically ruled out over-the-ear headphones because I can't wear them very long, and ruled out wired earbuds for convenience. To me these are acceptable compromises.)

I was considering the Sony WF-1000XM4, but didn't want to pay that much for casual listening. I was also considering the new Soundcore Liberty 4, which on paper seems to be a great product. But I decided to try this "Liberty 2 Pro Upgraded" pair to see if was good enough for a lot less money.

So far I'm really very pleased: the sound is excellent for all my favorite music genres: classical, country, pop, rock, and latin pop, and after replacing the earpiece flaps and cushions I'm finding them very comfortable to wear as I work at my desk.

Important: to get the sound right, I had to do several things. First, I downloaded the Soundcore app, connected the earbuds, set the audio quality to LDAC (in settings). Then on my Android phone (Pixel), I went to the bluetooth advanced settings (usually hidden under developer options: do a web search for more details), and set the Audio Codec to LDAP, the LDAC quality to 900kbps, and made sure that the other BT settings (such as sample rate, bits per sample) were at the highest for good audio. Finally, I went back to the Soundcore app and played with the equalizer settings until I had what sounded best to my ears. The app has a neat little personal-hearing tester, which is worth a try, especially if your ears are getting older. After all this I had nice clean well-balanced sound. You might try different EQ settings for different music genres if you like, it does make a difference, but perhaps not huge enough to matter.

I've read many grumbles about LDAC, but I wonder if those are based on using the default settings: in my experience getting the settings right makes a very big difference.

PS It seems that the LDAC settings on Android go back to "best efforts" everytime the earbuds are disconnected. Quite annoying: I have to set them back to 900kbps every time. The other settings are stable.

review_title: Excellent hardware at a great price, but configuration is too complicated.
review_text:
This is a superb piece of hardware at a great price. In my initial testing I was really pleased and impressed with the performance. So if you're a professional with deep understanding of how to set this up, go for it. (But read the rest of my comments here first.)

But it was frankly just a giant pain. The website guide and the forum were barely helpful, especially when professionals argued with one another about how to best do something. At this point I decided to accept defeat, rather than spend another day trying to figure it all out. I sent it back, thank goodness for Amazon's excellent return policy.

I wish Mikrotik would invest in a really nice GUI, and a small set of config wizards: yes, that would add cost, because good software costs money. But I think it would greatly increase the appeal of their products. Even pros like "ease of use", because it saves time and hassle and reduces chances of error.

The sound from the multiple speakers is very good, probably as good as you can get from a modern tv. I'm considering getting a decent (but not overly expensive) soundbar to try, see if it makes the sound noticeably better.

review_title: Died after about two years, no battery backup now
review_text:

I used this with my desktop computer, to bridge the 2-3 minutes it takes between the main power going off and my generator kicking on automatically. It did that job perfectly for about two years, but recently just stopped providing backup power. The computer thinks the battery is fine, and is charging, but with any loss of supply power, this thing just fails to provide the backup power and the computer essentially crashes. I suspect that either the battery isn't good or (more likely) the cutover circuitry isn't functioning properly.

I decided to switch to a TrippLite UPS instead (the AVR series): it gives you a much better system for just a few extra bucks.

I was looking for a 1TB SSD to upgrade the storage in my computer. Background: I have a tower computer I built about 3 years ago, and at that time I used a 500GB SSD for the system drive, and two 1TB hard drives for pretty much everything that didn't have to be on the system drive. Note: If I were building a new computer today I'd use an M.2 SSD for the main drive. In fact that's what I did in the new computer I recently built for my son.

review_title: Pretty good miniature flash drive, with useful free encryption program
review_text:
It's pretty amazing to me that you can pack so much data now in such a tiny drive. It's about the same size as my Logitech mouse "nano" receiver.

The drive capacity is almost exactly 32 billion bytes (that's really 29.8GB, not 32GB, but the marketers have defeated the engineers on this). For some reason it was connecting at USB2 on my front port, where other USB3 drives connect just fine. Once I got it connected on another port at USB3, I did see better behavior. However, file transfer speeds are limited by Windows (and perhaps my computer hardware) more than anything else. Even transferring to/from an internal SSD drive I didn't get sustained speeds over about 38MB/s (that's megabytes, not megabits). I've read tech journals that say that the smaller USB3 drives can't transfer at the same speeds as the super-duper larger ones, but for real-world file transfer (as opposed to lab benchmarks) it doesn't seem to matter. Suffice it to say that I get about 10x speeds on USB3 drives vs. USB2 drives, and this one works as well as my other USB3 drives.

The drive came with a basic file encryption program (you can download it from the Lexar website as well). This easy-to-use program encrypts files using AES-256 (more detail wasn't given); you can buy an upgraded version which allows upto AES-1024, and has a few other features. Each file you encrypt is stored in a separate folder hierarchy (labeled the Vault), there isn't a separate encrypted file system. It's probably secure enough for general consumer use, and is certainly a convenience making it easy to protect your data. There was a Windows version and an Apple version of the program, so I think it means that encrypted files can be shared with either type of system. Not being a Mac user, I couldn't verify this.

Overall, this is a very nice product for an attractively low price. There are 64GB and 128GB versions as well for those who need more storage.

review_title: Useful backup power for phones/tablets and such
review_text:
This is a handy little item if you need power backup for a phone or tablet, when you expect to have an extended period away from a power source. I'm planning to carry it with me when travelling, for example, and it might be handy on a hike as well.

I plugged in my regular micro-usb phone charger (the specs call for 2.1A at 5V) to fully charge it. Then I tested it on a phone (Samsung S4) and a tablet (Tab S), and found the results quite satisfactory. The specs say that the two USB ports will provide 2.4A at 5V simultaneously, and I was certainly able to charge my two devices at the same time without problems.

There's some discussion in the instructions about "smart charging", but I can't verify if that makes any real difference. (The idea seems to be that you can tell the charger to dialog with your device to select an optimal charge profile. Nice idea, but I didn't see a difference after I did what they asked. Maybe it was optimal already ...)

The flashlight is a nice touch, but I don't know that I'd ever use it. I'd carry a flashlight if I think I might one, rather than depending on one charger to provide backup power as well as a light source.

Finally, the charger is well-made, and compact in design. Easy to slip into a backpack for instance. One important limitation to keep in mind: you will probably need to carry a separate USB-microUSB cord (I have a 1 foot cord I use), because the cord that comes with it has a fat rubberized head, making it impossible to fit into some recessed charging slots (such as my tablet when it's inside a case).

Given that I paid about $30 extra just for the HDMI input, which apparently hasn't been well tested, I'm not delighted. I'll still consider other VS monitors, since they often represent good value for money, but perhaps avoiding the newest products is wise.

I myself wouldn't use this mouse for travelling; for that I prefer a smaller Logitech mouse which allows the usb key to be inserted into the mouse. (See the V450 for example.)

Check the Logitech website for driver support for other operating systems.

review_text:
This drive meets most of my requirements for a flash drive. There are so few well made flash drives that I gotta rate it as 5 stars simply for filling this niche fairly well.

First and foremost, I need a flash drive with a real SSD controller, not the cheapo craptastic "flash controllers" used by almost every other flash drive. Real SSD controllers offer things like better reliability (e.g. error detection and correction, wear leveling), higher performance (especially for random reads and writes), and secure erase. A real SSD controller should also mean that you can treat the flash drive just like an internal SSD. For example, it should support partitioning, and have software that lets you specify the amount of over provisioning. Maybe it also ought to support the TRIM command and S.M.A.R.T. drive performance and health monitoring?

Second, I need a drive that is physically robust. I want a strong case, with zero moving parts, and ideally it meets some good dust and water resistance standard (e.g. IP68; see trustedreviews's article on "IP67 vs IP68: Waterproof IP ratings explained"). Since the drive must have no moving parts, its connector must be protected by a cap, and to help avoid losing the cap, the drive must let you put the cap on the non-connector end when it is in use.

I am not sure where I stand about encryption. In principle, I support it. In practice, manufacturers always seem to use proprietary solutions, which makes them intrinsically bad; when closely examined by real security professionals, they usually turn out to be rubbish (e.g. Western Digital's line of "My Passport" hard drives ~2015). Furthermore, depending on how it is implemented, you may have issues with the host operating system (e.g. if some custom driver is needed).

So, how does the VisionTek 900903 measure up?

First, it claims to use "a high-performance Silicon Motion controller". Off to a good start. Benchmarks below go into further details, but the conclusion is that it offers decent performance.

Second, this drive is an all metal rectangular case ("tough aircraft-grade aluminum housing" according to the manufacturer). Its case is solid: there are no moving parts except for the cap, and the cap can be put on the rear of the drive when you have it inserted. Good, tho the cap could fit a tad more snugly. There are ridges on the drive that allow an excellent grip, which is a nice touch. Sole defects are the 4 corners of the case which are slightly sharper than they ought to be, and the drive seems to meet no official dust and water resistance spec.

Contrast VisionTek's case with that of a Sandisk Extreme Pro USB 3.0 128 GB (model #: SDCZ88) that I also own. The Sandisk case is only partly metal. The metal came from a sheet that was stamped and then folded. Part of the metal near the connector end, where the slider is, is dangerously sharp--an idiotic design... The metal is way too smooth (is hard to pull the drive out in some situations). The slider mechanism is made of plastic and is weak (I have had 2 drives fail on me).

Concerning performance, attached are 5 CrystalDiskMark screenshots. The first 3 benchmark this VisionTek 900903 under 3 different disk formats (FAT32, exFAT, and NTFS); default format parameters (e.g. Allocation unit size) were consistently used (tweaking might improve performance). For reference, in the other 2 screenshots, I also benchmarked my Sandisk Extreme Pro (SDCZ88) as well as my internal SSD (a Samsung 840 EVO).

The disk format does not make too much of a difference; to my surprise, NTFS came out slightly ahead in most categories (I would have guessed exFAT would be). To be sure, the differences are small enough that maybe this was just measurement noise (did not have time to try multiple runs).

Comparing the VisionTek 900903 to the Samsung 840 EVO, the Samsung is clearly faster in every test, altho the VisionTek's Sequential Read and 4K random Write are respectable for a drive so small. (You should probably ignore the Q32 = queue depth 32 results, as they are not relevant for most desktop users, only servers.)

Comparing the VisionTek 900903 to the Sandisk Extreme Pro, the VisionTek is faster in 3 out of the 4 tests. The Visiontek is much better in Sequential Reads, and blows away the Sandisk in random 4k Writes. (Is that due to it having a real SSD controller?) It only loses moderately in Sequential Writes.

The sole performance disappointment with this drive is its 4k random Reads. That's a sore spot for the Samsung 840 EVO too, indeed, even Samsung's latest and greatest PCIe NVMe 960 Pro has awful 4K random read performance. It must be hard to achieve with current flash technology. The Sequential Write performance of the VisionTek 900903 could also be a bit higher.

All in all, I am pleased with this drive.

Altho I hate its past case designs, SanDisk has just announced at CES its new Extreme Pro USB 3.1 flash drive, which claims to offer "read speeds up to 420MB/s and write speeds up to 380MB/s" (when attached to a USB 3.1 port). Those are surely its Sequential specs; the fact that they do not mention its random specs makes me suspect that they are still bad.

Another case design I dislike is Corsair's way too fat Flash Voyager GTX, as it causes port crowding. A tragedy, since it otherwise is one of the few flash drives that claims to use a real SSD controller.

Speaking of CES, some other announcements for the small storage enthusiast to check out are Longsyss SATA Disk in Package (SDP) and Toshiba's BG Ultra Mobile SSD.

review_title: pretty good but expensive wireless headset
review_text:
The Klipsch KG-300 Pro Audio Wireless Gaming Headset is a very nice headset and easy to install - right out of the box you can plug in the base via USB (batteries included in the headset) and start using them. The audio is pretty good for a gaming headset, with the sounds of the game coming through clear, and people on the other end can easily hear what is being said. The headset is mostly comfortable - they're not the lightest and a bit bulky/padded, but they fit well.
Now, for the price of this headset, one thing that did surprise me is how much background noise DID come through. While it is true that they don't claim to be noise cancelling, considering the price and the padding, I didn't expect to be picking up so much background noise while wearing them. Definitely won't have to worry about anyone sneaking up on you while wearing these.

review_text:
I didn't have that much of a problem applying the screen protector to my kindle HDX, but I'll admit that I've had previous (and recent) experience applying screens to my smart phones (and watching the videos that were suggested for one of those brands). That probably helps, having previous experience. If you're a newbie at the application process, you may be a bit frustrated at the 'IKEA' type of instructions included with these screens.

First, you want to be in as clean of an environment as possible to apply it. I've been told in the past it helps to be in the bathroom, but really, just wipe the area down around you, don't kick up any dust and hope for the best. Once you peel off the first protective layer of the screen, if dust is floating around, it'll stick to it. So be in a clean, dust-free environment, clean your hands, clean your screen (you may want to wipe it down and dry it), and have everything ready BEFORE you peel off the protective layer.

If you have any type of wrap or decal on your HDX, you're gonna have to remove it before putting on the screen. :-(

There will be bubbles when you put on the screen. I didn't have too much trouble repositioning the screen or smoothing them out after removing the second protective layer. So far, so good with the screen, but it doesn't seem the stickiest, so not sure that I'll be able to put a decal wrap back on the HDX w/out peeling the screen back off by any attempt to reposition it.

The nice thing is, there are two screens included in the kit - I know in the past it's taken me two tries to learn how to apply a screen. This kit wasn't too difficult to use and so far, don't impact the use of the kindle or muck up too quickly with fingerprints.

review_text:
Okay, I have officially bought into Amazon's kindle crack. This is not my first kindle (or second, or...). This tablet is definitely an improvement over the previous versions, it's more responsive, it handles video and web browsing so much better than the previous Fire generation, and I love the slimmed down version.

The overall design is an improvement. The video quality is great, and music does play with a decent quality. Love the feature where it can display lyrics while playing song (if the mp3 has the information), thanks to the whole X-Ray/Lyrics feature. There's a lot of new touches here that are fun. I really appreciate the volume and the power buttons being on the opposite sides of the kindle now (don't know how many times I've hit the wrong one on my Fire >.<).

Also, being able to have more than two browsers open on Silk now w/out it crashing all of the time is a great improvement.

Some minor quirks - not sure if it's me or the tablet, but still trying to figure out how to get pictures already taken from my phone onto the tablet and directly into the photo folder.

Have installed several apps without a problem, downloaded files and opened them, so far so good. The kindle goes everywhere with me (literally, it's the perfect size to fit in my purse). I wish there were more cover options for the 7", but it seems to be increasing the longer the kindle is out, and I think a cover/case is a must for one of these. This is the kindle that I do take everywhere, and on a recent trip, I used this more than my Surface as it has my most frequently used personal emails installed on it (easy to set up), I can access my social accounts, my music, and of course my books.

The battery is... eh, decent. I can keep it on and play music for a few hours, video less, and use it to read books for most of a day. It could use some improvement.

All in all, it's a great tablet that you can take with you.

review_text:
This is one of the smaller external HD's that I've received lately, and while the size and weight is nice for a portable HD, it does feel a little on the flimsy side (not as thick plastic) which would make me more concerned while carrying it around than with other HD's. That said, it looks nice, and more importantly, it works well. I'd just tuck it inside of something better than the little cloth bag they so kindly included with the drive. There's a small bluish/white light on the side that lets you know when it's linked, transferring and safe to disconnect.

It supports USB 3.0 connectivity, and is very fast in transferring files on my pc. There's very nice, detailed information on setting up the back-up functionality on the drive as well as any files you need (maybe too much - if you're just going to use the drive as a regular portable HD, then I'd delete the folders/programs to clear up space - or clean up after you get what you need off of it after setting up as a backup). I was a bit surprised to see that they send you to Dropbox for the cloud backup, considering that there's an associated cost for large file size storage (kickback much?).

So basically it's a small, lightweight drive that is very fast (if you've the right connection) and a decent price if you want to use it as a backup drive. It helps you back up to the cloud, but you'll be paying for your own storage.

review_text:
I must say, I love this keyboard. I am a medical student and I type a lot of my notes into my macbook from online lectures, text-books, review books, ect. Doing so on my lap is fine, but, for practical reasons I need to type on a table to keep all my books, ect in front of me. The macbook keyboard is not meant to be used on an elevated surface like a table for extended periods to time. After a while I noticed that my wrists were getting some carpal-tunnel like symptoms as well as tendonitis. I promptly bought this keyboard from Microsoft and have been very happy with the purchase and my wrists and hands have also thanked me.

Pros: The keyboard is beautiful. It is black, with some reflective black trim on the top. The keys are angled, to put less stress on the wrists and it is a full keyboard. It has the number pad, the directional buttons, function keys, page navigating buttons and some short-cut buttons. Not all the buttons work natively when I connect it to the macbook (for example the home and end keys don't always work in web browsers), the calculator short-cut key doesn't work. However, the most important keys for my purposes work. The function keys enable a mac user to use expose and panels, and the volume short-cut keys work as well. The keys have a good response, and I can definitely type much faster (and with less fatigue and typos) with the microsoft keyboard than my built-in macbook keyboard. Considering it is a full keyboard, it does feel pleasantly light and portable. I can't fit it in my satchel bag, but I do carry it around to the library / conference room to work, without any hassel. Another pro, the price is right.

Cons: It doesn't bother me, but the keys do make more noise than my laptop when typing. I feel badly sometimes when I start vigorously making notes and I know other people in the library hear the clackity-clackity of my key strokes. I don't think its worse than your typical desktop keyboard, but if there were one thing I could change about it, I would make it quieter. I've only been using the keyboard for a month or two, so I can't vouch for its durability, but at the price, I could easily buy another when it breaks.

review_text:
Ordered one from Amazon, $35. Like that camera can sit inside on window sill, flush to the glass of the window, and perfect video picture, night vision is spectacular (have read some ambient light outside is required). No need to worry about batteries or wiring, it plugs into the wall. You also do not need a subscription for just basic usage, but it will only film an event and notify you once every 5 minutes if you opt for no subscription. For $15/year, it is unlimited with no 5 minute pause between even detections. Has a micro SD slot (micro SD card not included), we just used one we had, but not necessary for camera operation. It can also be paired with other appliances through an IFTT app like a garage door.
The MAJOR ISSUE is that even though you may set your detection area, the detection is via a change in pixels (where Ring, Blink, etc. are infrared and detect a heat source) and we receive an EXCESSIVE DETECTION NOTIFICATIONS when the sun sets and shines through the leaves or at night when car headlights flash across the detection area. We have also read where people receive excessive detection notifications when it rains or bugs attracted to light, but we have not had an opportunity to put it to the test with these. The only solution to minimize these notifications for these non-events is to move the camera or to set up rules to silence events during certain times of the day. For the cost, we decided we can live with this. Our walk around for now, is to just have one family member's phone receive alerts. And the other family members must block the alerts for this specific app in the settings of their phone (not within the app, or it blocks everyone's notifications).
Only the initial person who sets up the camera on the app, can make a lot of the changes to the camera within the app. And other family members are just shared access to the camera and can set up their own rules. The initial person who did the set up will receive notifications a split second before the people it is shared with.
Ordered a 2nd one that was supposed to be new, but WAS OPENED and still had the UPS stickers on it with the customer's name and address who had returned it. So returning the 2nd camera and ordering a replacement, hopefully this one will be new.
Realize with any electronics that receive updates (like with cell phones, fitness trackers, etc), they do not have an infinite life due to technology restrictions so another reason to go for this budget friendly option. I believe Wyze retired support for their 1st model after 5 years.
Price on Wyze website was $29.99 ($57.98 for 2) plus $5.99 shipping, but decided buying it from amazon would make sure we had free returns with Prime. Wyze is a company started by former Amazon employees and it is based in Seattle.
Update: very sensitive to raindrops on the window, birds, neighbors' lights turning on and creates an event and notification.

review_title: Great right-angle adapter for phones and MP3 players
review_text:
I purchased this for my Sansa Clip+, which I keep in my pocket when running and hiking. I specifically needed the relatively low-profile right-angle plug, since this greatly reduces the strain put on both the MP3 player's jack and the headphone's plug, the latter of which would otherwise function as a lever and apply constant torque to the connection.

I previously had the Seadream right-angle adapters (ASIN: B01DCBJ51I) which is about the lowest profile I've seen, but that one cable became stiff over the next two/three years, which eventually torqued it's own internal wires so much that it stopped working. If you really need as low-profile as possible, that's the better choice, just keep that in mind. It's also a bit shorter, so you don't end up with extra cable on your headphones, but the difference is only 3", so not a big deal.

This adapter is far more flexible, seems better built in general, and has a standoff only 50%-ish greater than the Seadream, minimizing additional torque. I was leery of this at first, but having used it a few times now I'm happy with the outcome. I intend to continue using this one indefinitely into the future, and would recommend to others.

review_title: Flexible, low-profile, great for MP3 players
review_text:
I use this to connect my MP3 player to a 3.5mm jack I installed in my car's center console. The low-profile 3.5mm connector was very important to me because I wanted to make the connection as slim as possible to avoid accidentally torquing it, catching things on it, or applying pressure to the jack when moving things in and out of the console.

It works quite well for this purpose. the connector is slim - about as slim as they come, such that it basically clamps right up against the side of the player and the wall of the console. The plug itself feels solid and has a small snap when connecting to things. The cable is soft and almost as flexible as a woven cord, even if it does prefer some orientations to others. Sound quality is typical - which is to say, as good as every other cable I've owned.

The only thing I didn't like about the cable was the colors - it really doesn't go with the car interior and stuck out as a result, a bit distracting. So I used a Sharpie Pro - the big chisel-tip type - to turn it black. It is cotton sheathing, so this is quite viable. I was careful - after inking the entire cable and letting it dry, I washed it in warm water, then dried it and ran a soft, clean rag over it about a hundred times, until it came away basically clean. After the fact, while you could tell the original black bits from the inked threads, it's just different shades of black, rather than looking blotchy. I imagine using something like RIT black dye would be about equally effective, if you heated it and let it soak for a good long while.

So I would recommend it. The braided cable looks premium and is much easier to work with than its equally-thick rubber counterparts. This makes it easy to handle the MP3 player while it is still plugged in.

Aside from those two things, I would easily recommend this to hobbyists, tinkerers, and designers as a far preferable way to step up/down voltage without needing to use those tiny boards which require a meter to configure.

If they have a model that can handle greater amperage, I will be interested in procuring it.

Would recommend.

review_title: Great for a small apartment or upstairs WiFi router
review_text:
I purchased this specifically for my system in the upper-corner of the house, to compliment the main router in the basement and the first-floor router in the family room. The main draws of it were its reasonable range, decent price, and gigabit Ethernet jacks in the back, which allows me high-speed access to the NAS. I have been using it for almost two months now and am quite satisfied with its performance. I run mostly Ethernet up there; the WiFi is only for the smartphone and the tablets, which I rarely use while at home. So I can speak to the performance of the router's hardline connections more than its wireless ones.

I am an IT professional and work in system administration, among other domains, so setup for me was easy. The Archer offers more than sufficient customization options for a standard household, I found, but the basic guided setup option also seemed to me to be easy enough to follow. I don't think I'd recommend it as the primary router of a household of more than, say, three people or more than two floors, especially if data use is high, but it works as a secondary unit. I ended up setting it up with its own subnet, rather than making it a mere extender of the primary. I can send documents to the downstairs printer (all printers run via Ethernet to the primary router), but all traffic in that part of the house is kept local, which is fine for my purposes.

Would recommend.

review_title: Remarkably effective at what it does
review_text:
I only purchased a smartphone about a year ago, previously being in the flip-phone-for-life crowd, due to the requirements of a job I was on. Since then I have slowly been picking up the various accouterments of such devices, the latest being this magnetic mount. I bought it mostly so I can use Google Maps for navigation.

It is remarkably effective. I have a Motorola Moto X4, in a slim silicon case, and an 05 Subaru Outback. The kit comes with the magnetic mount, two metal plates with adhesive (a rectangular one and a little circular one), a clear adhesive interposer, and, as a nice surprise, an alternate, black bezel.

What you do is attach the metal plate to the outside of your case, the inside of your case, or your phone. If you choose the lattermost option, then you don't attach it directly to the phone, but to the clear adhesive interposer (just a clear plastic sheet with adhesive on both sides), likely to prevent surface damage and dampen shock/reduce possible strain. If you have one of those pop-socket devices, you attach the little metal circle to the center of that instead. Then, you fit the magnetic mount to one of the grilles of your car's vent system, wherever it is most convenient. Now you can mount your phone to it, the magnet clinging to the metal plate.

I attached the metal plate to the inside of my case. It is very thin - I would say 1mm or less - and even on my slim silicon case it leaves only a very slight rise, hardly visible from the outside. I also attached it about 2/5ths of the way up from the bottom of the phone, as recommended (the Moto X4 does not have wireless charging). The magnet adheres quite well to the phone - the silicon case actually slightly pulls away when detaching the phone from the mount - not nearly enough to dislodge the case, but enough to let you know that the magnet is really sticking. As the mount has a rubber pad, and my case has a rubber texture, the phone does not slide at all in any lateral direction, the shear resistance is quite high. I am not concerned about the phone just falling off during normal operation of the car.

The tines of the mount grip the vents quite well - I have only had the mount pull off the vents once when detaching the phone after parking. There are two sizes of gaps - narrow and wide - and the narrow gap seems to fit pretty well on the Subaru. I like how you can pivot the mount a little to the left or right, and use the vent's own hinge to pivot it up and down.

There are some basic shortcomings of design. Obviously you can only attach this to the vents of the car, which limits your choice of positioning. I tried putting it on the left vent, but that caught too many outside reflections. I tried the right vent, but my hand was mostly blocking the screen. I tried the left passenger-side vent, but found that this took my eyes too far off the road while checking the navigation. In the end, I went with the driver's side right vent, since it required the lease eye-movement to check navigation and it was actually helpful to have my had block the screen, so as to avoid distraction. The tines hold, but they are not as secure as a hard mount would be. Likewise, the magnet could, in theory, be bumped out of position by kids/pets/carelessness and fall down into the foot well.

However, I would generally recommend this, at least as someone's first mount, to get a feel for what they are looking for if nothing else.

review_text:
I bought a pair of these to use with my dashcam (a Viofo A119v3), and so far have not had any problems. No problem recording 2560x1600 video, and can store about a week of my commute before it needs to start overwriting it, good stuff. Obviously the endurance component will need to be tested over time, but even regular SD cards have lasted years for me, I don't imagine these will be failing any time soon.

Value is decent - the PRO Endurance versions are about 2x as expensive as the regular cards. For most uses I wouldn't care, but for dashcam use, I am more than willing to spend the extra money up front, especially since you can get so much space for so little these days. If it comes down to it, I would purchase a smaller-capacity PRO Endurance card than a larger-capacity standard micro-SD, at least for this use case.

I typically install one in the camera and keep a second with a USB-C SD card reader ( an uni Sturdy USB C to Micro SD adapter) in my car. This way, if I do witness an accident I can backup the video onto my phone, surrender the one SD-Card to the officer on duty, and install the backup one for my trip home. It also is useful as a fallback in case the one MicroSD fails, is lost (dropped in some inaccessible place in the car) or damaged in some way.

Anyway, would recommend thus far. Will leave an update if anything comes up.

review_text:
I purchased this as a "desk unit", by which I mean I want it to be visible with the rest of my workstation. As such, it was important to me that it look good. And it does! It looks quite nice with its aluminium body, much better than the plastic bodies typical of seven-port hubs. Works well too, high transfer speeds and everything. No general complaints about the product itself.

It is a little expensive for what you get. I would like more power delivery across all ports, or at least one that supports Fast Charge. I would appreciate it if the unit was a bit heavier, it sort of skids around a bit in its current state - I may add some weight to it myself for stabilization purposes.

I think it's worth about $30, rather than $50, so if you can get it for that price, I recommend you do so.

EDIT: Just like other users, I have started to experience the "frequent dropout" problem, where some or all devices connected to the USB hub occasionally just disconnect, almost constantly, regardless of the port I have it connected to. As I purchased this 11 months ago, I will contact the MFTR for warranty service.

EDIT2: I have purchased three of these, and all three have the issue. After checking my system logs, I can see the hub dropping connection every three or four minutes or so, constantly. I have also seen the same thing with units we purchased for my work, so it isn't just my system or me. Started at four stars, dropped to three with the initial issue, but seeing that this is a widespread problem, one star.
