review_title: A vast improvement over standard Corsair PSU cables
review_text:
I purchased these for the RM650x in my new build. to clean up the appearance of my case, as the default Corsair cables are serviceable but neither flexible nor visually appealing. Do I have a fancy case? It's a Fractal Define Mini C, so, sorta. Do I have a side window? No. Will anyone ever see the interior of this case aside from me and randos and I'm flexing on? Certainly not.

Why get cables like these? Call it an eccentricity. I don't like chaos hiding right out of sight. Sure, the Mini C would have the outward appearance of a stocky monolith of unalloyed order, but inside there would be a twisting madness of PVC and copper, heaving silently against the surface. There would be no evidence of it, sure, but I would know.

I would know.

So anyway, I purchased these to extend the relentless teleology of the IC into the broader world, and to this end I was successful. The cables are much more flexible than the default ones and the paracord is an interesting contrast against the typical circuit boards and enameled aluminum panels. They are a bit pricey for what you get, that's definitely the case - you might be better served by getting a different brand or shorter extensions rather than the full PSU set. I just happened to have the money for the CableMods.

Caveats: if you are using velcro ties inside the case, then you have to be careful with the ModFlex, as the hook-side can pull threads from it. I presume ModMesh, being nylon, would not have that issue. to get around it, I used rubber/silicon bands, since unlike zipties they can be removed and adjusted relatively easily.

Would I recommend them? If you have a side-window or transparent case, they are a definitely aesthetically on point. ModFlex or ModMesh, either should be suitable. If not, unless you too are eccentric, it probably isn't worth it. The improvement in airflow and the reduction in strain on the components are minimal so long as you are implementing reasonable cable management techniques. I'm still happy I purchased them though, since I'm pretty sure I'll be able to use them in the next two-three builds and they did make it a bit easier to get everything where I wanted it.

Definitely would recommend as replacement fan cables.

review_title: About what you'd expect for the price
review_text:
When my much more expensive Bluetooth on-ear headphones broke I was a bit frustrated and decided to go back to something cheaper. As expected, this product is less comfortable and clearly uses cheaper materials and construction, but I can't really complain given the price. The sound quality is fine as far as I can tell. The battery life is decent but noticeably shorter than my previous headphones. Also, the low battery warning is a very annoying loud series of beeps that repeats periodically until you charge it. So if you just want to listen for 5 more minutes or get through the last couple of minutes of that video and then charge it, well too bad, because the beeps are going to annoy the **** out of you until you charge it. Also, the pictures in the instructions were not clear to me at all, and it took me a while to find the charging port (you have to tilt one of the earphones to reveal the port which is otherwise hidden behind the headband).

Also, unlike my previous headphones, this one does not work well with my tablet's media volume sync (when the headphones are turned on they always revert to a default volume, they don't remember the last volume used), so I had to turn sync off to avoid constantly having to recalibrate the volume of the headset relative to the tablet.

review_title: In terms of audio performance these seem good. They are a bit uncomfortable to wear for ...
review_text:
In terms of audio performance these seem good. They are a bit uncomfortable to wear for longer periods of time, e.g. more than say 45 minutes (rough approximation) and they start to hurt my ears a bit. I do have asymmetrical ears, one has a larger fold on the top than the other, this could be a factor in the comfort (along with possibly other head/ear size/shape differences among people). As a result of this discomfort alone it is hard for me to give them more than 3 stars. I found the best way for me to wear them when I am not on the move is in reverse, with the neck bar over my chin. There is enough tension to keep them on as long as I am basically just lying back or reclining, and in that configuration they don't hurt my ears.

Another con is the type-C USB connector. Yes it is mentioned down in the wall of text of the product page so perhaps it is my fault for not noticing. But to me there is no excuse for any product of this nature not to use a standard micro-USB connector. Now I have to make sure I keep track of this cable for this device which is the only one of this type that I have, since all the other use micro-USB. I can't just plug it in to all the other micro-USB cables I have lying around my apartment.

I'm also not getting any kind of audible low battery warning, which other similar headsets always had.

The other functions such as the equalizer and locator app are fine/nice, though honestly I don't really use them.

review_text:
The MHBT0545W is a simple blah, as much as you might expect, given the kind of reviews, number consumer responses, manufacture details-specs, and the retailers you would generally find these at. While trying to understand what market these are aimed towards, given the MSRP, you would think Memorex or the OEM would have given these more respect.

Packaging aside, what you find them here on Amazon, price wise is really what they are worth, or a bit less. So with that I am not that impressed. The shrink wrap is not every sophisticated and they very well might have been rewrapped. The sleeve cover slides off and reveals front flap to the headphones which sit in a velvety plastic tray. Under neath is a gold tipped red flat wire aux cable, which reminds me of the cable on the Sony MDR-V55 head phones. Also included is a micro USB charging cable. Although I had expected it, there was no carrying pouch. While doing my research I was under the impression a pouch was included. There is a 90 day warranty card, and a fold out instruction sheet, in both English and Spanish. The headphones seem to have been fully charged, as they powered up out of the box, and when I charged them they stopped charging very quickly.

They sound okay. A bit too bass for me and not clear at that. However because they have an adjustable equalizer, I prefer the treble boost setting, the most. They are not "over the ear" but more or less on the ear for me. They do well at isolating sound, the cups are soft, but the headphones keep my ears and the surrounding area warm or hot. The band has a nice plushy cushion over the head, and the cups are quite tight on my ears. I will have to see what I can do about that. The buttons are labeled well, but until I get used to them I have to take the phones off and look. So with that in mind, they are not intuitive. The lower cost model of Memorex headphones have touch controls in obvious locations on the outside ear cup - for comparisons sake, I am wondering what is up with that? These are $70 ear phones and more difficult to use.

I was able to pair them with my laptop and phone, and while connected at the same time, will switch to the source of the audio, automatically. They will not auto connect to your second device, only to the first one - which is the last device you used or paired, then you have to go to the second one and manually select connect. There is a slight gap in audio, as it detects and plays the source of sound, or start your source.

There are no voice prompts that I have noticed. The headphones have basic alert tones which do not seem very loud. Some customers will understand and appreciate what I am writing here. I will have to come back to this part and update as I get more use out of them.

Double clicking the play/pause/power button activates SIRI. However SIRI does not understand anything I say and when she speaks it's the worst quality I have ever heard. This is not particularly important, as SIRI is not an advertised feature. I will get back to this in a moment.

Conclusion, these headphones are using circuitry and a chipset, meant for $80+ headphones. Although not mentioned, they are using a CSR 8645 chipset which by specification, can multi-point connect to two phones or other combination of bluetooth audio sources. They do not advertise what codecs are supported but again by definition the chipset is meant to support Apt-X, Low Latency, and ACC, please see [...] for reference. I am led to believe, they use the chip for it's most basic features, Bluetooth 4.1, half of the available slots meant for equalizer settings, and nothing else. SIRI sounding as bad as she does, is a victim of this basic configuration, and I am surprised she actually does anything at all.

The phones look good, sound okay and worth the amount of money I paid for them. However I will be buying something else at some future date, as the bluetooth headphone market matures.

(I will be editing for grammar other mistakes)

I recently purchased a monitor and keyboard to use at my desk. I have been using ThinkPad laptops exclusively for a few years.
I selected the Preferred Pro USB Keyboard. I almost went with one of the TrackPad keyboards ([[ASIN:B00C32FWJC ThinkPad Compact Bluetooth Keyboard with TrackPoint - US English]] or [[ASIN:B00F3U4TQS Lenovo ThinkPad Compact USB Keyboard with TrackPoint - US English]] ), because I love the TrackPoint. However, I needed a numeric keypad, and I didn't like the idea of having a separate one. I chose the Preferred Pro on the strength of reviews. I was not disappointed.

The keyboard is comfortable to type on. They tops of the keys are textured, and they feel nice under my fingers. The key travel feels wonderful, and I can type faster on this keyboard than on a laptop. The built-in wrist rest is also very comfortable to use. The only issue I've had with the keyboard is that I keep hitting the Windows key instead of control because I'm used to the layout being Fn-Ctrl-Win. I'm sure with time I'll stop making this minor mistake.

Pros: Traditional key layout and spacing. 3 simple lights for Caps Lock, Num Lock, and Scroll Lock. Keytops are slightly textured. Great Key travel. Built-in wrist rest. Professional black, dark gray, & blue color scheme.
Neutral: No keys for controlling volume, brightness, etc.
Cons: Takes time to get used to a full-sized keyboard.

review_title: Quite the bargain for a compact yet sturdy mini tripod
review_text:
I'm impressed. First of all, the [[ASIN:B00DRA4CW2 Mefoto A0320Q00B DayTrip Tripod Kit (Blue)]] lightweight aluminum mini tripod is lovely. It is housed in a nice black cardboard box that makes a good first impression. The tripod inside is protected by a black carrying case with orange piping trim. There's an attached lightweight adjustable carrying strap that functions without any padding. Inside of the case is a side zippered pocket that contains a hex tool and the owner's manual which is very well written in two languages. The English is easy to understand and without many grammatical or spelling errors. The two pages of diagrams are also well done and the publication is very basic. I'm happy that too much money didn't go into this part of the package and there weren't additional packing materials either!

The tripod I received is an appealing blue which reminds me of the Caribbean waters. It's definitely a color I would have selected in a B&M store. The entire tripod weighs less than 2 pounds and stands a maximum of about 24 inches tall. You can safely mount a camera of a maximum of 8.8 pounds. Each part of the tripod seems well constructed and very well designed. My favorite little treat is the bubble level which is recessed in the mounting platform, underneath the easily removable mounting plate. The ballhead allows for a relatively smooth head movement, better than I'd expected. I appreciate the retractable weight hook for situations where a bit of extra stability is required. Another feature is the reversible center column which I use quite often for shooting table top close ups. Having the tripod legs fold up greatly reduces the packing and carrying size of this tripod, and it can be folded and stored in the bag very quickly if necessary while on the go.

I must say that when I first read "Mefoto", I saw it as "Manfroto". They are not the same company or products, but for the cost of this great little tripod, I don't care what it's named. It's a bargain that securely allows you to better use a camera in situations where a full sized tripod is either inconvenient, overkill or simply too cumbersome. I'll likely purchase a couple as holiday gifts this year and will also check out their other products! This was a fine introduction for me.

review_title: So happy and feeling safer now
review_text: I'm one of the folks who had a hard drive crash without having backed up for several months.  That was all it took for me to realize the importance of backing up my hard drive regularly and not simply putting current files on a flash drive.  I'd been using a Western Digital drive for the past three or four years, then was told that hard drives have a limited life span.  That made sense, so I decided to replace the external drive which is used to backup my MacBook.  I almost purchased the Seagate FreeAgent GoFlex 500 GB USB 2.0 Ultra-Portable External Hard Drive STAA500100, then decided that I don't take the external drive with me and didn't need it to be portable.  Enter the Seagate FreeAgent GoFlex Desk 2 TB Desktop External Hard Drive STAC2000100, a shiny black drive that looks much sleeker and way more shiny than the dull Western Digital.  2 TB seemed like more than I need, but I went for it anyway.  Before the package arrived, I watched the videos available on the Seagate website, so I was prepared for this drive and felt comfortable using it as my new backup drive.  My only question was whether or not to format it for use with Mac and PC or just the Mac.  Decided on the Mac only and didn't install the other options onto my MacBook.  Since I use Time Machine, I immediately proceeded to backup the hard drive.  Not having purchased the optional Firewire, eSATA or USB 3.0, the transfer is not faster than on the other external drives I've used, but this one sure is quiet and it's much nicer to look at.  It also doesn't weigh as much as other desktop external drives.  Looks like the attractive Seagate sleek shape, just bigger.  There is no button to push, just plug in and connect, then go to Time Machine.  I cannot review the included Memeo backup because I've not installed it.  Can't imagine that it would be better than Time Machine.  This meets my needs and exceeds my expectations.  It also looks nicer when locked up in my fire retardant portable safe than any other drive.

When the huge box arrived, I thought I'd made a mistake by ordering the Altec Lansing VS4621 Octane 7, 2.1 Computer Speaker. Fortunately, the shipping box was much larger than the item, so my blood pressure was quickly reduced. The speakers do have a small footprint and the taller contemporary shape is quite attractive. The subwoofer size is compact enough and unobtrusive in it's solid black boxy shape. I now have it placed on the bare wood floor, so my downstairs neighbors are likely not too happy with me right now. I will be placing a small carpet beneath it this afternoon.

Installation was intuitive and quite simple -- the most time consuming aspect was removing all the plastic. I didn't even notice the visual directions for set up are imprinted on the inside top flaps of the box. Because there is no bottom covering on the speakers by design, I'm especially careful when moving the speakers from one position to another. You'll get a different sound depending upon what surface you place the speakers. In the past hour, I've listened to Bob Dylan, The Grateful Dead, Johnny Cash, Radiohead, Sigur Ros, M.I.A., my Dad's dictation of his life story, Charles Mingus Lama Karta, The Black Lips, David Sedaris and Luka Bloom. The least pleasing on these speakers was a classical piece by Schubert which demonstrated the "muddy" nature of this sort of speaker system. Now this is a wide variety of music and sounds and my impression is that this is a really nice system which for the most part I would recommend. There's also an AUX input on the front of the speaker with controls so it can be hooked up to another electronic device of choice. Being able to adjust the volume, treble and bass gives me simple control options but by using the iTunes Equalizer, I can adjust to my preference with each cut. Throughout the years, I've purchased and used various speakers for my stereo, iPod, computer and entertainment systems, and I'm very impressed with these! Can't now wait to watch a movie and hear how these speakers reproduce the sound!

review_title: Groovy GPS when used with Fresh Maps update
review_text:
I first bought this GPS several months ago when Costco had it on sale but ended up returning it because I was not pleased with the time it took to recognize my location. More specifically, I would be on the Capital Beltway surrounding DC and the stern female voice would repeatedly tell me to make a U-turn. Impossible. I then used a friend's hand-me-down Magellan which would not hold a charge, not recognize the location and simply needed to be retired. Enter Amazon and their great price for the Navigon 2100 max. Since I'd read that the device was improved with the Fresh Maps update, I purchased Fresh Maps and I highly recommend you do the same if you're contemplating this beautifully sleek GPS.

If you have a PC, you are able to upgrade by connecting the GPS directly to your computer. If you have a Mac, then it's a little more complicated but so worth the effort. You need to remove the SD card from the GPS and transfer the downloaded software to the SD card with a card reader/writer and then reinsert the card into the GPS. I kept a backup of the original software on my hard drive just in case, but have had no need since the upgrade immediately worked. Now on to what I really like about this system.

The 4.3 inch screen is easier to view than the 3.5, particularly if you have many of the POI's selected for display. I first chose them all, then realized they obstructed my map because I'm in the DC metro area. Mine connects with a satellite in only a few seconds each time and reroutes immediately if I change my route. Previously, it would announce that it was rerouting, but it no longer does that, just does the work. Three choices for trip planning are fine enough for me, I tend to choose the Optimal Route. I love being able to select different destinations, too, if I'm going to different places. The address book is easy to access and locations are easier to save. Traffic support is a great asset and now comes free with this device -- I've been saved from many a jam and not have to be tuned into the radio for traffic reports on the 8's. I have the screen set to automatically change from day to night and have had no problem viewing the screen at any time. With the new software, you are able to turn off the GPS from the touchscreen in addition to the usual power button at the upper right hand edge. I love the 2D/3D view, especially when I'm approaching a multi-lane area and I'm unsure as to which lane I need to take. Two voice selections are fine for my needs, Dagmar is more pleasant, but the higher pitched Sarah gives the text to speech option (TTS), so that's the one I've selected. She's not very pushy, either, as some voices I've heard on GPS systems. In the pre-update version, her voice sounded more Germanic, I assume from its origin of Germany, but it's not as odd now. For me, this GPS is intuitive to use and I can make any adjustments from the touchscreen very quickly. I've yet to have a freeze of the system and it has always known where I was with one exception when I was off road on a gravel trail.

My only real criticism of this unit is the rigid cord which extends straight out of the bottom of the device, being so inflexible that I sometimes dislodge it when attaching the mount to the windshield. I'm not crazy about the mount either, but am trying to decide how to approach a new mounting system. I do not want the display obstructing my field of vision but am not ready yet to get a sandbag type dashboard mount. I'm thinking of constructing something myself using the little plastic disc which was included with this GPS system. Also included is the USB cord, but no AC power supply.

review_title: Tomato Compatible and Cheaper Alternative to ASUS RT-AC66U
review_text:
I picked this router up at another online retailer for $50 on the right rebate day. I had my eye on the Tenda 1800/1801 routers for a while before that though, as these seem to be the only decent Gigabit / AC routers that are directly compatible with Tomato right out of the box, that don't break the bank!

My router is essentially the same thing as the much more expensive ASUS RT-AC66U, but with less memory. Having less memory on a router is not really the same thing as less memory on a computer. In other words, most people (including myself) will not notice the difference.

Hardware Look and Feel:
This Tenda sports the basic router design, and includes wall mounting screw holes that are 6” apart, and 3 movable antennas that are easy to install. There is lots of good ventilation on the sides and bottom, and a glossy white top. Altogether, the router seems will made, and doesn't feel cheap at all. Glad to say that it doesn't have a gimmicky cylindrical shape, or a stupid upright design, with an even more stupid non-adjustable plastic stand. I don’t mind at all that I can't take selfies next to my neat looking stylish black router to post on Facebook; Boring routers are just plain under-rated!

Stock Firmware:
I spent about 5-minutes poking around in the stock firmware before flashing to Tomato. To me the stock firmware seemed like an unpolished version of Asus firmware. This is not necessarily a bad thing, but why settle for stock when there is a specific version of the very stable, configurable, and admired Tomato USB written just for routers just like this! Enter Shibby K26RT-AC...

Tomato Flashing Process:
No feverish searching the internet for firmware “that will work” with your router, simply go to the Shibby download page, find the latest version for your router, download the compressed file, and unzip it.
Then unplug your WAN cable, open your routers firmware page, go to tools, upgrade, navigate to the folder your just unzipped, select the .TRX file, click upgrade, and wait about 10 minutes. Once it is done, you might want to do a factory reset in Tomato to clear the RAM.

That’s it people, no messing around with cumbersome flash utilities, no 30/30/30 resets in restore mode while holding your nose and saying the alphabet backwards in Pig Latin while crossing your fingers that you won’t brick your router. This one is as simple as it gets!

review_title: Get it! It is a very good radio.
review_text: Compared to a Kaito KA500, this is a fantastic radio. The battery holds power on WB Alert overnight; this is more than the Kaito can do on its limited battery. The Sidekick uses LESS than 1/4 of the battery doing this same task. While the buttons on top of the radio are tiny print, thankfully, I can still read them easily, though I haven’t tried reading them by candlelight. I am trying to use the radio every day so that using it becomes second nature and I don’t need to read the buttons. I may try labeling them different colors but I’m not there yet. The best thing about the radio is that it will charge while you are using it! I have listened to podcasts through the radio's Bluetooth while charging it. It charged fast. I love that the Sidekick is not too complicated even though it is digital. The 6.5-inch x 3.5-inch manual is a total of 14 pages, including the illustrations and warranty fine print.

review_text:
The internal battery wasn't holding overnight so I put in 3 AA alkaline batteries because the area was expecting a storm. I set the radio to WB Alert and overnight the batteries were dead or close enough so that the radio just gasps noise and will not work. Nowhere in the manual does it state what size the internal battery is. Other reviews state 600mah to 2000mah. I have a different brand weather radio as a backup with a 2000mah internal battery that lasts several days. So, either the rechargeable battery holds a tiny charge or it is defective. Not to mention that THREE AA batteries are not enough to sustain it on WB Alert OVERNIGHT. So does it have an electrical issue?! When I called their customer service a few days ago regarding the internal battery, I got a tech specialist who I had to prompt for a solution. I had to suggest a battery replacement which thinking back he probably didn't think would work which is why he didn't suggest it. I ended up paying for a $10 battery that is still in the mail when I should have just called it quits.

***Since it is easy to find a WATERPROOF radio with a *5000mah* internal battery for $20 LESS, you don't need this one. ***

---
I doubt I would purchase this version of Kaito's radio again. Choose a version other than KA500. I threw away the box so I'm stuck. I'm glad I bought two radios from two different brands as back ups for each other. The other radio cost twice as much but I like it better. These are this radio's faults: 1) The manual references an IN OUT switch (number 23 in the manual) on the Input and Output Functions Dock (number 18 in the manual) but there is no such thing. The switch is actually labeled OFF ON on the radio. I'm not planning on charging my phone or anything from this unit so I'm not going to worry about it. 2) I inevitably lose manuals but I cannot find a digital copy of the manual that came with my radio. I have found other versions that look nothing like my 5.5" by 8" version. I have looked everywhere, especially Kaito's website which does have other radio manuals. 3) I cannot take out the included green plastic-coated rechargeable battery. It seems to be glued in. I hope I can replace it when it becomes necessary. 4) The antenna does not swivel around. It only opens or closes (goes up or down).
